24. Consider iron studies, including ferritin and transferrin saturation, if anemia, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, or occult blood loss is suspected.  
25. Consider erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein if systemic inflammatory or malignant disease is clinically suspected.  
26. Ensure colorectal cancer screening is current; arrange colonoscopy if she is overdue, has alarm symptoms, iron-deficiency anemia, positive stool testing, or relevant family history.  
27. Consider fecal immunochemical testing only if average-risk colorectal screening is due and colonoscopy is not otherwise indicated.  
28. Ensure breast cancer screening is current with screening mammography; arrange diagnostic mammography and targeted ultrasound if breast symptoms or examination findings are present.  
29. Confirm whether cervical cancer screening is still indicated based on prior screening history, hysterectomy status, and age-based guidelines.  
30. Consider pelvic examination and transvaginal ultrasound only if pelvic symptoms, abnormal examination findings, or other concern for gynecologic malignancy is present.  
31. Consider referral to gastroenterology for colonoscopy and/or upper endoscopy if there are gastrointestinal alarm symptoms, anemia, unexplained weight loss, or high clinical concern for occult gastrointestinal malignancy.  
32. Consider upper endoscopy if dysphagia, early satiety, persistent vomiting, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, unexplained iron-deficiency anemia, or concern for gastric/esophageal malignancy is present.  
33. Consider chest imaging, beginning with chest radiography or diagnostic chest CT, if there are new pulmonary symptoms, abnormal examination findings, unexplained systemic symptoms, or concern for lung malignancy.  
34. Discuss whether low-dose CT lung cancer screening is indicated based on current age and pack-year/quit-date eligibility criteria; her reported 10-pack-year history may not meet standard screening thresholds.  
35. Consider CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast if there is a convincing abrupt Leser-Trélat-like eruption plus systemic symptoms, abnormal laboratory findings, abnormal examination, or a malignancy signal from initial testing.  
36. Avoid routine broad tumor-marker testing unless guided by symptoms, imaging, examination, or a specific suspected malignancy.  
37. Refer to dermatology routinely or urgently depending on lesion atypia, diagnostic uncertainty, rapid evolution, or concern for melanoma/nonmelanoma skin cancer.  
38. Refer to dermatology for biopsy confirmation if the primary clinician cannot confidently distinguish the lesions from malignant or premalignant mimics.  
39. Refer to primary care or an internal medicine clinician for coordination of age-appropriate cancer screening and systemic evaluation.  
40. Refer to oncology promptly if biopsy, imaging, laboratory results, or examination identifies a probable or confirmed malignancy.  
41. Reassure that seborrheic keratoses are common benign age-associated lesions, while explaining that a rapid eruptive increase can occasionally warrant evaluation for associated disease rather than being dismissed as routine.  
42. Counsel her to report new weight loss, persistent abdominal symptoms, blood in stool, black stool, dysphagia, hemoptysis, postmenopausal bleeding, new breast mass, or rapidly changing skin lesions.  
43. Counsel on smoking abstinence, COPD inhaler adherence if prescribed, vaccination, and prompt assessment of any new respiratory symptoms.  
44. Offer no lesion-directed medication if the seborrheic keratoses are asymptomatic and cosmetically acceptable.  
45. Offer cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen for selected symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome lesions, with counseling about blistering, dyspigmentation, scarring, and possible need for repeat treatment.  
46. Offer curettage with or without electrodessication for selected lesions after diagnostic confidence or biopsy confirmation.  
47. Offer shave removal for irritated, traumatized, or cosmetically bothersome lesions, with histopathologic examination when clinically indicated.  
48. Consider topical hydrogen peroxide 40% solution applied in-office for appropriate raised seborrheic keratoses, recognizing variable efficacy and risks of local irritation or pigment change.  
49. Treat pruritus, if present, with skin moisturization, avoidance of friction, and consideration of a short course of a topical corticosteroid for inflamed surrounding skin rather than attempting to eliminate every lesion.  
50. Arrange follow-up after the initial evaluation—such as within 2–6 weeks for biopsy/laboratory/imaging review, sooner for concerning findings—and escalate urgently if biopsy suggests melanoma or another malignancy, if systemic red-flag symptoms develop, or if lesions continue to erupt rapidly.

1. Obtain a focused history of the rate and extent of seborrheic keratosis (SK) eruption, including whether lesions appeared abruptly over weeks to months versus gradually.  
2. Document associated symptoms that may support an eruptive SK syndrome, including generalized pruritus, weight loss, anorexia, fatigue, fevers, or night sweats.  
3. Ask about gastrointestinal symptoms, including dysphagia, persistent reflux, early satiety, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, melena, hematochezia, and change in bowel habits.  
4. Ask about breast, gynecologic, respiratory, urinary, and constitutional cancer-related symptoms.  
5. Review prior skin lesion history, including previous SKs, atypical nevi, skin cancers, biopsies, and family history of melanoma or internal malignancy.  
6. Review all new medications, supplements, topical products, immunotherapies, chemotherapy agents, and systemic corticosteroid exposure that could be temporally associated with skin changes.  
7. Review smoking history in pack-years, current tobacco use, vaping, occupational exposures, and secondhand-smoke exposure.  
8. Perform a complete skin examination, not limited to the back, including scalp, face, trunk, extremities, palms, soles, nails, and mucosal surfaces when indicated.  
9. Photograph representative lesions and document lesion count, distribution, morphology, size, pigmentation, inflammation, and evidence of excoriation for comparison over time.  
10. Perform dermoscopy of representative lesions to confirm features consistent with seborrheic keratoses and identify lesions requiring biopsy.  
11. Examine for signs of the “sign of Leser-Trélat,” including numerous abruptly eruptive SK-like lesions, particularly with associated pruritus or acanthosis nigricans.  
12. Examine for acanthosis nigricans, tripe palms, dermatomyositis-like findings, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, breast masses, or other paraneoplastic clues.  
13. Palpate accessible lymph node regions, including cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal nodes.  
14. Perform a focused abdominal examination for masses, tenderness, ascites, hepatomegaly, or other concerning findings.  
15. Obtain a diagnostic shave biopsy of any lesion with atypical pigment pattern, irregular border, ulceration, bleeding, rapid enlargement, marked asymmetry, or uncertain diagnosis.  
16. Consider punch or excisional biopsy rather than shave biopsy for lesions where melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, or another invasive malignancy cannot be adequately excluded by shave sampling.  
17. Send biopsied tissue for dermatopathology review, with clinicopathologic correlation if pathology is discordant with the clinical appearance.  
18. Refer to dermatology on a routine-to-urgent basis depending on diagnostic uncertainty, lesion atypia, speed of eruption, and associated systemic symptoms.  
19. Consider expedited dermatology assessment if the eruption is truly abrupt, widespread, intensely pruritic, or accompanied by other paraneoplastic physical findings.  
20. Obtain a complete blood count with differential as a baseline evaluation for anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, or hematologic abnormalities when systemic disease is suspected.  
21. Obtain a comprehensive metabolic panel, including liver enzymes, bilirubin, creatinine, calcium, and albumin, if constitutional symptoms or malignancy concern is present.  
22. Consider thyroid-stimulating hormone testing if symptoms suggest thyroid disease or if diffuse pruritus lacks an obvious skin-based explanation.  
23. Consider fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, particularly if acanthosis nigricans or metabolic risk factors are present.  
24. Consider iron studies, hepatitis testing, renal evaluation, or other pruritus-directed laboratory testing if generalized itch is prominent and examination does not explain it.  
25. Review whether the patient is up to date with age-appropriate colorectal cancer screening; arrange colonoscopy or stool-based screening if overdue or if alarm gastrointestinal symptoms are present.  
26. Review breast cancer screening status and arrange screening mammography if overdue; arrange diagnostic breast imaging if a breast symptom or examination abnormality is present.  
27. Review cervical cancer screening status and arrange Pap/HPV testing according to age, prior results, and hysterectomy history.  
28. Review lung cancer screening eligibility using current criteria; consider annual low-dose chest CT only if she meets age and smoking-exposure eligibility criteria or has concerning pulmonary symptoms.  
29. Obtain diagnostic chest imaging, such as chest radiograph or CT, rather than screening CT if she has new hemoptysis, unexplained worsening cough, persistent chest pain, unexplained dyspnea, or weight loss.  
30. Consider CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast if there are concerning gastrointestinal, abdominal, pelvic, laboratory, or examination findings suggesting occult internal malignancy.  
31. Consider upper endoscopy if she has dysphagia, persistent upper-GI symptoms, iron-deficiency anemia, weight loss, early satiety, or other indications for evaluation of upper gastrointestinal malignancy.  
32. Refer to gastroenterology promptly if alarm GI symptoms, iron-deficiency anemia, positive colorectal screening, or imaging abnormalities are present.  
33. Refer to oncology or the relevant organ-specific specialty urgently if testing identifies suspected or confirmed malignancy.  
34. Avoid labeling the eruption as a definitive paraneoplastic syndrome solely on the basis of increased SK number, since SKs commonly increase with age and the Leser-Trélat association is debated.  
35. Provide reassurance that individual clinically typical SKs are benign and do not themselves transform into melanoma.  
36. Counsel the patient to report lesions that bleed, ulcerate, become painful, rapidly enlarge, change markedly in color or shape, or fail to resemble her other lesions.  
37. Counsel on sun protection, including broad-spectrum SPF 30 or greater sunscreen, protective clothing, and avoidance of tanning beds, while clarifying that sun protection will not remove existing SKs.  
38. If lesions are symptomatic, itchy, inflamed, or repeatedly traumatized by clothing, consider treatment with liquid-nitrogen cryotherapy.  
39. Consider curettage, electrodessication, shave removal, or laser therapy for selected symptomatic or cosmetically bothersome lesions after diagnostic confidence is established.  
40. Discuss that cosmetic removal may not be covered by insurance and that treatment can cause pain, blistering, pigment alteration, scarring, or recurrence/new lesions elsewhere.  
41. For pruritic lesions, consider a short course of a low- to medium-potency topical corticosteroid to inflamed surrounding skin, selected according to body site and skin thickness.  
42. For generalized itch interfering with sleep, consider an oral antihistamine such as cetirizine 10 mg orally daily or hydroxyzine 10–25 mg orally at bedtime as needed, accounting for sedation, anticholinergic effects, and comorbidities.  
43. Avoid empiric systemic corticosteroids or systemic anticancer therapy for eruptive SKs unless another specific diagnosis establishes an indication.  
44. Review COPD control, current inhalers, exacerbation frequency, oxygen needs, vaccination status, and whether respiratory symptoms could represent COPD progression versus another pulmonary condition.  
45. Offer smoking-cessation counseling and treatment options, including nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, or bupropion when appropriate, despite the relatively modest reported pack-year history.  
46. Arrange primary-care follow-up within approximately 2–6 weeks to review biopsy results, laboratory findings, screening status, and whether lesions continue to multiply.  
47. Arrange earlier follow-up, within days to 1–2 weeks, if any lesion is suspicious for melanoma or nonmelanoma skin cancer, if biopsy is pending for a concerning lesion, or if systemic symptoms are present.  
48. At follow-up, compare lesion photographs and counts; if the eruption continues rapidly over another several weeks or months despite benign initial assessment, reconsider dermatology reassessment and targeted internal-malignancy evaluation.  
49. If unexplained weight loss greater than 5% of body weight over 6–12 months, persistent fevers, drenching night sweats, iron-deficiency anemia, palpable lymphadenopathy, GI bleeding, hemoptysis, or abnormal examination findings develop, escalate to urgent diagnostic evaluation.  
50. If all lesions are clinically and/or histologically typical SKs, no systemic symptoms or concerning findings are present, and routine cancer screening is current, manage with observation and periodic skin examination rather than broad invasive malignancy testing.

1. Obtain urgent oncology assessment for suspected capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), given painful erythema, swelling, fissuring, and chemotherapy exposure.  

2. Perform a focused severity grading of hand-foot syndrome (pain, erythema, desquamation, fissures, functional limitation, ability to walk/use hands, ulceration, blistering).  

3. Document exact capecitabine regimen, dose in mg/m², schedule, start date, cumulative exposure, recent dose changes, renal-dose adjustments, and date of last oxaliplatin infusion.  

4. Review all medications for contributors to edema, rash, neuropathy, renal dysfunction, or drug interactions, including the recent pantoprazole exposure.  

5. Obtain vital signs, including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and weight, to assess for infection, systemic illness, and volume overload.  

6. Examine hands and feet for warmth, sharply demarcated erythema, fluctuance, purulence, bullae, ulceration, necrosis, lymphangitic streaking, asymmetric involvement, and neurovascular compromise.  

7. Assess for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy from oxaliplatin, including sensory loss, dysesthesia, allodynia, gait instability, and reduced protective sensation.  

8. Assess range of motion and tenderness of individual finger/toe joints, wrists, ankles, and other joints to evaluate inflammatory arthritis, crystal arthritis, or tenosynovitis.  

9. Obtain CBC with differential to assess neutropenia, leukocytosis, anemia, and thrombocytopenia before systemic corticosteroids or invasive procedures.  

10. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel including creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, AST/ALT, bilirubin, albumin, and glucose for chemotherapy safety and medication dosing.  

11. Obtain CRP and ESR as inflammatory baselines if inflammatory arthritis, infection, or vasculitis remains a consideration.  

12. Obtain serum uric acid, recognizing that a normal result does not exclude acute gout, if acute crystal arthritis is in the differential.  

13. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if fever, rigors, hypotension, neutropenia, or concern for bacteremia is present.  

14. Culture any drainage, erosion, ulcer, or fissure with suspected secondary infection.  

15. Consider hand/foot radiographs if focal bony tenderness, trauma, severe joint-localized pain, suspected fracture, erosive arthritis, osteomyelitis, or atypical presentation is present.  

16. Consider musculoskeletal ultrasound of symptomatic joints/tendon sheaths if synovitis, effusion, tenosynovitis, or crystal arthritis is suspected.  

17. Perform arthrocentesis of any accessible swollen joint with effusion if septic arthritis or crystal arthritis is plausible; send synovial fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystals.  

18. Consider dermatology consultation, urgently if there are bullae, erosions, ulceration, diagnostic uncertainty, suspected severe drug eruption, or failure to improve with supportive measures.  

19. Consider rheumatology consultation if there is objective polyarthritis, prolonged morning stiffness, tenosynovitis, elevated inflammatory markers, or uncertainty between chemotherapy toxicity and inflammatory rheumatic disease.  

20. Hold capecitabine temporarily pending oncology evaluation if symptoms are moderate-to-severe, painful, function-limiting, associated with fissuring/desquamation, or consistent with grade 2 or higher hand-foot syndrome.  

21. Resume capecitabine only after clinical improvement to mild symptoms or baseline, with oncology-directed dose reduction or schedule modification if toxicity recurs.  

22. Consider permanent discontinuation or alternative systemic cancer therapy if severe recurrent hand-foot syndrome persists despite dose interruption, dose reduction, and intensive supportive care.  

23. Review whether oxaliplatin should continue on schedule, be delayed, or be dose-adjusted based on concurrent neuropathy, functional impairment, cytopenias, renal function, and oncology treatment goals.  

24. Start intensive bland emollient therapy to palms, soles, toes, and fissured skin, such as petrolatum or thick fragrance-free cream, applied at least twice daily and after bathing.  

25. Use a keratolytic moisturizer such as urea 10–20% cream for hyperkeratosis/callus-prone areas if skin is intact and not severely inflamed or ulcerated.  

26. Apply petrolatum ointment and protective dressings to painful fissures; consider hydrocolloid or nonadherent dressings when there is cracking or superficial erosion.  

27. Avoid friction, pressure, repetitive gripping, prolonged walking, hot water exposure, tight shoes, ill-fitting socks, and vigorous exercise while symptoms are active.  

28. Use soft padded footwear, cushioned insoles, loose cotton socks, gloves for manual tasks, and off-loading of painful plantar areas.  

29. Consider podiatry referral for callus management, footwear modification, fissure care, nail care, and pressure off-loading, especially given age, CKD, impaired mobility, and painful plantar involvement.  

30. Use acetaminophen for pain, such as 325–650 mg orally every 4–6 hours as needed, with a conservative maximum daily dose individualized for liver function, frailty, alcohol use, and combination products.  

31. Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen because of CKD, CAD, hypertension, bleeding risk, and potential chemotherapy-related renal or platelet issues.  

32. Consider a short course of low-potency topical corticosteroid for inflammatory erythema/pruritus of intact skin, such as hydrocortisone 1–2.5% topical twice daily for up to 7–14 days.  

33. Consider a medium- to high-potency topical corticosteroid for more substantial inflammatory dermatitis on intact palms/soles, such as triamcinolone 0.1% or clobetasol 0.05% topical, with duration and potency individualized by dermatology/oncology.  

34. Avoid applying potent topical corticosteroids directly to infected, ulcerated, necrotic, or undiagnosed lesions without reassessment for infection.  

35. Consider topical anesthetic or local pain-relief strategies for severely painful intact areas, while avoiding use on extensive broken skin because of systemic absorption risk.  

36. Consider oral prednisone only after assessment for infection and discussion with oncology; potential regimens for a confirmed inflammatory process could include prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for a brief course with a defined taper plan if treatment extends beyond several days.  

37. Avoid initiating systemic prednisone as sole treatment for presumed chemotherapy-associated hand-foot syndrome when dose interruption, topical care, friction reduction, and oncology-directed chemotherapy modification are the primary management options.  

38. If systemic prednisone is used, monitor blood pressure, blood glucose, mental status, fluid retention, infection signs, insomnia, and interaction with the patient’s cancer-treatment plan.  

39. Consider proton-pump inhibitor continuation, discontinuation, or substitution only after reviewing whether there is a convincing temporal or morphologic concern for a drug eruption; symptoms predating pantoprazole makes causality less likely.  

40. Start empiric antibiotics if there is evidence of cellulitis or secondary skin infection, such as fever, progressive unilateral warmth, purulence, spreading erythema, lymphangitis, leukocytosis, or neutropenia-associated skin infection; select agent and renal dose based on severity and local guidance.  

41. Arrange emergency department evaluation and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics if fever of at least 38.0°C (100.4°F), ANC below 500/µL, hemodynamic instability, rapidly progressive erythema, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, necrosis, or inability to bear weight develops.  

42. Arrange urgent surgical/orthopedic/hand evaluation if concern arises for necrotizing soft-tissue infection, compartment syndrome, flexor tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, deep abscess, or threatened digit perfusion.  

43. Evaluate for venous thromboembolism with venous duplex ultrasound if swelling is markedly asymmetric, extends beyond the hands/feet, is associated with calf/arm pain, or occurs with dyspnea/chest pain.  

44. Consider cardiac/renal volume-status evaluation if edema is generalized or accompanied by weight gain, dyspnea, orthopnea, elevated jugular venous pressure, or worsening renal function.  

45. Check for hyperglycemia and consider hemoglobin A1c if corticosteroids are contemplated or if impaired wound healing/recurrent skin infection is present.  

46. Educate the patient and caregivers to inspect hands and feet daily for new blisters, open areas, drainage, color change, worsening cracks, or loss of sensation, particularly because neuropathy may blunt warning pain.  

47. Provide explicit return precautions for fever, rapidly worsening redness/swelling, drainage, new ulcers, black or blue discoloration, severe uncontrolled pain, inability to walk or use hands, confusion, reduced urine output, or shortness of breath.  

48. Reassess clinically within 24–72 hours if symptoms are significant, if prednisone or antibiotics are started, or if chemotherapy is held; otherwise reassess before the next chemotherapy cycle.  

49. At follow-up, document symptom grade, pain score, walking/hand-function status, skin integrity, infection signs, CBC/renal function, and whether toxicity has improved sufficiently for chemotherapy resumption.  

50. Coordinate a joint plan among oncology, primary care, dermatology/rheumatology as indicated, pharmacy, and wound/podiatry services to define chemotherapy modifications, skin-care regimen, analgesia, and escalation thresholds.

1. **Diagnostics:** Obtain a focused history of timing relative to each capecitabine cycle and oxaliplatin infusion, cumulative capecitabine dose, recent dose changes, and effect on walking, hand use, and activities of daily living.  

2. **Diagnostics:** Grade the skin toxicity using CTCAE hand-foot syndrome/palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia criteria, including pain severity, peeling, blistering, ulceration, and functional impairment.  

3. **Diagnostics:** Perform complete skin examination of palms, soles, digits, nail folds, interdigital spaces, dorsal hands/feet, oral mucosa, and other body surfaces for alternative drug eruptions or infection.  

4. **Diagnostics:** Document presence or absence of fever, chills, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, rapidly progressive erythema, purulence, lymphangitis, bullae, necrosis, or pain out of proportion.  

5. **Diagnostics:** Examine for symmetric versus asymmetric swelling, focal joint effusions, range-of-motion restriction, synovitis, dactylitis, and tenosynovitis.  

6. **Diagnostics:** Obtain CBC with differential, including absolute neutrophil count, to assess for chemotherapy-associated neutropenia and infection risk.  

7. **Diagnostics:** Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel with creatinine/eGFR, liver tests, electrolytes, albumin, and calcium before medication changes and to assess chemotherapy tolerance.  

8. **Diagnostics:** Obtain ESR and CRP if an inflammatory arthritis, cellulitis, vasculitis, or systemic inflammatory process remains under consideration.  

9. **Diagnostics:** Obtain serum uric acid as part of evaluation for gout, while recognizing that a normal uric acid does not exclude an acute flare.  

10. **Diagnostics:** Consider rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies if examination suggests persistent symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis rather than primarily cutaneous hand-foot syndrome.  

11. **Diagnostics:** Consider ANA, complement levels, ANCA, and urinalysis only if features suggest systemic autoimmune disease or vasculitis.  

12. **Diagnostics:** Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if febrile, systemically ill, neutropenic, or suspected to have bacteremia.  

13. **Diagnostics:** Culture drainage or obtain bacterial/fungal culture from fissures, ulcers, or purulent lesions if infection is suspected.  

14. **Diagnostics:** Consider KOH preparation and/or fungal culture of scaling plantar/interdigital lesions if tinea pedis is a plausible contributor to cracking and erythema.  

15. **Diagnostics:** Obtain bilateral hand/foot radiographs if focal bony tenderness, suspected fracture, erosive arthritis, osteomyelitis, or alternative structural pathology is present.  

16. **Diagnostics:** Obtain musculoskeletal ultrasound or MRI of an affected hand/foot if there is concern for occult synovitis, tenosynovitis, abscess, osteomyelitis, or deep soft-tissue infection.  

17. **Diagnostics:** Perform joint aspiration with synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain/culture, and crystal analysis if a discrete swollen joint or effusion raises concern for septic arthritis or crystal arthritis.  

18. **Diagnostics:** Review all medications, including recent antibiotics, diuretics, immunotherapies, over-the-counter drugs, and supplements, for alternative causes of rash, edema, arthritis, or drug interaction.  

19. **Diagnostics:** Verify capecitabine dosing against body-surface area and renal function, since reduced kidney function can increase capecitabine exposure and toxicity.  

20. **Diagnostics:** Review whether DPYD/DPD deficiency testing has been performed and consider testing or oncology/pharmacology review if toxicity is unusually early, severe, or disproportionate.  

21. **Medications:** Contact the treating oncology team urgently to discuss temporary interruption of capecitabine for suspected clinically significant hand-foot syndrome.  

22. **Medications:** Discuss capecitabine dose reduction upon symptom improvement and before rechallenge, guided by toxicity grade and the oncology protocol.  

23. **Medications:** Consider continuing capecitabine with intensified supportive skin care if symptoms are mild and do not impair function, with close reassessment.  

24. **Medications:** Consider delaying the next oxaliplatin infusion until the cause and severity of the extremity findings are clarified, particularly if there is substantial functional limitation or possible infection.  

25. **Medications:** Start intensive emollient therapy such as urea 10–20% cream, ammonium lactate-containing emollient if tolerated, or thick petrolatum-based moisturizer to hands and feet at least twice daily.  

26. **Medications:** Apply petrolatum ointment to painful fissures and cover with nonadherent dressings, cotton gloves, or cotton socks, changing daily or as needed.  

27. **Medications:** Consider topical high-potency corticosteroid treatment for inflammatory erythema, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment to intact inflamed palms/soles once or twice daily for up to 1–2 weeks, avoiding open wounds or suspected infection.  

28. **Medications:** Consider topical medium-potency corticosteroid therapy, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily, if a lower-potency option is preferred because of skin integrity concerns.  

29. **Medications:** Use acetaminophen for pain, for example 325–650 mg orally every 4–6 hours as needed, with a patient-specific daily maximum based on liver function, alcohol use, and oncology guidance.  

30. **Medications:** Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen because of CKD, CAD, hypertension, bleeding risk, and potential chemotherapy-related renal toxicity.  

31. **Medications:** Consider topical diclofenac gel for localized musculoskeletal pain only if skin is intact and renal/cardiovascular risks are reviewed.  

32. **Medications:** Consider a short course of opioid analgesia for severe pain limiting ambulation or hand use if non-opioid measures are inadequate, with renal-adjusted selection and bowel-regimen planning.  

33. **Medications:** Consider oral prednisone only after cellulitis, septic arthritis, disseminated infection, and severe chemotherapy-related skin toxicity requiring treatment modification have been reasonably excluded.  

34. **Medications:** If inflammatory arthritis is strongly supported and infection is excluded, consider prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for a short course (for example 5–7 days) followed by reassessment or a brief taper depending on duration and response.  

35. **Medications:** If prednisone is used, monitor blood pressure, glucose, mental status, fluid retention, infection signs, and interaction with the patient’s cancer-treatment plan.  

36. **Medications:** Avoid initiating systemic corticosteroids as sole treatment for presumed hand-foot syndrome if symptoms are more consistent with capecitabine toxicity and chemotherapy dose interruption/supportive care has not been addressed.  

37. **Medications:** Start systemic antibiotics promptly if cellulitis is clinically suspected, with regimen selected for purulent versus nonpurulent infection, renal function, local resistance patterns, and neutropenic status.  

38. **Medications:** Initiate urgent broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and hospital-based care if febrile neutropenia, sepsis, rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection, or necrotizing infection is suspected.  

39. **Procedures:** Debride only loose devitalized skin or hyperkeratotic callus conservatively, preferably through podiatry/wound care, and avoid aggressive paring of painful fissured skin.  

40. **Procedures:** Use protective nonadherent dressings, silicone toe sleeves, padded socks, or off-loading footwear if plantar fissures, pressure points, or walking pain are prominent.  

41. **Referrals:** Arrange same-day or next-business-day oncology review for suspected capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome and decisions about treatment interruption, dose modification, or rechallenge.  

42. **Referrals:** Refer urgently to dermatology if diagnosis is uncertain, lesions are severe, blistering/ulcerative, widespread, refractory to supportive measures, or concerning for severe cutaneous adverse drug reaction.  

43. **Referrals:** Refer to rheumatology if there is objective synovitis, persistent dactylitis, inflammatory-pattern morning stiffness, recurrent episodes, or laboratory/imaging evidence suggesting inflammatory arthritis.  

44. **Referrals:** Refer to podiatry or wound care for painful plantar fissures, impaired ambulation, pressure redistribution, nail/skin care, or concern for secondary infection.  

45. **Counseling:** Counsel on avoiding heat exposure, hot water, friction, repetitive gripping, prolonged walking, running, tight shoes, and other pressure-producing activities during active symptoms.  

46. **Counseling:** Counsel to use cool—not ice—compresses or cool water soaks for short periods for symptomatic relief, avoiding direct ice contact that could damage fragile skin.  

47. **Counseling:** Counsel to wear loose, breathable shoes, thick soft socks, cushioned insoles, and gloves for household tasks; avoid adhesive bandages directly on fragile or fissured skin.  

48. **Follow-up and monitoring:** Reassess clinically within 48–72 hours if pain, erythema, or swelling is substantial; document pain score, ability to walk/use hands, skin integrity, temperature, and progression of redness.  

49. **Follow-up and monitoring:** Repeat CBC and renal function promptly if symptoms worsen, infection is suspected, capecitabine is continued despite toxicity, or systemic medications such as antibiotics or corticosteroids are started.  

50. **Contingencies:** Direct urgent emergency evaluation if temperature is at least 38.0°C (100.4°F), ANC is low, redness spreads rapidly, pain becomes disproportionate, there is purulence/bullae/necrosis, new confusion or hypotension occurs, inability to ambulate develops, or there is concern for septic arthritis or necrotizing infection.

1. Perform same-day oncology assessment for suspected capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), with grading of pain, erythema, edema, fissuring, desquamation, and functional impairment.  

2. Document a full skin and joint examination, including palms, soles, dorsal hands/feet, nail folds, oral mucosa, wrists, ankles, and range of motion of affected joints.  

3. Obtain clinical photographs of hands and feet for baseline severity documentation and comparison during treatment.  

4. Record vital signs, including temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and weight, to assess for infection, systemic inflammation, and fluid status.  

5. Obtain CBC with differential and platelet count to evaluate for neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, anemia, or leukocytosis before immunosuppression or chemotherapy decisions.  

6. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel, including creatinine/eGFR, AST/ALT, bilirubin, albumin, electrolytes, and calcium, for chemotherapy toxicity assessment and medication dosing.  

7. Obtain ESR and CRP to assess the degree of systemic inflammation and provide a baseline if inflammatory arthritis or infection remains under consideration.  

8. Obtain serum uric acid, recognizing that a normal result does not exclude acute gout, if the pattern includes abrupt severe joint inflammation.  

9. Consider rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies if there is persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis or concern for new inflammatory polyarthritis.  

10. Consider ANA with reflex connective-tissue-disease testing if there are systemic autoimmune features such as rash beyond the hands/feet, Raynaud symptoms, serositis, cytopenias, or renal abnormalities.  

11. Obtain blood cultures before corticosteroids or antibiotics if fever, rigors, hypotension, neutropenia, or other features raise concern for bacteremia.  

12. Culture any purulent drainage, ulcer base, or suspicious fissure if there is drainage, crusting, expanding erythema, malodor, or concern for bacterial superinfection.  

13. Obtain fungal testing (KOH preparation and/or fungal culture) from plantar scaling or toe-web maceration if tinea pedis is suspected as a contributor to fissuring or cellulitis risk.  

14. Consider hand/foot radiographs if there is focal bony tenderness, concern for fracture, erosive inflammatory arthritis, osteomyelitis, calcinosis, or unexpected severe pain.  

15. Consider musculoskeletal ultrasound of painful joints or tendon sheaths to distinguish synovitis, tenosynovitis, edema, and soft-tissue inflammation.  

16. Consider arthrocentesis of any clearly swollen accessible joint if septic arthritis or crystal arthritis is possible; send synovial fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.  

17. Assess whether the capecitabine regimen is continuous daily dosing or a standard cycle schedule, and calculate cumulative exposure and timing relative to symptom onset.  

18. Review the chemotherapy record for prior fluoropyrimidine toxicity, prior capecitabine dose reductions, renal-dose adjustments, and any prior hand-foot syndrome.  

19. Review for concurrent medications that may worsen edema, skin dryness, renal function, bleeding risk, or inflammatory symptoms, including antihypertensives, diuretics, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and supplements.  

20. Consider temporary interruption/holding of capecitabine pending oncology review if symptoms are painful, interfere with walking or hand function, have fissuring, or meet grade 2 or higher hand-foot syndrome criteria.  

21. Consider resuming capecitabine only after improvement to grade 0–1, with oncology-directed dose reduction or schedule adjustment if toxicity recurs.  

22. Consider switching from capecitabine to an alternative systemic cancer regimen if recurrent or severe hand-foot syndrome persists despite dose interruption, dose reduction, and supportive measures.  

23. Coordinate with oncology regarding whether oxaliplatin should continue on schedule, be delayed, or be modified based on overall toxicity and functional status.

25. Add a keratolytic moisturizer for hyperkeratosis/fissuring, such as urea 10–20% cream to intact thickened plantar skin once or twice daily; avoid use directly in deep open fissures if it causes burning.  

26. Apply petrolatum ointment to fissures and cover with nonadherent dressings, hydrocolloid dressings, or cotton socks/gloves overnight as tolerated.  

27. Consider liquid bandage, skin adhesive, or protective fissure dressings for painful superficial cracks if there is no infection and tissue is adequately dry.  

28. Use cool compresses or cool-water soaks for 15–20 minutes several times daily for symptomatic relief, while avoiding prolonged soaking that worsens skin breakdown.  

29. Counsel avoidance of friction, pressure, heat, and repetitive trauma: avoid long walks, tight shoes, high-impact exercise, hot baths, heating pads, and prolonged gripping.  

30. Recommend soft padded socks, wide toe-box footwear, cushioned insoles, and protective gloves for household activities to reduce pressure on palms and soles.  

31. Arrange podiatry or wound-care assessment for painful plantar fissures, callus management, off-loading strategies, and surveillance for secondary infection.  

32. Use acetaminophen for pain, for example 325–650 mg orally every 4–6 hours as needed (maximum daily dose individualized for liver function, frailty, and concurrent products).  

33. Avoid or limit oral NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen because of CKD, CAD, hypertension, and potential bleeding/renal risks; consider only if the treating clinicians determine benefits outweigh risks.  

34. Consider topical diclofenac gel for focal joint pain if skin is intact and renal/cardiovascular risks make systemic NSAIDs undesirable.  

35. Consider short-course opioid analgesia for severe pain impairing ambulation or self-care, with renal-adjusted agent selection, bowel regimen, fall-risk counseling, and reassessment within days.  

36. Start a high-potency topical corticosteroid to inflamed intact skin, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment thinly twice daily for up to 1–2 weeks, avoiding open fissures, ulcerated skin, and untreated infection.  

37. Consider a medium-potency topical corticosteroid, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily, if a lower-potency approach is preferred because of frailty, skin fragility, or diagnostic uncertainty.  

38. Consider topical anesthetic therapy, such as lidocaine 4% cream or patch applied to intact painful areas, if pain remains limiting despite moisturization and systemic analgesia.  

39. Consider oral pyridoxine (vitamin B6), for example 50–100 mg orally daily, only as an oncology-discussed supportive option given mixed evidence for prevention/treatment of capecitabine hand-foot syndrome.  

40. Consider oral celecoxib only after oncology/primary-care review of CKD, CAD, blood pressure, antiplatelet/anticoagulant use, and gastrointestinal risk, recognizing that evidence for hand-foot syndrome prevention is limited and cardiovascular/renal risks may be substantial.  

41. Consider oral prednisone only after infection, septic arthritis, uncontrolled diabetes, and major chemotherapy-related contraindications have been assessed; possible debated regimens include prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for 3–5 days with a rapid taper, or weight-based dosing if true inflammatory arthritis is diagnosed.  

42. If prednisone is started, prescribe the lowest effective dose and shortest duration, monitor glucose, blood pressure, mood, fluid retention, delirium, infection signs, and gastrointestinal risk, and coordinate with oncology because of active chemotherapy.  

43. Do not use systemic corticosteroids as sole treatment for suspected bacterial cellulitis, septic arthritis, or neutropenic infection; initiate urgent infectious evaluation and appropriate antimicrobials instead.  

44. Start empiric oral antibiotics for cellulitis only if there is clinical evidence such as expanding unilateral warmth/erythema, purulence, fever, lymphangitis, or elevated inflammatory markers, with renal-adjusted selection and MRSA coverage based on local risk factors.  

45. Refer urgently to dermatology, ideally within days, if diagnosis is uncertain, lesions are severe, blistering/ulcerative, atypical for hand-foot syndrome, or not improving after chemotherapy modification and topical care.  

46. Refer to rheumatology if there is objective synovitis, persistent morning stiffness, elevated inflammatory markers, recurrent episodes, positive autoimmune serology, or concern for paraneoplastic/inflammatory arthritis.  

47. Refer to infectious diseases or send to the emergency department urgently for fever, neutropenia, rapidly progressive redness, severe swelling, hemodynamic instability, suspected deep infection, or failure of initial antimicrobial therapy.  

48. Screen for functional decline and fall risk caused by painful ambulation; arrange physical therapy, occupational therapy, mobility aids, or home-safety assessment if walking or hand use is impaired.  

49. Reassess symptoms and skin findings within 48–72 hours if systemic steroids, antibiotics, or a chemotherapy hold is initiated, and reassess again before the next capecitabine cycle or oxaliplatin infusion.  

50. Instruct the patient to seek immediate care for temperature at or above 38.0°C (100.4°F), shaking chills, rapidly spreading redness, new pus, black/blue discoloration, blistering, inability to bear weight, severe uncontrolled pain, confusion, reduced urine output, or shortness of breath.

1. Obtain urgent oncology assessment to evaluate for capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia) and determine chemotherapy modifications.  

2. Document severity of hand-foot symptoms using a standardized grading system (eg, CTCAE grade 1–3), including pain, functional impairment, blistering, desquamation, ulceration, and inability to walk/use hands.  

3. Perform full skin examination for sharply demarcated erythema, hyperkeratosis, fissures, blisters, erosions, ulceration, drainage, necrosis, and involvement beyond palms/soles.  

4. Examine joints for synovitis, warmth, effusions, range-of-motion limitation, dactylitis, tenosynovitis, and distribution suggestive of inflammatory arthritis or crystal arthritis.  

5. Assess vital signs and systemic symptoms, including fever, chills, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion, malaise, and decreased oral intake, to exclude infection or sepsis.  

6. Obtain CBC with differential, including neutrophil count, to assess for chemotherapy-related cytopenias and infection risk.  

7. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel, including creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, AST/ALT, bilirubin, and albumin, for chemotherapy safety and medication dosing.  

8. Obtain ESR and CRP as inflammatory baselines if inflammatory arthritis, vasculitis, or infection remains under consideration.  

9. Obtain serum uric acid, recognizing that a normal value does not exclude acute gout.  

10. Consider rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies if persistent symmetric small-joint inflammatory arthritis is suspected.  

11. Consider ANA, complement testing, CK, and other autoimmune testing only if examination or systemic features suggest connective-tissue disease or myositis.  

12. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if febrile, systemically ill, neutropenic, or if bacteremia is a concern.  

13. Culture any purulent drainage, open fissure with suspected infection, or ulcerated lesion before targeted antimicrobial treatment when feasible.  

14. Consider plain radiographs of hands and feet if severe pain, focal bony tenderness, suspected erosive arthritis, fracture, osteomyelitis, or alternative structural pathology is present.  

15. Obtain musculoskeletal ultrasound of painful joints/tendon sheaths if the presence of synovitis, tenosynovitis, effusion, or crystal arthritis is uncertain.  

16. Perform arthrocentesis of any accessible joint effusion for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis if septic arthritis or gout/pseudogout is plausible.  

17. Consider dermatology consultation, urgently if there is blistering, ulceration, extensive desquamation, diagnostic uncertainty, or concern for severe drug eruption.  

18. Consider rheumatology consultation if true inflammatory polyarthritis, dactylitis, persistent synovitis, vasculitis, or crystal arthropathy is suspected.  

19. Consider infectious-disease consultation if cellulitis, neutropenic infection, osteomyelitis, unusual infection, or recurrent infected fissures are suspected.  

20. Hold capecitabine temporarily pending oncology review if symptoms are moderate to severe, painful, function-limiting, associated with fissuring/blistering, or consistent with grade 2 or higher hand-foot syndrome.  

21. Resume capecitabine only after improvement to mild/grade 1 symptoms or baseline, with oncology-directed dose reduction or altered schedule if toxicity recurs.  

22. Consider permanent discontinuation or change of systemic anticancer regimen if severe recurrent hand-foot syndrome persists despite dose interruption, dose reduction, and supportive care.  

23. Review timing of oxaliplatin doses and assess for concurrent oxaliplatin toxicities, including neuropathy, hypersensitivity phenomena, cytopenias, and functional decline.  

24. Continue pantoprazole if clinically necessary while documenting that symptoms preceded its initiation; consider a trial discontinuation or substitution only if a drug eruption remains plausible.  

25. Review all medications for agents that may worsen edema, skin reactions, renal function, bleeding risk, or immunosuppression, including NSAIDs, anticoagulants, diuretics, calcium-channel blockers, and recent antibiotics.  

26. Start frequent bland emollient therapy, such as petrolatum-based ointment or urea-containing cream, applied generously to hands and feet at least twice daily and after washing.  

27. Consider urea 10–20% cream or salicylic-acid–containing keratolytic treatment for marked hyperkeratosis, avoiding application to deep painful fissures or open erosions.  

28. Apply petrolatum ointment with cotton gloves/socks overnight to improve xerosis and fissuring.  

29. Use liquid bandage, hydrocolloid dressing, protective padding, or fissure dressings for painful cracks when there is no active infection.  

30. Start a high-potency topical corticosteroid for inflamed intact palmar/plantar skin, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily for 7–14 days, with reassessment for response and skin breakdown.  

31. Consider a medium- or high-potency topical corticosteroid under limited occlusion for severe localized inflammatory erythema, avoiding infected, ulcerated, or macerated areas.  

32. Use topical lidocaine preparations or other local analgesic measures for focal painful fissures if skin integrity permits.  

33. Use acetaminophen for pain, with a conservative maximum daily dose adjusted for liver function, frailty, alcohol use, and concomitant medications.  

34. Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs because of CKD, CAD, hypertension, advanced age, and potential chemotherapy-related renal or bleeding risks; consider only a short monitored course if benefits outweigh risks.  

35. Consider topical diclofenac for localized musculoskeletal pain if intact skin and renal/cardiovascular risk assessment support its use.  

36. Consider oral prednisone only after infection, septic arthritis, and severe drug-related skin toxicity have been reasonably excluded and if there is convincing inflammatory arthritis or another steroid-responsive inflammatory diagnosis.  

37. If oral prednisone is used for suspected inflammatory arthritis, consider a short course such as prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for 5–10 days with a rapid taper or stop plan, coordinated with oncology and adjusted to response.  

38. Avoid empiric systemic prednisone, or stop it promptly, if there is fever, neutropenia, purulence, progressive cellulitis, suspected septic arthritis, uncontrolled diabetes, delirium, gastrointestinal bleeding risk, or concern that steroids could mask infection.  

39. If systemic prednisone is started, monitor blood pressure, glucose, mental status, fluid retention, infection signs, sleep disturbance, and renal function, particularly given age, hypertension, CAD, and CKD.  

40. Start empiric antibiotics directed at cellulitis only if clinical findings support bacterial infection (eg, unilateral spreading warmth/erythema, purulence, fever, leukocytosis, or rapidly worsening fissures), with renal-dose adjustment and neutropenic-fever pathways as applicable.  

41. Send the patient for emergency evaluation and IV broad-spectrum antibiotics if febrile with neutropenia, hemodynamic instability, rapidly progressive erythema, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, or concern for necrotizing infection.  

42. Counsel on avoidance of friction, pressure, repetitive gripping, prolonged walking, hot water, tight shoes, and vigorous exercise while symptoms are active.  

43. Recommend soft, well-cushioned shoes, thick socks, padded insoles, gloves for manual tasks, and off-loading of painful plantar areas.  

44. Advise against peeling, cutting, or aggressively debriding callused or cracked skin at home; arrange professional podiatric care if needed.  

45. Refer to podiatry for management of painful plantar fissures, callus reduction, pressure off-loading, nail care, footwear guidance, and evaluation for secondary infection.  

46. Refer to wound care if fissures are deep, ulcerated, draining, slow to heal, or impair ambulation.  

47. Evaluate for peripheral neuropathy and sensory loss from oxaliplatin, including fall risk and unnoticed foot trauma; consider physical therapy or occupational therapy if gait or hand function is impaired.  

48. Provide return precautions for fever of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher, rapidly increasing redness/swelling, new drainage, inability to bear weight, severe uncontrolled pain, new blisters/ulcers, confusion, or reduced urine output.  

49. Arrange close follow-up within 24–72 hours if symptoms are severe, evolving, or infection has not been definitively excluded; otherwise reassess within approximately 1 week after supportive measures or chemotherapy changes.  

50. At follow-up, reassess symptom grade, functional status, skin integrity, joint findings, CBC/renal function where indicated, analgesic use, steroid adverse effects if used, and readiness for the next capecitabine/oxaliplatin treatment cycle.

17. Resume capecitabine only after improvement to mild/baseline toxicity, with oncology-directed consideration of dose reduction, schedule modification, or discontinuation based on toxicity grade and recurrence.  

18. Review the capecitabine dose against current renal function; consider dose adjustment or discontinuation if renal impairment is substantial or has worsened.  

19. Review whether the patient has previously had DPYD/DPD deficiency testing; consider testing or oncology/pharmacology review if toxicity is early, unusually severe, accompanied by severe diarrhea/mucositis/cytopenias, or otherwise disproportionate.  

20. Review timing of oxaliplatin relative to symptoms and assess for acute neurotoxicity, cold-triggered dysesthesia, neuropathic pain, hypersensitivity reaction, or infusion-related symptoms.  

21. Consider holding or modifying oxaliplatin only in coordination with oncology if there is evidence that it is contributing to neuropathy, hypersensitivity, or another treatment-limiting toxicity.  

22. Do not attribute the eruption solely to pantoprazole without assessment; review the full medication and over-the-counter exposure history for other potentially causative drugs or contact allergens.  

23. Consider holding pantoprazole temporarily if a drug eruption remains plausible and there is no high-risk indication requiring uninterrupted acid suppression; substitute another acid-suppression strategy if needed.  

24. Start frequent bland emollient therapy, such as petrolatum-based ointment, applied generously to hands and feet at least 2–4 times daily and after bathing.  

25. Start keratolytic moisturization for hyperkeratosis and fissuring, such as urea 10–20% cream to intact thickened plantar/palmar skin once or twice daily; avoid application directly into open or deeply painful fissures if it burns.  

26. Consider higher-strength urea (eg, 20–40%) or salicylic-acid-containing keratolytic preparations for marked callus/hyperkeratosis only with dermatology/podiatry guidance and avoidance of broken skin.  

27. Use a high-potency topical corticosteroid, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment applied thinly to inflamed intact palmar/plantar skin once or twice daily for up to 1–2 weeks, with reassessment.  

28. Consider a medium-potency topical corticosteroid, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily, if high-potency therapy is felt excessive or if large areas require treatment.  

29. Avoid applying potent topical corticosteroids directly into infected, ulcerated, or draining skin unless infection has been assessed and treated.  

30. Treat painful fissures with petrolatum, hydrocolloid dressing, liquid bandage/cyanoacrylate skin protectant, or protective padding, depending on depth, drainage, and infection risk.  

31. Consider podiatry or wound-care referral for painful plantar fissures, callus debridement, pressure redistribution, dressing selection, or impaired ambulation.  

32. Use nonpharmacologic cooling measures such as cool water soaks or cool packs for short intervals as tolerated, while avoiding ice injury and prolonged soaking that may worsen fissuring.  

33. Counsel the patient to avoid heat exposure, hot baths, prolonged walking, running, friction, repetitive manual tasks, tight footwear, and pressure on affected palms and soles during active symptoms.  

34. Counsel use of cushioned, well-fitting shoes, soft socks, padded insoles, gloves for manual activity, and avoidance of friction-producing footwear or tools.  

35. Use acetaminophen for pain, for example 325–650 mg orally every 4–6 hours as needed, with a conservative maximum daily dose tailored to liver status, frailty, and alcohol use.  

36. Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, naproxen) because of CKD, advanced age, hypertension, CAD, bleeding risk, and potential chemotherapy-related renal or hematologic toxicity; consider only if a clinician determines benefits outweigh risks.  

37. Consider topical diclofenac gel for focal musculoskeletal pain only if skin is intact and renal/cardiovascular risks are reviewed; avoid applying to fissured or inflamed palmar/plantar skin.  

38. Consider a short course of oral prednisone only after infection, septic arthritis, and severe cutaneous drug reaction have been reasonably excluded and after oncology review; possible regimens for an inflammatory alternative diagnosis include prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for 3–5 days with rapid reassessment or taper as clinically indicated.  

39. If oral prednisone is used, monitor blood pressure, glucose, edema/heart failure symptoms, delirium or insomnia, infection signs, and interactions with the patient’s cancer treatment plan.  

40. Avoid initiating prolonged systemic corticosteroids for presumed hand-foot syndrome without reassessing the diagnosis and chemotherapy management, because dose interruption/modification and topical/supportive measures may be more relevant.  

41. Start empiric antibiotics only if there are convincing findings of cellulitis, infected fissures, purulence, systemic infection, or neutropenia-related infection; select agent and renal-adjusted dose according to local guidance and severity.  

42. Send the patient to the emergency department immediately for fever of at least 38.0°C (100.4°F), neutropenia with fever, rapidly spreading redness, severe uncontrolled pain, inability to walk/use hands, bullae or skin sloughing, mucosal involvement, purpura, hypotension, confusion, or concern for sepsis/SJS-TEN.  

43. Reassess clinically within 48–72 hours after medication changes and supportive treatment, sooner if symptoms progress, to document pain, function, erythema, swelling, fissures, and infection signs.  

44. Recheck CBC and renal/hepatic function before the next capecitabine cycle or earlier if systemic symptoms, diarrhea, mucositis, poor oral intake, or other chemotherapy toxicity develops.  

45. At follow-up, determine whether symptoms improve after holding capecitabine; improvement supports chemotherapy-associated hand-foot syndrome, whereas persistent synovitis, progressive rash, or systemic findings should trigger expanded dermatologic/rheumatologic/infectious evaluation.

1. Perform urgent oncology assessment for suspected capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), including formal CTCAE severity grading.  

2. Obtain a complete symptom history: fever, chills, rash elsewhere, mouth sores, diarrhea, neuropathy, morning stiffness duration, preceding trauma, prior gout, psoriasis, and functional impairment.  

3. Document whether pain is predominantly cutaneous/burning versus intra-articular, and whether swelling involves joints, tendons, or diffuse digits.  

4. Examine for cellulitis, lymphangitis, fluctuance, purulence, ulceration, ischemia, nail-fold infection, and signs of systemic infection.  

5. Examine for true synovitis in MCP, PIP, DIP, wrist, ankle, and MTP joints to distinguish inflammatory arthritis from chemotherapy-related skin toxicity.  

6. Assess for dactylitis, enthesitis, psoriasis, nail pitting, and other findings that could suggest psoriatic or seronegative inflammatory arthritis.  

7. Obtain vital signs, including temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and weight; evaluate for hemodynamic instability or sepsis.  

8. Obtain CBC with differential and platelet count to identify neutropenia, leukocytosis, anemia, or thrombocytopenia before anti-inflammatory treatment.  

9. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel, including creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, AST/ALT, bilirubin, albumin, and calcium for chemotherapy toxicity and medication dosing.  

10. Obtain ESR and CRP as baseline inflammatory markers if inflammatory arthritis, infection, or drug reaction remains possible.  

11. Obtain serum uric acid, recognizing that a normal level does not exclude acute gout.  

12. Consider rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies if persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis is present.  

13. Consider ANA and additional autoimmune testing only if history or examination suggests connective-tissue disease.  

14. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if fever, rigors, hypotension, neutropenia, or concern for bacteremia is present.  

15. Culture any open fissure, ulcer, drainage, or purulent skin lesion if infection is suspected.  

16. Obtain plain radiographs of symptomatic hands and feet if there is concern for fracture, erosive arthritis, chondrocalcinosis, severe osteoarthritis flare, or metastatic bone disease.  

17. Consider musculoskeletal ultrasound of hands/feet to distinguish synovitis, tenosynovitis, effusion, crystal arthritis, and diffuse soft-tissue edema.  

18. Perform arthrocentesis of any accessible swollen joint with effusion for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis if septic arthritis or crystalline arthritis is plausible.  

19. Consider venous duplex ultrasound of an affected limb if swelling is asymmetric or there is concern for venous thrombosis.  

20. Notify the treating medical oncologist promptly before the next capecitabine dose or oxaliplatin infusion.  

21. Consider temporarily holding capecitabine while the severity and etiology of the palmar/plantar findings are evaluated, particularly if pain limits activities of daily living or there is skin breakdown.  

22. Consider capecitabine dose interruption followed by protocol-directed dose reduction on rechallenge if symptoms meet moderate or severe hand-foot syndrome criteria.  

23. Consider delaying the next oxaliplatin infusion pending oncology assessment if symptoms may represent a serious treatment-related toxicity or systemic inflammatory process.  

24. Review the chemotherapy regimen, capecitabine dose, renal-dose appropriateness, timing of symptoms relative to cycles, and prior toxicities.  

25. Confirm renal function–appropriate capecitabine dosing, given CKD and increased risk of fluoropyrimidine toxicity with reduced renal clearance.  

26. Consider testing for DPYD deficiency or reviewing prior DPYD status if toxicity is unusually early, severe, or accompanied by mucositis, diarrhea, cytopenias, or other fluoropyrimidine toxicities.  

27. Start intensive bland emollient therapy to palms, soles, toes, and fissures, such as petrolatum-based ointment several times daily.  

28. Consider keratolytic moisturizers containing urea 10–20% for hyperkeratosis and fissuring if skin is intact and not severely inflamed or ulcerated.  

29. Consider topical high-potency corticosteroid treatment to markedly inflamed palms/soles for a limited course, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment twice daily for 7–14 days, avoiding open or infected areas.  

30. Consider topical medium-potency corticosteroid treatment instead, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily, if a lower-potency approach is preferred.  

31. Consider topical lidocaine or other local analgesic measures for painful fissures if there are no contraindications and intact skin permits use.  

32. Use acetaminophen for pain control, with a conservative maximum daily dose appropriate to liver function, frailty, alcohol use, and concomitant medications.  

33. Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs because of CKD, hypertension, CAD, older age, and potential bleeding or renal risks; if considered, use the lowest dose for the shortest duration with renal and blood-pressure monitoring.  

34. Consider a short course of low-dose opioid analgesia for severe pain impairing ambulation or self-care when nonopioid measures are inadequate, with bowel regimen and fall-risk precautions.  

35. Consider oral prednisone only after assessment for infection, septic arthritis, and chemotherapy-related skin toxicity; candidate regimens include prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily for 5–7 days with a taper or stop plan based on response.  

36. Consider avoiding systemic prednisone if findings are most consistent with capecitabine hand-foot syndrome without substantial inflammatory synovitis, because drug interruption and local skin-directed measures may be more appropriate.  

37. Consider a higher short prednisone course, such as 0.3–0.5 mg/kg/day, only if a rheumatologic inflammatory arthritis is strongly suspected and infection has been reasonably excluded, ideally with rheumatology input.  

38. If prednisone is started, monitor glucose, blood pressure, mood/sleep changes, fluid retention, infection signs, and worsening edema; consider gastroprotection only after reviewing whether pantoprazole is necessary and appropriate.  

39. Do not attribute the syndrome solely to recently initiated pantoprazole without evaluating chemotherapy toxicity and inflammatory/infectious alternatives; consider holding pantoprazole if a drug eruption remains plausible and there is no strong indication.  

40. Counsel on avoidance of friction, pressure, heat exposure, vigorous exercise, prolonged walking, tight footwear, hot water, and repetitive hand activities while symptoms are active.  

41. Advise use of cushioned shoes, soft socks, gloves for manual tasks, silicone toe protection, and avoidance of adhesive products over fragile skin.  

42. Recommend gentle skin care: lukewarm water, fragrance-free cleanser, careful drying between toes, avoidance of alcohol-containing products, and prompt treatment of cracks.  

43. Consider podiatry referral for painful plantar fissures, callus management, off-loading strategies, footwear modification, and surveillance for secondary infection.  

44. Refer to dermatology urgently if diagnosis is uncertain, there is extensive desquamation, blistering, ulceration, atypical rash, concern for severe cutaneous adverse reaction, or failure of initial measures.  

45. Refer to rheumatology within days to 1–2 weeks if objective synovitis, dactylitis, recurrent episodes, elevated inflammatory markers, positive serologies, or persistent symptoms suggest inflammatory arthritis.  

46. Refer to emergency care immediately for fever ≥38.0°C, neutropenia, rapidly spreading erythema, severe warmth, purulence, hypotension, confusion, inability to bear weight, or concern for septic arthritis/cellulitis.  

47. Start empiric antimicrobial therapy only if clinical findings support cellulitis, infected fissures, neutropenic infection, or septic arthritis, with agent selection adjusted for renal function and local protocols.  

48. Arrange follow-up contact within 24–72 hours to reassess pain, swelling, redness, functional status, skin integrity, fever, laboratory results, and the decision about chemotherapy continuation.  

49. Reassess in person before resuming or escalating capecitabine, documenting hand-foot syndrome grade and whether symptoms have improved to a tolerable baseline.  

50. If symptoms fail to improve within 3–7 days after chemotherapy modification and supportive treatment, or worsen despite treatment, broaden evaluation for infection, crystal arthritis, autoimmune disease, vascular causes, and alternative drug reactions.

1. Obtain an urgent oncology assessment for suspected capecitabine-associated hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia), including grading severity by pain, erythema, edema, desquamation, fissuring, and impact on activities of daily living.  

2. Contact the treating oncology team before administering oral prednisone or changing chemotherapy, given ongoing capecitabine/oxaliplatin treatment and possible chemotherapy toxicity.  

3. Hold capecitabine temporarily pending oncology evaluation if symptoms are moderate-to-severe, painful, associated with fissuring, or impair walking/hand function.  

4. Resume capecitabine only after improvement to mild symptoms or baseline, using the oncology protocol for possible dose reduction or altered schedule.  

5. Consider permanent capecitabine dose reduction for recurrent grade 2 or any severe/grade 3 hand-foot syndrome after recovery.  

6. Evaluate whether continuous daily capecitabine dosing, renal impairment, age, or drug interactions may be increasing fluoropyrimidine exposure and toxicity risk.  

7. Obtain current renal function (BMP/CMP including creatinine/eGFR) to assess whether capecitabine dosing is appropriate for CKD.  

8. Review the capecitabine prescription, actual dose, dosing schedule, adherence, recent dose changes, and whether it is being taken with food as prescribed.  

9. Review all medications and over-the-counter products for agents that may worsen renal function, skin injury, bleeding risk, or inflammatory symptoms.  

10. Document a complete skin examination of palms, soles, digits, nail folds, dorsal hands/feet, lower legs, and oral mucosa to characterize chemotherapy toxicity and identify alternate diagnoses.  

11. Examine for focal warmth, fluctuance, purulence, lymphangitic streaking, ulceration, necrosis, or unilateral predominance that would suggest cellulitis, abscess, or another infection.  

12. Obtain CBC with differential to assess for neutropenia, leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and chemotherapy-related marrow toxicity.  

13. Measure temperature and assess for systemic infection symptoms, including fever, chills, hypotension, confusion, malaise, and tachycardia.  

14. Obtain blood cultures promptly if fever is present, if the patient is neutropenic, or if there are systemic signs of infection.  

15. Obtain CRP and ESR if inflammatory arthritis, vasculitis, infection, or another systemic inflammatory condition remains a concern.  

16. Check serum uric acid only as supportive data if acute gout is suspected; do not use a normal uric acid level to exclude gout.  

17. Consider rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP testing if there is persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis rather than primarily cutaneous palmar-plantar toxicity.  

18. Consider ANA, complement levels, urinalysis, and other autoimmune testing only if examination or systemic features raise concern for connective-tissue disease or vasculitis.  

19. Obtain bilateral hand/foot radiographs if there is true joint swelling, concern for erosive disease, fracture, osteomyelitis, calcification, or an alternate structural diagnosis.  

20. Use musculoskeletal ultrasound of symptomatic joints or tendon sheaths if it is unclear whether swelling is synovitis/tenosynovitis versus soft-tissue edema from hand-foot syndrome.  

21. Aspirate any clearly swollen joint urgently if septic arthritis or crystal arthritis is plausible, with synovial fluid cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.  

22. Avoid empiric systemic oral prednisone until infection, septic arthritis, and major chemotherapy toxicity considerations have been assessed, unless a specialist determines benefits outweigh risks.  

23. Consider a short oral prednisone course only if an inflammatory rheumatologic diagnosis is supported, infection is reasonably excluded, and the oncology team agrees; use the lowest effective dose and shortest duration.  

24. If systemic prednisone is used, define a specific dose, duration, taper plan if indicated, glucose monitoring plan, blood-pressure monitoring plan, and infection precautions.  

25. Avoid prolonged systemic corticosteroids because of advanced age, malignancy, infection risk, hypertension, CAD, skin fragility, and potential metabolic adverse effects.  

26. Use frequent bland emollients/barrier ointments to hands and feet, such as petrolatum-based products, especially after bathing and before sleep.  

27. Start keratolytic moisturizing therapy for hyperkeratosis/fissuring, such as urea 10–20% cream to intact thickened plantar skin; avoid applying high-strength products to deeply open or severely inflamed fissures.  

28. Consider urea 20–40% cream or salicylic-acid-containing keratolytics under dermatology/oncology guidance for marked hyperkeratosis if skin is intact.  

29. Use topical medium- to high-potency corticosteroid treatment for localized inflammatory erythema if judged appropriate, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily for a limited course, avoiding open wounds and areas with suspected infection.  

30. Consider a more potent topical steroid, such as clobetasol 0.05% ointment, for short-term use on severely inflamed intact palms/soles only with clinician guidance and reassessment.  

31. Treat painful fissures with protective dressings, liquid bandage products where appropriate, hydrocolloid dressings, or nonadherent dressings depending on drainage and skin integrity.  

32. Consider topical antibiotic treatment only for small superficial fissures with localized impetiginization; avoid routine topical antibiotics on noninfected skin because of contact dermatitis and resistance risk.  

33. Start systemic antibiotics only if cellulitis, wound infection, neutropenic infection, or another bacterial process is clinically suspected; tailor selection to severity, neutropenia status, renal function, and local resistance patterns.  

34. Use acetaminophen for pain if no contraindication, with a conservative maximum daily dose appropriate for age, liver function, alcohol use, and concomitant medications.  

35. Avoid or minimize oral NSAIDs because of CKD, hypertension, CAD, advanced age, and possible chemotherapy-related renal or bleeding risks.  

36. Consider short-term opioid analgesia only for severe pain preventing ambulation or self-care when safer measures are inadequate, with bowel regimen, fall-risk counseling, and close reassessment.  

37. Advise avoidance of friction, pressure, repetitive gripping, long walks, running, kneeling, hot water exposure, and other mechanical stressors on palms and soles.  

38. Recommend soft, well-cushioned footwear, moisture-wicking socks, padded insoles, gloves for household tasks, and avoidance of tight shoes or pressure points.  

39. Advise against picking, cutting, or aggressively filing peeling skin/calluses; arrange professional foot care if needed rather than self-debridement.  

40. Counsel on daily inspection of hands and feet for worsening cracks, bleeding, drainage, ulcers, increasing redness, black discoloration, or new focal tenderness.  

41. Refer to dermatology urgently or semi-urgently if diagnosis is uncertain, lesions are severe, blistering/desquamating, refractory to initial supportive care, or there is concern for a serious drug eruption.  

42. Refer to rheumatology if persistent objective synovitis, inflammatory morning stiffness, dactylitis, or recurrent symptoms remain after chemotherapy toxicity and infection are addressed.  

43. Refer to podiatry or wound care for painful plantar fissures, impaired ambulation, ulceration, difficult callus management, or concern for secondary infection.  

44. Consider physical therapy, occupational therapy, mobility aids, or home-safety assessment if hand/foot pain or swelling limits walking, transfers, footwear use, or activities of daily living.  

45. Reassess symptoms, skin findings, pain control, mobility, temperature, CBC, and renal function within 24–72 hours if chemotherapy is held, infection is possible, or symptoms are functionally significant.  

46. Reassess before the next oxaliplatin infusion and before restarting capecitabine, documenting toxicity grade and a chemotherapy dose-modification plan.  

47. Escalate to same-day emergency evaluation for fever of at least 38.0°C (100.4°F), especially during chemotherapy, or for chills, hypotension, confusion, or other possible neutropenic sepsis features.  

48. Escalate urgently for rapidly spreading erythema, severe focal warmth, purulent drainage, lymphangitic streaking, new ulceration/necrosis, inability to bear weight, or pain out of proportion to examination.  

49. Escalate urgently for a hot, markedly painful swollen joint with restricted passive motion, because septic arthritis requires prompt aspiration and treatment.  

50. Educate the patient and spouse to notify oncology immediately for worsening pain, blistering, inability to use hands or walk, or failure to improve after chemotherapy interruption and supportive skin care.

39. Consider topical anesthetic measures for painful intact skin, such as lidocaine 4% topical preparation, while avoiding excessive application over broken skin.  

40. If cellulitis or secondary bacterial infection is suspected, initiate systemic antibiotics directed at likely streptococcal/staphylococcal pathogens after examination and culture when feasible, with renal dose adjustment.  

41. If neutropenic fever, rapidly spreading erythema, purulence, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, necrosis, or hemodynamic instability occurs, send the patient to the emergency department for urgent IV antibiotics and inpatient evaluation.

43. Counsel to use soft, well-fitting shoes, padded socks, cushioned insoles, gloves for household tasks, and mobility assistance if walking is painful or unsafe.
