21. Obtain venous duplex ultrasonography of the lower extremities if unilateral swelling, pain, asymmetry, or otherwise concerning DVT features occur.  
22. Consider BNP, chest radiograph, ECG, and echocardiography if edema is accompanied by dyspnea or concern for cardiac decompensation.  
23. Contact the treating oncologist urgently before the next capecitabine dose to discuss chemotherapy-related hand-foot syndrome and treatment modification.  
24. Hold capecitabine temporarily pending oncology review if symptoms meet moderate-to-severe hand-foot syndrome criteria, significantly impair function, or involve painful fissuring/ulceration.  
25. Resume capecitabine only after improvement to a lower toxicity grade, with oncology-directed dose reduction, altered schedule, or discontinuation if toxicity recurs.  
26. Consider reducing the next capecitabine dose according to the oncology protocol after recovery from clinically significant hand-foot syndrome.  
27. Consider delaying or modifying oxaliplatin if neuropathy, severe acral toxicity, or another oxaliplatin-related adverse reaction is suspected.  
28. Start frequent thick emollient therapy to palms, soles, toes, and fissured areas, such as petrolatum- or ceramide-based ointment applied at least twice daily and after washing.  
29. Apply urea 10%–20% cream or keratolytic moisturizer to hyperkeratotic, dry, cracked plantar surfaces if skin is intact enough to tolerate it.  
30. Use petrolatum ointment with cotton gloves or socks overnight for occlusion of severely dry, fissured skin, avoiding occlusion of infected, macerated, or draining areas.  
31. Consider topical medium- to high-potency corticosteroid treatment for painful inflammatory erythema without evidence of infection, such as triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily for 7–14 days.  
32. Consider clobetasol 0.05% ointment for short, localized courses on markedly inflamed thick palmar/plantar skin, with dermatology or oncology input.  
33. Consider topical anesthetic measures for focal pain, such as lidocaine-containing preparations, while avoiding use on extensive denuded skin.  
34. Use acetaminophen for pain, for example 325–650 mg orally every 4–6 hours as needed, with a patient-specific maximum daily dose based on liver function and frailty.  
35. Avoid or minimize systemic NSAIDs because of CKD, CAD, hypertension, edema, bleeding risk, and potential interaction with the patient’s overall oncology status.  
36. Consider short-course opioid analgesia only for severe pain limiting ambulation or self-care after assessment of fall risk, constipation risk, renal function, and concurrent sedating medications.  
37. Consider oral prednisone only after infection, uncontrolled diabetes risk, severe chemotherapy-related skin toxicity, and other mimics have been assessed; potential regimens for an inflammatory arthritis-type presentation include prednisone 10–20 mg orally daily with a short taper individualized to response.  
38. Avoid initiating systemic prednisone alone if cellulitis, bacteremia, neutropenic infection, uncontrolled fungal infection, or another untreated infection is suspected.  
39. If systemic corticosteroids are started, monitor glucose, blood pressure, fluid retention, delirium, infection symptoms, mood changes, and interaction with ongoing cancer treatment.  
40. Start empiric antibiotics directed at skin/soft-tissue infection if there is spreading erythema, focal warmth, purulence, fever, leukocytosis, or rapidly progressive tenderness, with renal dose adjustment.  
41. Arrange urgent emergency evaluation and intravenous antibiotics if there is fever, neutropenia, hypotension, rapidly spreading redness, severe pain out of proportion, bullae, necrosis, or concern for sepsis/necrotizing infection.  
42. Refer to dermatology urgently for diagnostic confirmation, grading of chemotherapy-associated skin toxicity, consideration of biopsy, and management of severe or atypical lesions.  
43. Refer to rheumatology if objective synovitis, persistent inflammatory stiffness, dactylitis, elevated inflammatory markers, or unclear inflammatory arthritis remains after initial assessment.  
44. Refer to podiatry or wound care for painful plantar fissures, pressure off-loading, nail care, ulcer prevention, or wounds that are slow to heal.  
45. Counsel on avoiding friction, repetitive pressure, long walks, tight footwear, hot water, vigorous exercise, and manual activities that worsen hand-foot symptoms.  
46. Counsel on wearing cushioned shoes, soft moisture-wicking socks, protective gloves for household tasks, and avoiding barefoot walking.  
47. Advise use of lukewarm water, mild fragrance-free cleansers, gentle drying, and avoidance of alcohol-based or irritating skin products on affected areas.  
48. Consider cooling measures during capecitabine exposure or around oxaliplatin infusion only after oncology guidance, recognizing that cold exposure may aggravate oxaliplatin-induced acute neuropathy.  
49. Reassess clinically within 24–72 hours if symptoms are severe, progressing, associated with edema, or infection has not been definitively excluded.  
50. Provide explicit return/ED precautions for temperature of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher, new shortness of breath, unilateral leg swelling, inability to walk or use hands, rapidly worsening redness/swelling, drainage, blistering, black discoloration, confusion, or reduced urine output.

1. Verify the current alendronate formulation, dose, weekly schedule, adherence, start date, and cumulative oral bisphosphonate exposure.  
2. Confirm the indication for alendronate and document fracture-risk status using prior fragility fractures, DXA results, vertebral imaging if available, and FRAX.  
3. Obtain or review the most recent DXA scan (lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck) as a baseline for assessing the consequence of any interruption in therapy.  
4. Review for additional MRONJ risk factors, including cancer, prior head/neck radiation, diabetes, smoking, glucocorticoid use, immunosuppression, poor oral hygiene, periodontitis, and prior antiresorptive exposure.  
5. Confirm that she has not received IV bisphosphonates, denosumab, romosozumab, antiangiogenic therapy, chemotherapy, or chronic systemic corticosteroids.  
6. Review renal function, calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase as osteoporosis-treatment and bone-healing baselines.  
7. Assess for symptoms or signs of existing jaw pathology, including exposed bone, nonhealing oral ulcers, jaw pain, swelling, drainage, loose teeth, or fistula.  
8. Obtain a dental examination and appropriate dental radiographs or cone-beam CT as determined by the oral surgeon to assess periodontal disease, infection, bone quality, and extraction complexity.  
9. Treat active dental infection, periodontal disease, abscess, or periapical pathology before or at the time of definitive extraction according to the dental specialist’s plan.  
10. Ask the oral surgeon to document whether extraction, grafting, and immediate implant placement are essential versus whether staged extraction and delayed implant placement are feasible.  
11. Discuss conservative alternatives to extraction when clinically appropriate, such as endodontic treatment, restoration, crown, periodontal treatment, or retention of the tooth/root.  
12. Refer for oral and maxillofacial surgery consultation before extraction because the procedure includes bone grafting and planned implant placement in a patient receiving an antiresorptive medication.  
13. Coordinate a shared treatment plan among the prescribing clinician, dentist/oral surgeon, and patient rather than having the patient independently stop alendronate.  
14. Continue alendronate without interruption through extraction, grafting, and implant placement as one reasonable approach, given the very low MRONJ incidence with osteoporosis-dose oral bisphosphonates.  
15. Consider holding alendronate beginning immediately before the extraction as an alternative individualized approach if the surgeon and osteoporosis clinician believe her local surgical risk outweighs short-term skeletal benefit.  
16. Consider a pre-procedure alendronate holiday of approximately 2 months before extraction as a debated strategy for patients with longer-term oral bisphosphonate exposure or additional MRONJ risk factors.  
17. Consider a shorter alendronate interruption of approximately 1 week before surgery, timed by omitting the scheduled weekly dose immediately preceding the procedure, as another possible practice pattern.  
18. Consider no preoperative hold because bisphosphonates remain bound in bone for years and short interruptions may not meaningfully reduce MRONJ risk.  
19. If alendronate is held, avoid substituting denosumab solely for the dental procedure because denosumab also carries MRONJ risk and creates rebound vertebral-fracture concerns if delayed or stopped.  
20. If alendronate is held, consider whether temporary non-antiresorptive osteoporosis management alone—adequate calcium, vitamin D, fall prevention, and surveillance—is sufficient during the interruption.  
21. Consider anabolic osteoporosis therapy referral (such as teriparatide or abaloparatide) if her fracture risk is confirmed to be very high and a prolonged antiresorptive interruption is contemplated.  
22. Avoid routine serum C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) or other bone-turnover-marker testing to predict MRONJ risk, because such testing is not validated for this purpose.  
23. Avoid using routine prophylactic “drug holiday” duration as a guarantee against MRONJ, and document that risk persists despite temporary interruption.  
24. Plan atraumatic extraction technique with preservation of soft tissue and bone where feasible.  
25. Consider primary mucosal closure over the extraction socket/graft when technically feasible to reduce exposed bone and promote healing.  
26. Consider staged treatment—extraction first, then bone grafting and/or implant placement after complete mucosal and radiographic healing—rather than immediate graft/implant placement.  
27. Consider deferring implant placement or using a removable prosthetic alternative if the oral surgeon judges implant-related risk or healing uncertainty to be unacceptable.  
28. Use local hemostatic measures and surgical-site protection as appropriate, particularly because she takes aspirin.  
29. Review the indication for aspirin (especially prior TIA) with the prescribing clinician before dental surgery.  
30. Continue low-dose aspirin for the dental procedure as one option, using local bleeding control, given the potential thrombotic risk of interruption after TIA.  
31. Consider a brief aspirin hold only if the oral surgeon believes bleeding risk is unusually high and the clinician managing her cerebrovascular risk agrees on a specific plan.  
32. Use perioperative antimicrobial mouth rinse, such as chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse, before and after the procedure if directed by the dental surgeon.  
33. Consider perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis or a short postoperative antibiotic course only if the oral surgeon identifies infection, extensive grafting, immunocompromise, or another procedure-specific indication.  
34. Provide analgesia with acetaminophen as first-line postoperative pain treatment if appropriate.  
35. Use NSAIDs cautiously or avoid them if bleeding risk, renal function, gastrointestinal risk, or concurrent aspirin use makes them undesirable.  
36. Continue atorvastatin unless another perioperative issue arises, as it does not require interruption for this dental procedure.  
37. Ensure calcium intake of approximately 1,000–1,200 mg/day from diet plus supplements if needed, accounting for total intake and kidney-stone history.  
38. Ensure vitamin D supplementation sufficient to maintain an adequate 25-hydroxyvitamin D level, with dose individualized to laboratory results and current intake.  
39. Counsel on meticulous oral hygiene, routine dental care, smoking avoidance, limiting heavy alcohol use, and prompt evaluation of dental infections.  
40. Counsel that MRONJ is rare with osteoporosis-dose oral alendronate, but that extraction, infection, poor healing, and invasive implant procedures are recognized risk contexts.  
41. Counsel that advanced age and low body weight increase fracture risk, so unnecessarily prolonged interruption of osteoporosis therapy may have skeletal consequences.  
42. Arrange postoperative dental review within approximately 1–2 weeks to assess soft-tissue closure, infection, pain, drainage, and exposed bone.  
43. Arrange continued oral-surgery follow-up until the extraction/graft site has complete mucosal healing and the surgeon is satisfied with osseous healing.  
44. If alendronate was held, resume it after complete mucosal healing—often after approximately 6–8 weeks or when the oral surgeon confirms adequate healing—as one common strategy.  
45. If bone grafting or implant placement requires prolonged healing, consider delaying alendronate resumption until graft integration and implant stability are documented, balancing this against fracture risk.  
46. If alendronate was not held, continue the usual weekly dosing schedule while monitoring closely for delayed healing or MRONJ symptoms.  
47. If exposed bone or a fistula probing to bone persists for more than 8 weeks, evaluate urgently for suspected MRONJ and refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery.  
48. If postoperative fever, progressive facial swelling, purulence, severe pain, dysphagia, trismus, or spreading infection occurs, arrange urgent dental/oral-surgical assessment and treat for infection or other complications.  
49. If the socket fails to heal, implant integration fails, or recurrent infection develops, defer further invasive dental procedures and reassess antiresorptive management with oral surgery and osteoporosis specialists.  
50. Reassess osteoporosis treatment after dental healing, including whether to restart/continue alendronate, change therapy, or plan a formal bisphosphonate holiday based on total duration of therapy, DXA, fractures, and updated fracture risk.

1. Verify the exact alendronate regimen, adherence, start date, cumulative exposure, renal function history, and whether she has ever received IV bisphosphonate, denosumab, romosozumab, chemotherapy, systemic glucocorticoids, or antiangiogenic therapy.  

2. Confirm the indication for alendronate and reassess current fracture risk using prior fragility-fracture history, DXA results, body weight/BMI, falls history, vertebral imaging if indicated, and updated FRAX inputs.  

3. Obtain or review the most recent DXA scan (hip and lumbar spine) as a baseline for osteoporosis management and for estimating consequences of any prolonged interruption.  

4. Check serum calcium, albumin, creatinine/eGFR, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and possibly phosphorus before making major osteoporosis-medication changes.  

5. Review for secondary contributors to skeletal fragility, including hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, thyroid disease, malabsorption, renal disease, and chronic glucocorticoid exposure if not previously evaluated.  

6. Take a focused oral history for jaw pain, exposed bone, loose teeth, nonhealing extraction sites, drainage, swelling, altered sensation, ill-fitting dentures, and prior dental infections.  

7. Obtain a pre-procedure dental examination with periodontal assessment and dental radiographs/panoramic imaging as determined by the dentist or oral surgeon.  

8. Evaluate for active odontogenic infection, periodontal disease, periapical pathology, or abscess that may independently increase risk of delayed healing and MRONJ.  

9. Refer to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon before extraction/bone graft/implant planning, particularly because the procedure involves osseous manipulation and staged implant work.  

10. Communicate directly among the prescribing clinician, dentist/oral surgeon, and patient regarding osteoporosis indication, alendronate exposure of approximately one year, fracture risk, and the planned procedural timeline.  

11. Document that oral alendronate for osteoporosis carries a substantially lower MRONJ risk than oncology-dose IV antiresorptive therapy, while acknowledging that the planned extraction and graft are local risk factors.  

12. Discuss proceeding with dental extraction without interrupting alendronate, given the limited evidence that a short oral-bisphosphonate interruption changes MRONJ risk.  

13. Discuss continuing alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly (or her verified prescribed dose) through extraction, grafting, and implant placement if fracture-risk concerns outweigh uncertain benefit of interruption.  

14. Discuss holding alendronate immediately before the extraction or after the last scheduled weekly dose, with no pre-procedure delay, if the clinicians and patient elect a precautionary pause despite uncertain benefit.  

15. Discuss a time-limited pre-procedure alendronate hold of approximately 2 months before extraction as an alternative protocol sometimes used in higher-concern situations, while recognizing that skeletal retention makes short holidays biologically uncertain.  

16. Discuss deferring the extraction/graft/implant until after a longer alendronate interruption only if the dental procedure is elective and the anticipated dental benefit outweighs the increased fracture concern from treatment interruption.  

17. Avoid an extended alendronate holiday solely for dental reasons unless osteoporosis specialists judge her fracture risk to be acceptably low during the interruption.  

18. If alendronate is held, define an explicit restart criterion, such as complete mucosal epithelialization and absence of pain, drainage, exposed bone, or infection at the extraction/graft site.  

19. Consider resuming alendronate after soft-tissue healing, commonly around 6–8 weeks after extraction if healing is uncomplicated, rather than waiting for complete osseous implant integration.  

20. Consider delaying alendronate resumption until the oral surgeon confirms stable graft healing and implant-site readiness if the procedure is complex or healing is delayed.  

21. If a prolonged interruption is anticipated, obtain endocrinology, osteoporosis-specialist, or geriatrics input regarding fracture-prevention alternatives and the shortest acceptable interruption duration.  

22. Do not use serum C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) or other bone-turnover markers as a stand-alone predictor of MRONJ risk or as the sole determinant of when to hold or resume alendronate.  

23. Consider obtaining a bone-turnover marker only if an osteoporosis specialist believes it may help assess general treatment effect or adherence, while not presenting it as a validated dental-clearance test.  

24. Continue nonpharmacologic osteoporosis measures during any interruption: adequate dietary calcium targeting roughly 1,000–1,200 mg/day total intake, vitamin D supplementation sufficient to maintain an adequate level, weight-bearing activity as safely tolerated, and fall-prevention measures.  

25. Review alendronate administration technique if it is continued or resumed: take with plain water on an empty stomach, remain upright for at least 30 minutes, and avoid food or other medications during that interval.  

26. Consider whether switching from alendronate to another osteoporosis medication before dental work would add benefit; avoid switching to denosumab solely to reduce MRONJ concern because denosumab also carries MRONJ risk and cannot be interrupted without rebound-fracture planning.  

27. Avoid initiating IV zoledronic acid or denosumab during an elective extraction/graft/implant sequence unless fracture risk requires urgent antiresorptive therapy and the dental and osteoporosis teams agree on timing.  

28. If oral alendronate must be discontinued for an extended period and fracture risk is judged very high, discuss an anabolic osteoporosis strategy (for example teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily, if otherwise appropriate) with an osteoporosis specialist rather than leaving her untreated indefinitely.  

29. Review aspirin indication and dose, particularly whether it is being used for secondary prevention after TIA.  

30. Coordinate aspirin management with the prescribing clinician and oral surgeon; consider continuing low-dose aspirin for a routine dental extraction when thrombotic risk outweighs manageable bleeding risk.  

31. If the proceduralist requests aspirin interruption, obtain explicit approval from the clinician managing her cerebrovascular risk rather than stopping aspirin independently.  

32. Continue atorvastatin at the verified prescribed dose unless a separate perioperative issue arises.  

33. Use an atraumatic extraction technique with minimization of periosteal stripping and bone trauma, as feasible for the involved tooth and graft plan.  

34. Consider primary mucosal closure or local flap coverage of the extraction site when technically feasible to reduce exposed bone and promote healing.  

35. Consider staging the treatment—extraction and healing first, followed by grafting and later implant placement—rather than performing extraction, graft, and implant placement simultaneously if local healing risk is a concern.  

36. Consider whether a removable prosthesis, bridge, or no implant restoration is an acceptable alternative if the oral surgeon believes graft/implant placement would carry unacceptable local risk.  

37. Use local hemostatic measures as needed, such as pressure, sutures, absorbable hemostatic material, or tranexamic-acid mouth-rinse protocols if clinically appropriate, especially if aspirin is continued.  

38. Consider perioperative antibiotic therapy only according to the oral surgeon’s assessment of infection risk, grafting complexity, and local practice; avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotics in the absence of infection.  

39. Consider chlorhexidine oral rinse (for example 0.12% rinse as directed by the dental surgeon) before and/or after surgery if not contraindicated, with counseling about staining and altered taste.  

40. Counsel on meticulous oral hygiene, gentle postoperative cleaning as instructed, avoiding smoking and tobacco exposure, maintaining nutrition and hydration, and promptly reporting delayed healing or infection.  

41. Counsel the patient to seek urgent dental/oral-surgical review for exposed bone persisting more than 8 weeks, increasing jaw pain, swelling, purulent drainage, fever, numbness, loose teeth, or a nonhealing extraction socket.  

42. Schedule oral-surgery follow-up within approximately 1–2 weeks after extraction and again until mucosal closure and graft-site healing are documented.  

43. Reassess the planned timing of graft placement and implant placement at each postoperative visit; defer the next stage if there is incomplete mucosal healing, infection, exposed bone, or unexplained pain.  

44. If suspected MRONJ develops, obtain prompt oral and maxillofacial surgery evaluation, assess with appropriate dental imaging, treat infection/pain conservatively or surgically as indicated, and reconsider antiresorptive timing jointly with osteoporosis specialists.  

45. If healing is uncomplicated and alendronate was not interrupted, continue routine osteoporosis follow-up with reassessment of fracture risk, falls, calcium/vitamin D status, medication tolerance, and interval DXA typically within 1–2 years or sooner if clinically indicated.

1. Verify the exact alendronate regimen, dose, adherence, start date, and cumulative exposure (approximately 1 year reported).  
2. Confirm that alendronate is being used at an osteoporosis dose rather than an oncology/high-dose intravenous bisphosphonate regimen.  
3. Obtain the indication and baseline bone data supporting treatment, including prior fragility fractures, DXA T-scores, height loss, and prior vertebral imaging if available.  
4. Recalculate fracture risk using current clinical information and FRAX, recognizing that FRAX may underestimate risk in advanced age/low body weight or vertebral fracture.  
5. Review whether she meets criteria for “very high” versus “high” fracture risk, which may affect the acceptability of a treatment interruption.  
6. Ask specifically about prior jaw radiation, oral cancer, chemotherapy, chronic glucocorticoid use, diabetes, immunosuppression, smoking, heavy alcohol use, or prior MRONJ.  
7. Document any oral symptoms before the procedure, including jaw pain, exposed bone, nonhealing ulcers, loose teeth, drainage, numbness, or swelling.  
8. Obtain a preoperative dental/oral surgery evaluation, including assessment for periodontal disease, active dental infection, denture trauma, and oral hygiene.  
9. Obtain appropriate dental imaging (periapical films and/or panoramic radiograph; cone-beam CT if the oral surgeon believes it is needed for graft/implant planning).  
10. Refer or communicate directly with the oral surgeon/dentist regarding the patient’s osteoporosis-dose alendronate exposure and estimated MRONJ risk.  
11. Consider consultation with an endocrinologist, osteoporosis specialist, or primary clinician managing bone health if the decision to interrupt antiresorptive therapy is uncertain.  
12. Counsel that MRONJ risk with oral alendronate for osteoporosis is low, particularly after only about 1 year of therapy, but is not zero.  
13. Counsel that tooth extraction, bone grafting, infection, poor oral hygiene, and implant surgery can increase local MRONJ risk.  
14. Counsel that stopping alendronate briefly may not rapidly remove its skeletal effects because bisphosphonates remain incorporated in bone for years.  
15. Counsel that professional societies differ in the strength of support for a pre-procedure bisphosphonate “drug holiday,” and evidence that it prevents MRONJ is limited.  
16. Continue alendronate without interruption through extraction, grafting, and implant placement as one reasonable management option for a patient on short-duration oral therapy.  
17. Alternatively, hold alendronate immediately once the procedure is scheduled, if the treating clinicians and patient prioritize reducing theoretical MRONJ risk despite limited evidence of benefit.  
18. Alternatively, hold alendronate for approximately 2 months before extraction if the procedure can safely be deferred and a more conservative oral-surgery protocol is chosen.  
19. Avoid delaying urgent extraction or treatment of active odontogenic infection solely to complete a preoperative alendronate hold.  
20. If alendronate is held, resume only after extraction and graft sites have achieved complete mucosal/soft-tissue healing and there is no exposed bone, drainage, or infection.  
21. Use a minimum post-extraction reassessment interval of approximately 6–8 weeks before considering alendronate resumption if a hold strategy is used.  
22. Delay alendronate resumption beyond 6–8 weeks if healing is incomplete, bone remains exposed, infection persists, or additional invasive oral surgery is planned.  
23. If implant placement is staged after the extraction/bone graft, coordinate whether alendronate is resumed after graft healing or remains held until implant surgery and subsequent soft-tissue healing.  
24. Consider limiting any elective drug interruption to the shortest feasible duration because of her age/low-weight fracture risk.  
25. Do not use serum CTX, urine NTX, or other bone-turnover markers as a validated test to predict individual MRONJ risk or determine surgical timing.  
26. Do not automatically substitute another potent antiresorptive agent, such as denosumab or intravenous zoledronic acid, during an alendronate interruption solely for dental-procedure coverage.  
27. If denosumab is being considered as a future alternative, avoid starting it immediately around the dental procedure without a long-term dosing/discontinuation plan because missed doses can cause rebound vertebral fracture risk.  
28. Consider whether anabolic osteoporosis therapy (such as teriparatide or abaloparatide) is appropriate for her overall fracture risk if prolonged antiresorptive interruption is contemplated; assess contraindications before use.  
29. Continue nonpharmacologic bone-health measures during any alendronate hold, including adequate calcium intake from diet/supplements and vitamin D adequacy.  
30. Check serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and replete deficiency before or during the perioperative period if clinically indicated.  
31. Check serum calcium and renal function if they have not been recently assessed for osteoporosis-treatment safety and to guide future therapy.  
32. Reinforce correct alendronate administration when resumed: take fasting with plain water, remain upright for at least 30 minutes, and avoid food, beverages, and other medications during that interval.  
33. Review whether upper gastrointestinal symptoms, dysphagia, inability to remain upright, renal impairment, or other factors provide an independent reason to stop or change alendronate.  
34. Continue atorvastatin unless the procedural clinician identifies a separate indication to change it.  
35. Review aspirin indication and dose, recognizing that she has a history of TIA and may be taking aspirin for secondary stroke prevention.  
36. Coordinate aspirin management with the oral surgeon and the clinician managing her cerebrovascular risk; avoid stopping secondary-prevention aspirin without a clear procedural plan.  
37. Consider continuing low-dose aspirin through routine extraction if the oral surgeon judges local hemostatic measures sufficient, rather than exposing her to avoidable thrombotic risk.  
38. If aspirin interruption is requested for an unusually extensive procedure, define the exact stop and restart dates with the prescriber and oral surgeon rather than allowing an open-ended hold.  
39. Use atraumatic extraction technique and primary soft-tissue closure where feasible, as determined by the oral surgeon.  
40. Treat active periodontal or periapical infection before or at the time of extraction using dental source control; use antibiotics only when clinically indicated by the dental surgeon rather than solely because of alendronate exposure.  
41. Consider chlorhexidine mouth rinse before and after the procedure if prescribed by the oral surgeon as part of the local surgical protocol.  
42. Counsel on meticulous oral hygiene, smoking avoidance, adequate nutrition/protein intake, and avoiding trauma to the surgical site during healing.  
43. Arrange postoperative oral-surgery follow-up within approximately 1–2 weeks to assess early wound healing and again until epithelial closure is confirmed.  
44. Arrange follow-up with the osteoporosis prescriber around 6–8 weeks after the procedure to document healing status and make an explicit alendronate restart decision.  
45. Monitor for MRONJ warning signs after extraction or implant work: exposed bone or a fistula probing to bone lasting more than 8 weeks, persistent pain, swelling, purulence, numbness, loose teeth, or delayed healing.  
46. If exposed bone, nonhealing mucosa, drainage, or suspected MRONJ develops, hold further elective invasive dental work and urgently refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery.  
47. If suspected MRONJ occurs, obtain specialist-directed imaging and manage with oral hygiene measures, antimicrobial rinses, pain control, treatment of secondary infection when present, and surgical debridement only as clinically indicated.  
48. If the extraction/graft is elective and her fracture risk is reassessed as extremely high (for example, recent vertebral/hip fragility fracture or very low T-score), discuss deferring elective implant work or proceeding without an extended alendronate interruption.  
49. If a prolonged alendronate hold exceeds several months because of delayed healing or multiple staged dental procedures, reassess fracture-prevention strategy, fall risk, calcium/vitamin D status, and need for alternative osteoporosis therapy.  
50. Document a shared decision with the patient, osteoporosis prescriber, and oral surgeon specifying whether alendronate is continued or held, the planned restart criterion, and responsibility for follow-up.

1. **Diagnostics:** Verify the exact alendronate formulation, dose (for example, 70 mg orally weekly), start date, adherence, and cumulative exposure; document that exposure has been approximately 1 year.  
2. **Diagnostics:** Confirm that alendronate is being used for osteoporosis/osteopenia rather than for malignancy-related bone disease or another high-dose intravenous bisphosphonate indication.  
3. **Diagnostics:** Obtain or review the most recent DXA scan, including hip and lumbar spine T-scores.  
4. **Diagnostics:** Recalculate fracture risk using FRAX with current weight, age, prior fracture history, smoking, glucocorticoid exposure, alcohol use, rheumatoid arthritis, and secondary osteoporosis factors.  
5. **Diagnostics:** Review for vertebral compression fractures by history, height loss, kyphosis, or available spine imaging.  
6. **Diagnostics:** Consider vertebral fracture assessment or spine radiographs if there is unexplained height loss, back pain, or suspected occult vertebral fracture.  
7. **Diagnostics:** Check serum calcium, albumin, creatinine/eGFR, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase as osteoporosis-treatment baseline data if not recently available.  
8. **Diagnostics:** Evaluate for secondary contributors to low bone density when clinically indicated, such as CBC, TSH, PTH, testosterone, celiac testing, or serum protein electrophoresis.  
9. **Diagnostics:** Obtain a detailed dental/oral examination and dental radiographs or cone-beam CT as determined by the oral surgeon to define infection, periodontal disease, bone quality, and extraction complexity.  
10. **Diagnostics:** Assess for active odontogenic infection, periodontal abscess, nonhealing mucosal lesions, exposed bone, fistula, or pre-existing jaw osteonecrosis before surgery.  
11. **Diagnostics:** Evaluate suspicious oral lesions for malignancy or other causes of jaw pathology before attributing findings to possible MRONJ.  
12. **Diagnostics:** Document MRONJ risk modifiers, including diabetes, tobacco/nicotine exposure, glucocorticoids, chemotherapy, antiangiogenic therapy, immunosuppression, poor oral hygiene, and ill-fitting dentures.  
13. **Diagnostics:** Verify there is no current or prior exposure to denosumab, intravenous zoledronic acid, pamidronate, romosozumab, or cancer-directed antiresorptive treatment.  
14. **Diagnostics:** Avoid using serum CTX or other bone-turnover markers as a sole determinant of MRONJ risk or timing of extraction, because predictive value is uncertain.  
15. **Medications:** Continue alendronate without interruption through extraction, grafting, and implant placement as an option, given low MRONJ incidence with short-duration oral bisphosphonate therapy.  
16. **Medications:** Hold alendronate for approximately 2 months before extraction as a debated elective drug-holiday option, particularly if the oral surgeon considers the procedure extensive or infection risk high.  
17. **Medications:** Hold alendronate beginning immediately if surgery is imminent and a preoperative 2-month interval is not feasible, recognizing that a shorter hold may not materially change skeletal bisphosphonate exposure.  
18. **Medications:** If alendronate is held, defer resumption until extraction sockets and grafted areas have achieved complete mucosal and clinical osseous healing, commonly at least 6–8 weeks after surgery.  
19. **Medications:** If alendronate is held and implant placement is staged, defer restarting until after implant placement and adequate soft-tissue/bony healing, if the fracture-risk tradeoff is considered acceptable.  
20. **Medications:** If alendronate is held, resume after the oral surgeon documents no exposed bone, drainage, infection, delayed epithelialization, or other healing complication.  
21. **Medications:** Consider continuing or promptly resuming alendronate if reassessment shows very high fracture risk, recent fragility fracture, vertebral fracture, or rapidly declining bone density.  
22. **Medications:** Avoid substituting denosumab solely to permit a bisphosphonate holiday, because denosumab discontinuation/delay can cause rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures.  
23. **Medications:** Consider endocrinology-directed alternative osteoporosis therapy, such as teriparatide or abaloparatide, if he is ultimately determined to be at very high fracture risk and prolonged interruption of antiresorptive therapy is desired.  
24. **Medications:** Continue atorvastatin unless another perioperative issue arises; it does not require interruption for routine dental extraction.  
25. **Medications:** Review aspirin indication with the clinician managing his prior TIA before any interruption; avoid stopping secondary-prevention aspirin without explicit risk-benefit discussion.  
26. **Medications:** Continue low-dose aspirin during simple extraction/implant surgery as an option, with local hemostatic measures, rather than exposing him to thrombotic risk from interruption.  
27. **Medications:** If the proceduralist requests aspirin interruption for a particularly extensive operation, coordinate with neurology/primary care and specify the stop and restart dates rather than allowing indefinite discontinuation.  
28. **Medications:** Provide perioperative analgesia with acetaminophen, such as 500–1,000 mg orally every 6–8 hours as needed (maximum adjusted for liver disease/alcohol use), if appropriate.  
29. **Medications:** Use NSAIDs only selectively, considering age, aspirin use, renal function, gastrointestinal risk, and bleeding risk.

47. Schedule additional oral-surgery follow-up around 6–8 weeks, or sooner as directed, to document complete healing before restarting alendronate if it was withheld.

1. Confirm the osteoporosis indication, baseline DXA results, prior fragility fractures, and calculated fracture risk before changing antiresorptive therapy.  

2. Verify the exact alendronate regimen (for example, 70 mg orally once weekly), start date, adherence, and cumulative duration of exposure.  

3. Confirm that alendronate is being used at an osteoporosis dose rather than a high-dose oncology regimen.  

4. Obtain a focused MRONJ risk history, including prior head/neck radiation, cancer, chemotherapy, chronic systemic glucocorticoid use, diabetes, smoking, immunosuppression, poor oral hygiene, periodontal disease, and prior MRONJ.  

5. Review the dental indication and urgency for extraction, bone grafting, and implant placement with the treating dentist/oral surgeon.  

6. Obtain dental imaging as determined by the oral surgeon (for example, periapical radiographs or cone-beam CT) to define infection, bone quality, extraction complexity, and implant planning.  

7. Evaluate for active periodontal disease, periapical infection, denture trauma, or other oral inflammatory conditions that may independently increase MRONJ risk.  

8. Obtain a baseline oral examination documenting exposed bone, fistula, nonhealing ulceration, swelling, purulence, loose teeth, pain, or altered sensation before the procedure.  

9. Refer to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for procedural planning if extraction/grafting/implant complexity or MRONJ concern exceeds the dentist’s usual scope.  

10. Communicate directly between the osteoporosis prescriber and dentist/oral surgeon regarding alendronate duration, fracture risk, and the planned extent of dentoalveolar surgery.  

11. Discuss proceeding with extraction without interrupting oral alendronate, given the low MRONJ incidence with osteoporosis-dose oral bisphosphonates and treatment duration of approximately one year.  

12. Discuss a pre-procedural alendronate hold as an individualized option, recognizing that the evidence that a brief drug holiday reduces MRONJ risk is limited and debated.  

13. If a pre-procedural hold is chosen, consider stopping alendronate immediately rather than waiting for a prolonged interval, because bisphosphonate remains in bone for years and short holds may have limited biologic effect.  

14. If a conservative drug-holiday strategy is chosen, consider holding alendronate for approximately 2 months before elective invasive dental surgery.  

15. Consider a longer pre-procedure interruption only if additional major MRONJ risk factors are identified, with explicit reassessment of the competing fracture risk.  

16. Avoid assuming that serum C-terminal telopeptide (CTX) or other bone turnover markers can reliably predict MRONJ risk or determine timing of surgery.  

17. Avoid using a normal CTX result as clearance to proceed with extraction or implant placement.  

18. Consider obtaining serum calcium, creatinine/eGFR, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, phosphorus, and alkaline phosphatase if osteoporosis management or alternative antiresorptive therapy is being reconsidered.  

19. Continue adequate calcium intake through diet and/or supplements, targeting approximately 1,200 mg/day total intake unless contraindicated.  

20. Continue vitamin D supplementation or adjust it to maintain adequate vitamin D status, commonly targeting 25-hydroxyvitamin D of at least 20–30 ng/mL depending on local practice.  

21. Maintain nonpharmacologic fracture-prevention measures during any alendronate interruption, including weight-bearing/resistance exercise as tolerated, fall prevention, vision review, and home-safety measures.  

22. Do not routinely substitute denosumab immediately before or around the dental procedure solely to replace alendronate, because denosumab also carries MRONJ risk and delayed doses/discontinuation can cause rebound vertebral fracture risk.  

23. Consider temporary use of an anabolic osteoporosis agent only if her overall fracture risk is very high, prolonged antiresorptive interruption is contemplated, or she develops an indication for escalation of osteoporosis therapy.  

24. Consider teriparatide or abaloparatide as an alternative osteoporosis strategy in selected high-fracture-risk patients if antiresorptive treatment must be avoided for an extended period, after evaluating contraindications and coverage.  

25. Consider romosozumab only after assessing cardiovascular history and stroke/TIA risk, because her prior TIA may make this option less favorable or contraindicated depending on risk assessment.  

26. Ensure the oral surgeon uses atraumatic extraction technique, preservation of viable soft tissue, smoothing of sharp bone edges as needed, and primary mucosal closure when feasible.  

27. Consider socket preservation/bone grafting only after discussion of whether the graft and planned implant meaningfully improve function versus the additional surgical burden.  

28. Consider delaying implant placement until the extraction site has demonstrated uncomplicated soft-tissue and bony healing.  

29. Consider a staged approach—extraction first, healing assessment, then grafting or implant—rather than immediate implant placement if local infection, poor tissue quality, or concern for impaired healing is present.  

30. Consider non-implant restorative alternatives, such as a removable partial denture, fixed bridge, or no replacement, if the surgical risk-benefit balance is unfavorable.  

31. Use perioperative antimicrobial mouth rinse, such as chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse, according to the oral surgeon’s protocol before and after invasive dental treatment.  

32. Consider perioperative systemic antibiotics when indicated by the complexity of extraction, presence of infection, bone grafting, or surgeon preference; select agent, dose, and duration based on dental standards, allergies, and renal function.  

33. Avoid prolonged prophylactic antibiotic courses without a specific dental indication because of adverse effects, resistance, and C. difficile risk.  

34. Continue low-dose aspirin unless the dentist/oral surgeon and prescribing clinician determine that bleeding risk from the specific procedure outweighs thrombotic risk from interruption, particularly given her TIA history.  

35. Avoid nonselective NSAIDs or use them cautiously for post-procedure pain if bleeding risk, renal function, GI risk, or concurrent aspirin use is a concern; consider acetaminophen as a primary analgesic option.  

36. Counsel her that osteoporosis-dose oral alendronate for about one year is associated with a very low absolute MRONJ risk, while stopping osteoporosis therapy may increase fracture risk over time.  

37. Counsel her that untreated oral infection and traumatic dental disease may themselves pose greater risk to jaw healing than appropriately performed necessary extraction.  

38. Counsel her to report persistent pain, swelling, drainage, exposed bone, a nonhealing extraction socket, numbness/tingling, loose teeth, foul taste, or fever promptly after the procedure.  

39. Counsel her to maintain meticulous oral hygiene, routine dental cleanings, smoking avoidance, adequate nutrition, and denture adjustment if applicable.  

40. Schedule post-extraction follow-up with the dentist/oral surgeon within approximately 1–2 weeks, with additional visits until mucosal healing is confirmed.  

41. Document the degree of extraction-site healing before resuming alendronate if a drug holiday was selected.  

42. If alendronate was held, consider resuming the prior dose once the oral surgeon confirms satisfactory soft-tissue healing and absence of infection, often after approximately 6–8 weeks but individualized to healing and procedure extent.  

43. If bone grafting or implant placement has delayed healing, defer alendronate resumption until the surgical site is clinically stable, while reassessing fracture risk if interruption becomes prolonged.  

44. If healing is uncomplicated and no drug holiday was selected, continue alendronate on its usual weekly schedule through the extraction and subsequent implant-related care.  

45. If exposed bone or a fistula persists for more than 8 weeks after antiresorptive exposure and no jaw radiation history is present, evaluate for possible MRONJ and refer urgently to oral and maxillofacial surgery.  

46. If there is progressive facial swelling, purulent drainage, fever, dysphagia, airway symptoms, or rapidly worsening pain after extraction, arrange urgent dental/oral surgery assessment and emergency evaluation when indicated.  

47. If MRONJ is diagnosed or strongly suspected, hold further antiresorptive dosing pending multidisciplinary discussion among oral surgery, dentistry, and the osteoporosis prescriber.  

48. If alendronate interruption extends beyond several months, reassess fracture risk, falls, interval fractures, calcium/vitamin D status, and the need for an alternative osteoporosis treatment plan.

1. Repeat a fasting early-morning serum prolactin level, ideally drawn 2–3 hours after waking.  

2. Ensure repeat prolactin sampling follows 20–30 minutes of quiet rest before phlebotomy.  

3. Avoid vigorous exercise, sexual activity, nipple/chest stimulation, acute pain, and major stress for 24 hours before repeat prolactin testing.  

4. Obtain serial prolactin samples through an indwelling catheter (for example, at 0, 20, and 40 minutes) if stress-related transient elevation remains a concern.  

5. Order macroprolactin testing (polyethylene glycol precipitation or laboratory equivalent) to identify macroprolactinemia.  

6. Ask specifically about intermittent or recently stopped medicines that can raise prolactin, including antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antidepressants, opioids, verapamil, estrogens, and antiemetics.  

7. Ask specifically about nonprescription products, bodybuilding agents, testosterone/anabolic steroids, cannabis, alcohol, supplements, and biotin-containing products.  

8. Verify the prolactin assay with the laboratory if results are discordant with the clinical picture or if assay interference is suspected.  

9. Obtain serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (free T4) to exclude primary hypothyroidism as a reversible cause of hyperprolactinemia.  

10. Obtain serum creatinine/eGFR to confirm normal renal function.  

11. Obtain liver enzymes and hepatic function testing if liver disease, heavy alcohol use, or other hepatic risk factors are suspected.  

12. Obtain total testosterone on two separate fasting morning samples to characterize androgen status.  

13. Obtain sex hormone-binding globulin and calculate free testosterone, or measure free testosterone with an appropriate validated assay, if total testosterone is borderline or SHBG abnormality is suspected.  

14. Obtain luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) to distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism.  

15. Obtain estradiol if obesity, gynecomastia, abnormal gonadotropins, or altered androgen metabolism is suspected.  

16. Obtain baseline complete blood count and metabolic panel if testosterone replacement or dopamine-agonist therapy may later be considered.  

17. Screen for other pituitary hormone abnormalities with morning serum cortisol, with further adrenal testing if cortisol is low or equivocal.  

18. Obtain insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) as screening for growth hormone excess if a pituitary lesion is found or if suggestive clinical features are present.  

19. Assess for symptoms of hypogonadism, including decreased libido, infertility, fatigue, reduced shaving frequency, loss of body hair, gynecomastia, and reduced muscle mass.  

20. Perform a focused examination for gynecomastia, galactorrhea, testicular size/consistency, visual fields by confrontation, and features of thyroid or pituitary disease.  

21. Perform a cardiovascular and metabolic erectile-dysfunction assessment, including blood pressure, BMI/waist circumference, fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c, and lipid profile.  

22. Screen for psychogenic, relationship-related, sleep-related, depressive, anxiety-related, and substance-related contributors to erectile dysfunction.  

23. Obtain a focused headache and neurologic history, including new persistent headache, cranial nerve symptoms, visual changes, polyuria/polydipsia, or symptoms of pituitary hormone deficiency.  

24. Order a dedicated pituitary/sellar MRI with and without gadolinium contrast to evaluate for pituitary microadenoma or other sellar/parasellar pathology.  

25. Defer pituitary MRI initially while confirming persistent monomeric hyperprolactinemia and excluding secondary causes such as hypothyroidism, assay artifact, macroprolactinemia, and occult medication exposure.  

26. Obtain pituitary MRI promptly if repeat monomeric prolactin remains elevated without a reversible explanation.  

27. Obtain pituitary MRI urgently if visual field symptoms, diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, severe or progressive headache, neurologic deficits, or other evidence of mass effect develops.  

28. Arrange formal automated visual-field testing if MRI shows a lesion near or contacting the optic chiasm, or if visual symptoms arise.  

29. Refer to endocrinology on a routine-to-expedited basis for persistent unexplained hyperprolactinemia, suspected pituitary adenoma, hypogonadism, or uncertainty regarding MRI interpretation.  

30. Refer to ophthalmology/neuro-ophthalmology urgently for formal visual-field assessment if any visual complaint or chiasmal compression is identified.  

31. Refer to urology or sexual-medicine services for persistent erectile dysfunction despite endocrine evaluation and initial risk-factor management.  

32. Refer to reproductive endocrinology/andrology or obtain semen analysis if fertility is desired, particularly before testosterone treatment is considered.  

33. Treat confirmed primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine, with dose individualized to TSH, free T4, age, body size, and cardiovascular status.  

34. Recheck prolactin after correction of hypothyroidism or another identified reversible cause to document normalization or persistence.  

35. Discontinue, substitute, or reduce any subsequently identified prolactin-elevating medication when clinically feasible, in coordination with the prescribing clinician.  

36. If a prolactinoma is confirmed and treatment is indicated, initiate cabergoline, such as 0.25 mg orally twice weekly, with titration according to prolactin response, symptoms, and tolerability.  

37. Use bromocriptine as an alternative dopamine agonist for confirmed prolactinoma when cabergoline is unavailable, contraindicated, not tolerated, or when a different risk-benefit profile is preferred.  

38. Monitor for dopamine-agonist adverse effects including nausea, orthostatic dizziness, headache, fatigue, mood changes, impulse-control symptoms, and rare psychiatric effects.  

39. Recheck serum prolactin approximately 4–8 weeks after starting or changing dopamine-agonist treatment, then at intervals based on biochemical response.  

40. Repeat pituitary MRI after medical therapy for a confirmed adenoma at an interval determined by lesion size, prolactin trend, symptoms, and endocrine specialist input.  

41. Refer to pituitary neurosurgery if there is visual compromise, hemorrhage/apoplexy, progressive mass effect, dopamine-agonist resistance or intolerance, diagnostic uncertainty requiring tissue diagnosis, or patient preference after counseling.  

42. Consider transsphenoidal pituitary surgery for a confirmed adenoma meeting neurosurgical indications.  

43. Avoid initiating testosterone replacement solely for erectile dysfunction until repeat testosterone testing, gonadotropin assessment, fertility goals, and the cause of hyperprolactinemia are clarified.  

44. If persistent symptomatic testosterone deficiency is confirmed and fertility is not desired, consider testosterone replacement using an appropriate formulation and dose, with hematocrit, PSA/prostate-risk assessment as appropriate, testosterone level, and symptom monitoring.  

45. If fertility is desired and secondary hypogonadism is present, avoid exogenous testosterone and consider endocrine-directed fertility-preserving options such as gonadotropin therapy or selective estrogen receptor modulator therapy when appropriate.  

46. Offer a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction after cardiovascular and medication contraindication review, such as sildenafil 25–50 mg orally about 1 hour before sexual activity, titratable up to 100 mg as needed.  

47. Avoid PDE5 inhibitors in combination with nitrates and assess for hypotension risk, unstable cardiovascular disease, and interacting alpha-blocker therapy before prescribing.  

48. Counsel regarding exercise, weight management, smoking cessation, alcohol moderation, sleep optimization, diabetes/lipid/blood-pressure control, and psychosocial/relationship interventions as part of erectile-dysfunction management.  

49. Arrange follow-up within approximately 4–12 weeks to review repeat prolactin, macroprolactin, thyroid/renal testing, testosterone-pituitary axis results, erectile-function response, and the need for MRI or specialty care.  

50. Advise urgent evaluation if he develops sudden severe headache, vomiting, new visual loss or diplopia, confusion, syncope, focal neurologic symptoms, or symptoms suggestive of pituitary apoplexy.

### Diagnostics
1. Repeat fasting morning serum prolactin after avoiding nipple/chest stimulation, strenuous exercise, sexual activity, acute illness, and significant stress for 24 hours before testing.  
2. Obtain the repeat prolactin with the patient resting quietly for 20–30 minutes before phlebotomy.  
3. Request laboratory evaluation for macroprolactin (polyethylene glycol precipitation or equivalent assay) to identify macroprolactinemia.  
4. Confirm that prolactin testing was not affected by assay interference; consider repeat measurement using an alternate assay platform if results remain unexplained.  
5. Obtain serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (free T4) to exclude primary hypothyroidism.  
6. Obtain morning total testosterone, ideally between 7 and 10 AM.  
7. Repeat total testosterone on a separate morning if the initial value is low or borderline low.  
8. Obtain sex hormone-binding globulin and calculate or measure free testosterone if total testosterone is borderline or altered by abnormal SHBG.  
9. Obtain luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) to distinguish primary from secondary hypogonadism.  
10. Obtain serum estradiol if there are symptoms or examination findings suggesting estrogen excess, obesity-related aromatization, or gynecomastia.  
11. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel including creatinine/eGFR and liver enzymes to exclude renal or hepatic causes of hyperprolactinemia.  
12. Obtain fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c as part of erectile-dysfunction and cardiometabolic assessment.  
13. Obtain fasting lipid panel as part of cardiovascular risk evaluation related to erectile dysfunction.  
14. Measure blood pressure, BMI, and waist circumference.  
15. Review for symptoms of hypogonadism, including reduced libido, infertility, reduced morning erections, fatigue, low energy, reduced shaving frequency, gynecomastia, and decreased body hair.  
16. Perform focused neurologic examination, including cranial nerves and visual fields by confrontation.  
17. Consider formal automated visual-field testing if there is a pituitary lesion, visual complaint, abnormal confrontation examination, or concern for optic-chiasm compression.  
18. Review all prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, supplements, recreational drugs, and recent antiemetic/antipsychotic exposure that can increase prolactin.  
19. Specifically ask about metoclopramide, domperidone, antipsychotics, SSRIs/SNRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, opioids, verapamil, methyldopa, cimetidine, estrogens, and cannabis.  
20. Ask about chest-wall trauma, herpes zoster, surgery, burns, chronic nipple stimulation, and seizure history as potential contributors to mild prolactin elevation.  
21. Obtain pituitary MRI with dedicated sellar protocol and gadolinium contrast to evaluate for pituitary adenoma.  
22. Consider deferring MRI until macroprolactin, thyroid disease, renal dysfunction, medication causes, and persistent true hyperprolactinemia have been clarified.  
23. If MRI is obtained, request assessment for microadenoma, macroadenoma, stalk deviation/compression, cavernous sinus involvement, and optic-chiasm proximity.  
24. If a pituitary lesion is found, obtain baseline pituitary-function testing including morning cortisol, ACTH as appropriate, insulin-like growth factor-1, free T4/TSH, LH/FSH, and testosterone.  
25. Consider semen analysis if fertility is currently desired or infertility is a concern.  

### Medications
26. Continue PRN albuterol for mild intermittent asthma if asthma remains controlled and no alternative cause of symptoms is suspected.  
27. Avoid initiating dopamine-agonist therapy until persistent monomeric hyperprolactinemia and a clinically relevant cause have been evaluated.  
28. If a prolactinoma or symptomatic persistent hyperprolactinemia is confirmed, consider cabergoline 0.25 mg orally once or twice weekly, with titration based on prolactin response and tolerability.  
29. If cabergoline is used, consider titration every 4–8 weeks toward normalization of prolactin, using the lowest effective dose.  
30. If cabergoline is unavailable, contraindicated, or not tolerated, consider bromocriptine 1.25–2.5 mg orally at bedtime initially, then titrate as tolerated.  
31. Counsel regarding dopamine-agonist adverse effects including nausea, orthostatic dizziness, headache, fatigue, mood change, and impulse-control symptoms.  
32. Screen for personal history of psychosis, mania, severe depression, or impulse-control disorder before starting a dopamine agonist.  
33. If a medication-associated cause of hyperprolactinemia is identified, consider stopping, reducing, or substituting the causative agent in coordination with the prescribing clinician.  
34. If testosterone deficiency is confirmed, evaluate and treat the cause before considering testosterone replacement therapy.

### Procedures
40. Arrange dedicated contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI if imaging is pursued after shared clinical decision-making.  
41. Obtain formal perimetry promptly if MRI demonstrates lesion contact with, compression of, or proximity to the optic chiasm.

### Referrals
44. Refer to endocrinology on a routine but timely basis for persistent unexplained hyperprolactinemia, interpretation of macroprolactin testing, pituitary imaging decisions, and management of any adenoma.  
45. Refer urgently to endocrinology and neurosurgery if MRI shows a macroadenoma with optic-chiasm compression, cavernous sinus involvement, pituitary apoplexy, or rapid symptom progression.

47. Refer to urology or sexual-medicine clinic if erectile dysfunction persists after endocrine and cardiovascular evaluation or if first-line ED therapy is ineffective.  
48. Refer to reproductive endocrinology/andrology or male infertility specialist if fertility is desired and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or abnormal semen analysis is found.  
49. Refer to primary care or cardiology for cardiovascular-risk assessment if diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, exertional symptoms, or elevated baseline cardiovascular risk is identified.  

### Counseling
50. Explain that prolactin values in the 27–30 ng/mL range represent mild elevation and can occur from physiologic variation, macroprolactin, hypothyroidism, medications, systemic illness, or pituitary disease.  
51. Discuss that absence of headache and visual symptoms lowers concern for a large compressive pituitary lesion but does not completely exclude a microadenoma.  
52. Explain the purpose, potential benefits, limitations, incidental findings, contrast exposure, and cost implications of pituitary MRI.  
53. Counsel on reporting new headache, visual blurring, loss of peripheral vision, diplopia, nausea/vomiting with severe headache, or neurologic deficits urgently.  
54. Counsel on lifestyle measures that may improve erectile function, including regular aerobic/resistance exercise, weight management, sleep optimization, smoking cessation, moderation of alcohol, and avoidance of recreational drugs.  
55. Discuss psychological, relationship, performance-anxiety, depression, sleep, and stress contributors to erectile dysfunction; consider validated screening for depression and anxiety.  
56. Advise avoiding unregulated testosterone products, “male enhancement” supplements, anabolic steroids, and dopamine-active supplements during evaluation.  

### Follow-up and Monitoring
57. Reassess prolactin after repeat testing and macroprolactin results are available, generally within several weeks.  
58. If no treatment is started and repeat monomeric prolactin remains mildly elevated, recheck prolactin in approximately 3–6 months.  
59. If cabergoline or bromocriptine is started, measure prolactin approximately 4–8 weeks after initiation and after each meaningful dose change.  
60. Monitor blood pressure, orthostatic symptoms, nausea, mood, compulsive behaviors, and sexual function during dopamine-agonist treatment.  
61. If a pituitary adenoma is identified and treated medically, repeat pituitary MRI at an interval based on tumor size and response, often around 6–12 months for a macroadenoma and about 1 year for a microadenoma.  
62. Monitor testosterone, gonadotropins, libido, morning erections, and erectile-function response after normalization or treatment of prolactin.  
63. If testosterone replacement is initiated, monitor hematocrit, testosterone concentration, PSA/prostate risk as age-appropriate, fertility goals, and clinical response.  

### Contingencies

18. Consider CT enterography or MR enterography if capsule endoscopy is contraindicated, nondiagnostic, retained, or if a small-bowel mass/inflammatory process is suspected.  
19. Consider device-assisted enteroscopy (single-balloon, double-balloon, or spiral enteroscopy) if capsule or imaging identifies a reachable small-bowel bleeding lesion requiring diagnosis or therapy.  
20. Consider push enteroscopy if a proximal jejunal lesion is suspected or if capsule findings localize pathology to the proximal small bowel.  
21. Reserve CT angiography, tagged red-cell imaging, or catheter angiography for development of overt or hemodynamically significant bleeding rather than isolated chronic occult blood loss.  
22. Refer to gastroenterology with nonemergent but expedited timing for evaluation of progressive iron-deficiency anemia despite prior EGD/colonoscopy and for selection/sequencing of repeat endoscopy versus small-bowel testing.  
23. Consider hematology referral if iron studies are atypical, anemia is disproportionate to demonstrated blood loss, there is poor response to iron replacement, or another hematologic disorder is suspected.  
24. Start or optimize oral iron replacement, such as ferrous sulfate 325 mg orally every other day or once daily as tolerated, with a planned reassessment of hemoglobin and iron indices.  
25. Consider alternate oral iron formulations or lower-frequency dosing if gastrointestinal intolerance limits adherence to ferrous sulfate.  
26. Administer intravenous iron, such as ferric carboxymaltose 750 mg IV on two doses at least 7 days apart or iron sucrose in divided doses, if oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, malabsorption is suspected, or faster repletion is needed.

36. Continue apixaban during the diagnostic workup if anemia remains stable and there is no active major bleeding, while recognizing the competing stroke risk associated with a CHADS-VASc score of 5.

38. If apixaban is held for major bleeding, consider reversal with andexanet alfa or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate according to local protocols, bleeding severity, availability, and thrombotic risk.  
39. Refer to cardiology/electrophysiology for discussion of long-term anticoagulation versus left atrial appendage closure, including whether the anemia represents a clinically meaningful contraindication or intolerance to indefinite anticoagulation.  
40. Evaluate left atrial appendage closure candidacy with review of nonvalvular AF status, transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac CT anatomy, left atrial appendage thrombus exclusion, vascular access feasibility, life expectancy, and procedural risk.  
41. Discuss that left atrial appendage closure typically still requires a short-term postimplant antithrombotic regimen, such as anticoagulation or dual antiplatelet therapy followed by antiplatelet therapy, which may still pose bleeding risk.

47. Establish urgent evaluation thresholds, including emergency assessment for hemodynamic symptoms, symptomatic anemia, overt bleeding, a substantial acute hemoglobin drop, or hemoglobin near or below a transfusion threshold individualized for CAD symptoms and clinical status.  
48. Consider red-blood-cell transfusion if anemia becomes symptomatic or severe, using an individualized threshold that accounts for coronary artery disease, active ischemic symptoms, hemodynamics, and hemoglobin trajectory.

14. Perform video capsule endoscopy to evaluate the small bowel for angioectasias, ulcers, tumors, Crohn disease, or other occult bleeding lesions.  

15. Consider CT enterography or MR enterography if capsule endoscopy is negative, contraindicated, retained, or if small-bowel mass/inflammatory disease is suspected.  

16. Obtain a patency capsule before video capsule endoscopy if there is concern for small-bowel stricture, obstruction, prior abdominal radiation, or Crohn disease.  

17. Pursue device-assisted enteroscopy (single-balloon, double-balloon, or spiral enteroscopy) if capsule or enterography identifies a treatable small-bowel lesion.

29. Avoid empiric off-label apixaban dose reduction solely for anemia if labeled dose-reduction criteria are not met.  

30. Check serum creatinine/eGFR, liver function, body weight, and interacting medications to confirm appropriate apixaban dosing and exposure.  

31. Review for strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors or inducers that could raise or lower apixaban concentrations.  

32. Hold apixaban for the minimum guideline-based interval before high-risk endoscopic interventions, with timing based on renal function and procedural bleeding risk.  

33. Resume apixaban promptly after endoscopy once hemostasis is secured, with timing individualized to whether biopsy, polypectomy, ablation, or treatment of an active lesion occurred.  

34. Avoid routine heparin bridging during temporary apixaban interruption for endoscopic procedures unless an exceptional thrombotic indication is identified.  

35. Refer to cardiology/electrophysiology or a structural-heart team for formal assessment of stroke prevention options in atrial fibrillation.  

36. Calculate and document HAS-BLED or another bleeding-risk assessment, while recognizing that bleeding scores do not by themselves determine whether anticoagulation should be stopped.  

37. Discuss that a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 5 confers substantial embolic stroke risk if anticoagulation is permanently discontinued.  

38. Assess whether the anemia represents clinically significant recurrent bleeding despite optimized GI evaluation and treatment, which may affect candidacy for left atrial appendage closure.  

39. Refer for left atrial appendage closure evaluation if there is recurrent major bleeding, transfusion dependence, inability to maintain anticoagulation, or an unacceptable long-term anticoagulation risk after multidisciplinary review.  

40. Obtain transesophageal echocardiography and/or cardiac CT as part of Watchman planning to assess left atrial appendage anatomy and exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.  

41. Review the need for temporary post-Watchman antithrombotic therapy, which may include short-term anticoagulation and/or antiplatelet therapy and can itself worsen bleeding risk.  

42. Consider alternative left atrial appendage closure strategies or surgical appendage exclusion only in consultation with structural cardiology/cardiac surgery when anatomy or antithrombotic constraints make standard Watchman treatment unsuitable.  

43. Optimize blood pressure control, including reassessment of amlodipine 5 mg daily and home blood-pressure readings, because uncontrolled hypertension increases hemorrhagic risk on anticoagulation.  

44. Counsel the patient to seek urgent evaluation for melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, syncope, new chest pain, dyspnea at rest, confusion, rapidly worsening fatigue, or signs of hemodynamic instability.  

45. Recheck hemoglobin, reticulocyte response, ferritin, and transferrin saturation about 2–4 weeks after initiating or changing iron therapy, then at intervals until stable.  

46. Escalate to urgent inpatient evaluation if hemoglobin falls rapidly, reaches a symptomatic/severely low range, overt bleeding develops, or there is hypotension, tachycardia, ischemic symptoms, or need for transfusion.

10. During repeat EGD, inspect specifically for Cameron lesions, gastric antral vascular ectasia, peptic ulcer disease, erosive gastritis, angioectasias, and duodenal lesions.  
11. Obtain gastric biopsies or noninvasive testing for *Helicobacter pylori* if not previously evaluated.

14. Consider anoscopy or colorectal examination to better characterize internal hemorrhoids and determine whether they plausibly account for the degree of iron-deficiency anemia.  
15. Proceed with video capsule endoscopy for small-bowel evaluation after negative or nondiagnostic high-quality EGD and colonoscopy.  
16. Use a patency capsule before video capsule endoscopy if there is concern for small-bowel obstruction, prior abdominal surgery, Crohn disease, or known strictures.  
17. Consider CT enterography or MR enterography to assess for small-bowel mass, inflammatory disease, or structural lesions, particularly if capsule endoscopy is contraindicated or nondiagnostic.  
18. Refer for device-assisted enteroscopy (single- or double-balloon enteroscopy) if capsule endoscopy identifies a potentially treatable small-bowel lesion.  
19. Treat small-bowel, gastric, or colonic angioectasias found on endoscopy with endoscopic therapy such as argon plasma coagulation, clipping, or other hemostatic intervention as anatomically appropriate.  
20. Reserve CT angiography, tagged red-blood-cell scan, or catheter angiography for development of overt or hemodynamically significant active GI bleeding rather than stable occult blood loss alone.  
21. Check fecal occult blood testing or fecal immunochemical testing only if it would clarify uncertainty about GI blood loss; do not use a negative result to exclude GI evaluation in confirmed iron-deficiency anemia.  
22. Start or continue oral iron replacement, such as ferrous sulfate 325 mg orally every other day or once daily as tolerated, with adjustment for constipation or gastrointestinal adverse effects.  
23. Consider intravenous iron replacement (for example iron sucrose or ferric carboxymaltose per local protocol) if oral iron is ineffective, poorly tolerated, malabsorbed, or insufficient to keep pace with ongoing losses.  
24. Recheck hemoglobin, reticulocyte response, ferritin, and transferrin saturation approximately 2–4 weeks after initiating or changing iron therapy, then at intervals based on response.

26. Review all medications for contributors to mucosal injury or bleeding, including aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, SSRIs/SNRIs, fish oil, herbal products, and alcohol use.  
27. Avoid nonselective NSAIDs and other unnecessary agents that increase GI bleeding risk.  
28. Confirm whether aspirin or a P2Y12 inhibitor remains indicated given the timing of prior coronary stenting and current CAD status; involve cardiology before stopping any antiplatelet therapy.  
29. If antiplatelet therapy is no longer required, consider discontinuation of aspirin or other antiplatelet therapy while maintaining the anticoagulation strategy appropriate for atrial fibrillation.  
30. Confirm that apixaban is being taken at the indicated atrial-fibrillation dose: typically 5 mg orally twice daily, reduced to 2.5 mg twice daily only when at least two of age 80 years or older, body weight 60 kg or less, and serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or greater are present.

32. Assess apixaban adherence, timing of doses, renal function, liver function, drug interactions, and use of CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors or inducers.  
33. Consider temporary interruption of apixaban only if there is clinically significant active bleeding, severe anemia requiring urgent evaluation, or a procedure requiring interruption, with a documented thromboembolic-risk plan.  
34. For elective high-risk endoscopic procedures, coordinate peri-procedural apixaban interruption based on renal function and procedural bleeding risk; generally avoid heparin bridging for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation unless a separate indication exists.  
35. Resume apixaban after endoscopy or endoscopic hemostasis according to procedural bleeding risk and adequacy of source control, with cardiology/GI coordination.  
36. Obtain cardiology or electrophysiology consultation to review stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5), bleeding history, CAD/stent-related antithrombotic needs, and long-term anticoagulation options.

38. Refer to a structural-heart/left atrial appendage closure program for Watchman or other LAA closure assessment if anemia represents recurrent clinically significant bleeding, anticoagulation becomes unsafe or intolerable, or a bleeding source cannot be controlled.  
39. During LAA closure evaluation, assess transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac CT suitability, left atrial appendage anatomy, left ventricular function, valvular status, existing atrial thrombus, vascular access, and procedural risk.  
40. Discuss that LAA closure generally requires a period of post-implant antithrombotic therapy (often anticoagulation and/or antiplatelet therapy depending on device and protocol), which may still pose short-term bleeding risk.  
41. Consider whether a switch from apixaban to another anticoagulant is justified only after reviewing the bleeding phenotype, renal function, drug interactions, and comparative bleeding risks; avoid assuming another anticoagulant will eliminate occult GI blood loss.  
42. Consider proton-pump inhibitor therapy, such as pantoprazole 40 mg orally daily, if upper-GI mucosal disease is present or if gastroprotection is warranted in the setting of necessary antithrombotic therapy.  
43. Monitor for symptoms of worsening anemia or occult bleeding, including dyspnea, angina, presyncope, fatigue, palpitations, melena, hematochezia, or new abdominal symptoms.  
44. Set a transfusion contingency: if hemoglobin falls to a severely low level (often approximately below 7–8 g/dL, with a higher threshold considered for active ischemia, angina, hemodynamic instability, or symptomatic CAD), evaluate urgently for transfusion and bleeding control.  
45. If overt melena, hematochezia, syncope, hypotension, tachycardia, chest pain, or rapid hemoglobin decline occurs, direct urgent emergency evaluation, repeat CBC/type-and-screen, hold anticoagulation temporarily as clinically appropriate, and pursue acute GI-bleeding evaluation.  
46. If a malignant lesion is identified, refer urgently to the appropriate oncology, surgery, gastroenterology, or radiation-oncology team for staging and treatment planning.  
47. If no source is found after high-quality upper, lower, and small-bowel evaluation, continue periodic CBC and iron studies, reassess medication-related bleeding risk, and reconsider repeat investigation if anemia recurs or worsens.  
48. Schedule coordinated follow-up with primary care, gastroenterology, cardiology/electrophysiology, and hematology as needed within weeks to review anemia response, completed investigations, and the long-term anticoagulation versus LAA-closure decision.
