9. Consider a toxin enzyme immunoassay plus glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) antigen assay with reflex NAAT for discordant results rather than NAAT alone.  
10. Consider NAAT/PCR testing alone only if the practice setting restricts testing to patients meeting strict clinical stool-submission criteria.  
11. Avoid submitting formed stool for *C. difficile* testing.  
12. Avoid repeat *C. difficile* testing within approximately 7 days during the same diarrheal episode unless the clinical situation substantially changes.  
13. Avoid using *C. difficile* testing as a test of cure after symptoms improve.  
14. If stool is not sufficiently unformed or frequency is below testing criteria, monitor clinically rather than sending a low-pretest-probability *C. difficile* assay.  
15. Send a CBC with differential to establish leukocyte count and assess for anemia after recent bloody stools.  
16. Send a basic metabolic panel or comprehensive metabolic panel to assess creatinine, electrolytes, bicarbonate, renal injury, and dehydration.  
17. Obtain albumin if concern exists for severe colitis, poor nutritional status, or recurrent infection severity stratification.  
18. Consider CRP and/or ESR if diarrhea persists, recurs with blood, or inflammatory bowel disease is being considered.  
19. Consider fecal calprotectin or lactoferrin if persistent inflammatory diarrhea, inflammatory bowel disease, or microscopic colitis is under consideration.  
20. Consider stool culture or multiplex gastrointestinal pathogen testing if diarrhea becomes more severe, persists, is associated with fever/blood, follows travel/exposure, or has outbreak risk.  
21. Consider testing for Shiga toxin-producing *E. coli* and other invasive enteric pathogens if bloody diarrhea recurs.  
22. Consider ova and parasite testing or targeted parasite testing only if prolonged diarrhea, travel, exposure, immunocompromise, or epidemiologic risk is identified.  
23. Test for COVID-19/influenza/other respiratory pathogens only as clinically indicated for the recent atypical pneumonia syndrome, rather than attributing all symptoms to azithromycin or *C. difficile*.  
24. Review whether azithromycin is still clinically necessary and discontinue it if the pneumonia treatment course is complete or an alternative diagnosis makes continued therapy unnecessary.  
25. If ongoing antimicrobial treatment for pneumonia is necessary, coordinate with the treating clinician to use the narrowest effective agent and shortest effective duration.  
26. Avoid empiric *C. difficile* therapy while awaiting testing in a clinically stable patient with mild loose stools unless testing is delayed or symptoms progress substantially.  
27. If *C. difficile* testing is positive and symptoms meet clinical criteria for active infection, consider fidaxomicin 200 mg orally twice daily for 10 days.  
28. If fidaxomicin is unavailable, contraindicated, or not feasible, consider vancomycin 125 mg orally four times daily for 10 days for nonfulminant confirmed infection.  
29. If this represents a confirmed recurrence, consider an extended-pulsed fidaxomicin regimen where appropriate, such as 200 mg orally twice daily for 5 days followed by 200 mg every other day for 20 days.  
30. If this represents a confirmed recurrence and fidaxomicin is not used, consider a tapered/pulsed oral vancomycin regimen, with the exact schedule individualized by infectious disease or gastroenterology.  
31. Consider bezlotoxumab 10 mg/kg intravenously once during standard antibacterial treatment for confirmed recurrent *C. difficile*, particularly given prior recurrence/FMT history.  
32. Review for congestive heart failure before bezlotoxumab and weigh its use carefully if heart failure is present.  
33. If fulminant *C. difficile* develops—hypotension/shock, ileus, toxic megacolon, marked abdominal distension, or severe systemic illness—initiate urgent inpatient management with oral/NG vancomycin 500 mg four times daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 8 hours.  
34. If fulminant disease with ileus develops, consider rectal vancomycin administration in addition to oral/NG therapy and obtain urgent gastroenterology, infectious disease, and surgical input.  
35. Avoid antimotility agents such as loperamide if *C. difficile* is suspected or confirmed and especially if fever, abdominal pain, distension, or bloody stool is present.  
36. Consider withholding nonessential proton-pump inhibitor therapy, while continuing acid suppression when there is a strong indication such as high-risk ulcer prevention.  
37. Encourage oral hydration with water, electrolyte-containing fluids, and adequate dietary intake; consider oral rehydration solution if stool losses increase.  
38. Advise temporary avoidance of alcohol, excess caffeine, high-fat foods, and individually recognized dietary triggers while diarrhea is active.  
39. Discuss that azithromycin and other antibiotics can cause non-*C. difficile* antibiotic-associated diarrhea, which may resolve after the antibiotic is stopped.  
40. Discuss that a positive NAAT without demonstrable toxin or compatible symptoms may represent colonization rather than active infection and should be interpreted with the clinical picture.  
41. Refer to gastroenterology nonurgently if loose stools persist beyond approximately 2–4 weeks, if bleeding recurs, if inflammatory markers are elevated, or if colonoscopy evaluation is needed.  
42. Refer to infectious diseases or an FMT/recurrent-*C. difficile* specialist if confirmed recurrence occurs after prior FMT, if multiple recurrences are documented, or if suppressive/preventive strategies are being considered.  
43. Consider colonoscopy with biopsies, after acute infectious causes are assessed, for recurrent hematochezia, unexplained persistent diarrhea, anemia, abnormal inflammatory markers, colorectal cancer screening needs, or concern for microscopic colitis/IBD.  
44. Consider CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast urgently if significant abdominal pain, distension, fever, leukocytosis, peritoneal findings, obstruction symptoms, or concern for colitis complication develops.  
45. Provide emergency precautions for new or recurrent substantial bloody stool, black/tarry stool, severe abdominal pain, fever, inability to maintain hydration, dizziness/syncope, reduced urine output, abdominal distension, confusion, or hypotension.  
46. Arrange follow-up contact within 24–72 hours if testing is sent or symptoms continue, with review of stool frequency, hydration, vital signs if available, laboratory results, and test interpretation.  
47. If diarrhea resolves promptly after azithromycin cessation and no qualifying unformed stool remains, document symptom resolution and avoid further *C. difficile* testing or treatment.  
48. If symptoms increase to at least 3 unformed stools per day, recur after initial improvement, or are accompanied by systemic features, obtain or repeat clinical evaluation promptly and reassess for *C. difficile* and alternate etiologies.

1. **Diagnostics:** Repeat serum creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphorus, albumin, and calculated race-free CKD-EPI eGFR within 1–4 weeks to confirm whether the rise to 1.4 mg/dL persists.  
2. **Diagnostics:** Repeat serum cystatin C with cystatin-C–based eGFR and combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR (eGFRcr-cys).  
3. **Diagnostics:** Verify the creatinine assay method and consider repeating creatinine using an enzymatic assay if interference with a Jaffe assay is possible.  
4. **Diagnostics:** Obtain prior creatinine values over several years to establish baseline, trajectory, and whether abnormality has persisted for at least 3 months.  
5. **Diagnostics:** Repeat complete urinalysis with microscopy, including assessment for hematuria, dysmorphic red cells, casts, pyuria, and urine specific gravity.  
6. **Diagnostics:** Repeat spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR).  
7. **Diagnostics:** Obtain spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR), because non-albumin proteinuria can be missed by UACR alone.  
8. **Diagnostics:** Consider a timed 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance and total protein if creatinine- and cystatin-C–based estimates remain discordant.  
9. **Diagnostics:** Consider formal measured GFR using an exogenous filtration marker (such as iohexol or iothalamate clearance) if the true GFR would affect diagnosis, medication dosing, occupational clearance, athletic evaluation, or kidney-donor considerations.  
10. **Diagnostics:** Measure creatine kinase (CK) if recent heavy exercise, high muscle mass, muscle symptoms, or rhabdomyolysis is possible.  
11. **Diagnostics:** Check serum uric acid if there is gout, nephrolithiasis, high-purine intake, or concern for urate-related kidney disease.  
12. **Diagnostics:** Obtain fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c as a baseline screen for diabetes-associated kidney risk.  
13. **Diagnostics:** Obtain a fasting lipid panel and assess overall cardiovascular risk if chronic kidney disease remains possible.  
14. **Diagnostics:** Obtain CBC to assess for anemia, eosinophilia, or other systemic clues if kidney dysfunction is confirmed.  
15. **Diagnostics:** Check liver tests if low creatinine generation, liver disease, or systemic illness is suspected as a contributor to discordant filtration estimates.  
16. **Diagnostics:** Check thyroid-stimulating hormone if thyroid disease is suspected, because thyroid status can affect cystatin C interpretation.  
17. **Diagnostics:** Consider CRP or ESR only if inflammatory disease, infection, obesity-related inflammation, or other cystatin-C confounders are clinically suspected.  
18. **Diagnostics:** Review body weight, body composition, muscularity, diet, and recent changes in exercise habits to assess whether increased creatinine generation explains the result.  
19. **Diagnostics:** Ask about a high-protein diet, recent cooked-meat intake, creatine supplements, protein powders, anabolic steroids, and bodybuilding supplements.  
20. **Diagnostics:** Repeat creatinine after avoiding unusually strenuous exercise for 48–72 hours and avoiding a large cooked-meat meal for approximately 12–24 hours before phlebotomy.  
21. **Diagnostics:** Perform standardized office blood-pressure measurements on more than one occasion, including consideration of home blood-pressure monitoring.  
22. **Diagnostics:** Consider ambulatory 24-hour blood-pressure monitoring if office readings are borderline, variable, or concern exists for masked hypertension.  
23. **Diagnostics:** Repeat renal/bladder ultrasound if creatinine elevation persists, worsens, or there are urinary symptoms, stone symptoms, recurrent infections, retention symptoms, or concern for obstruction despite a normal study 5 years ago.  
24. **Diagnostics:** Include post-void residual measurement with ultrasound if lower urinary tract symptoms, urinary retention, neurogenic bladder risk, or hydronephrosis is suspected.  
25. **Diagnostics:** Evaluate for nephrolithiasis with imaging if flank pain, hematuria, recurrent stones, or obstructive symptoms develop.  
26. **Diagnostics:** Obtain renal artery imaging only if resistant hypertension, recurrent flash pulmonary edema, asymmetric kidneys, abrupt unexplained worsening, or vascular risk factors raise concern for renovascular disease.  
27. **Diagnostics:** Obtain ANA, complement C3/C4, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, hepatitis B/C testing, HIV testing, and serum protein studies only if active urine sediment, proteinuria, systemic symptoms, or progressive renal dysfunction emerges.  
28. **Diagnostics:** Obtain serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains if unexplained proteinuria, anemia, hypercalcemia, neuropathy, or another plasma-cell disorder signal appears.  
29. **Diagnostics:** Review family history for chronic kidney disease, early dialysis, hearing loss, hematuria, stones, cystic kidneys, hypertension, diabetes, and known inherited renal disorders.  
30. **Diagnostics:** Consider genetic kidney-disease testing or genetics referral if there is a strong family history, early-onset CKD, persistent hematuria/proteinuria, structural abnormalities, or syndromic features.  
31. **Medications:** Conduct a complete prescription, over-the-counter, supplement, recreational-drug, and performance-enhancing-substance review for nephrotoxins or agents that raise creatinine without lowering GFR.  
32. **Medications:** Stop or avoid nonessential NSAIDs, including ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, and high-dose aspirin, if being used.  
33. **Medications:** Hold nonessential creatine supplementation before repeat creatinine testing and reassess creatinine after an appropriate washout period.  
34. **Medications:** Review for trimethoprim, cimetidine, cobicistat, dolutegravir, fenofibrate, chemotherapy agents, and other drugs that can increase serum creatinine through altered tubular secretion or renal effects.  
35. **Medications:** Avoid starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB solely for creatinine elevation in the absence of hypertension, albuminuria, diabetes, heart failure, or another established indication.  
36. **Medications:** Avoid empiric corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy unless a specific inflammatory or immune-mediated kidney disorder is identified.  
37. **Procedures:** Consider kidney biopsy only if there is progressive unexplained loss of kidney function, significant proteinuria, glomerular hematuria, active sediment, abnormal serologies, or another finding suggesting intrinsic renal disease.  
38. **Referrals:** Refer to nephrology nonurgently if creatinine elevation persists for at least 3 months, combined eGFR is reduced, the creatinine/cystatin-C discrepancy remains clinically consequential, or diagnostic uncertainty persists.  
39. **Referrals:** Expedite nephrology referral if eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², creatinine rises rapidly, UACR is at least 30 mg/g persistently, UPCR is elevated, hematuria/casts appear, or hypertension develops.  
40. **Referrals:** Refer to a renal dietitian if high-protein intake, supplements, recurrent stones, hyperkalemia, confirmed CKD, or dietary uncertainty is identified.  
41. **Counseling:** Counsel on maintaining adequate hydration, particularly around exercise, heat exposure, gastrointestinal illness, and other volume-depleting situations.  
42. **Counseling:** Counsel to avoid dehydration, binge alcohol use, illicit stimulants, unregulated supplements, and unnecessary nephrotoxic medications.  
43. **Counseling:** Counsel on maintaining normal blood pressure, regular exercise without extreme exertion immediately before testing, smoking avoidance, and a balanced diet with moderation of excessive protein intake.  
44. **Follow-up and monitoring:** Recheck creatinine/eGFR, cystatin C, urinalysis, UACR, UPCR, and blood pressure in approximately 1–3 months if repeat testing is stable but unexplained.  
45. **Follow-up and monitoring:** If kidney function and urine testing remain normal and combined eGFR is reassuring, monitor creatinine, urinalysis/UACR, and blood pressure annually or sooner if clinical circumstances change.  
46. **Contingency:** If repeat creatinine returns to the prior 1.0–1.2 mg/dL range after exercise/diet/supplement adjustment and cystatin-C eGFR remains normal, document likely non-GFR-related creatinine elevation and continue periodic surveillance.  
47. **Contingency:** If creatinine rises by more than 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, by at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or there is oliguria, evaluate urgently for acute kidney injury, obstruction, volume depletion, rhabdomyolysis, and nephrotoxic exposure.  
48. **Contingency:** If new edema, dyspnea, gross hematuria, markedly decreased urine output, severe flank pain, fever with urinary symptoms, or blood pressure above 180/120 mmHg occurs, seek urgent or emergency evaluation.

2. **Diagnostics:** Repeat cystatin C with cystatin-C–based eGFR and calculate combined creatinine–cystatin C eGFR.  
3. **Diagnostics:** Obtain a basic metabolic panel on the same day as creatinine/cystatin C testing to assess potassium, bicarbonate, and other evidence of impaired renal function.  
4. **Diagnostics:** Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, including assessment for hematuria, pyuria, casts, crystals, and urine specific gravity.  
5. **Diagnostics:** Repeat spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR).  
6. **Diagnostics:** Obtain spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) to assess non-albumin proteinuria.  
7. **Diagnostics:** Consider a first-morning urine specimen for UACR/UPCR to reduce effects of exercise, hydration, and orthostatic proteinuria.  
8. **Diagnostics:** Review the trajectory of all prior creatinine values, eGFR estimates, cystatin C results, weights, and urine studies to determine whether the rise is persistent versus transient.  
9. **Diagnostics:** Confirm whether the creatinine increase occurred after intense exercise, dehydration, high-protein intake, cooked meat consumption, or use of creatine-containing supplements.  
10. **Diagnostics:** Repeat creatinine after avoiding strenuous exercise for 24–48 hours and avoiding unusually large cooked-meat meals before testing.  
11. **Diagnostics:** Assess hydration status and repeat kidney function testing when euvolemic rather than after prolonged fasting, illness, heavy exercise, or poor oral intake.  
12. **Diagnostics:** Obtain creatine kinase (CK) if there is substantial exercise exposure, muscle symptoms, supplement use, or concern for increased creatinine generation from muscle injury.  
13. **Diagnostics:** Consider measured GFR using an exogenous filtration marker (such as iohexol or nuclear-medicine clearance testing) if creatinine and cystatin C estimates remain discordant and the result would affect clinical decisions.  
14. **Diagnostics:** Consider a 24-hour urine creatinine clearance collection as an alternative assessment of filtration and creatinine generation, with counseling regarding collection limitations.  
15. **Diagnostics:** Assess body habitus, muscle mass, diet, and recent weight change as potential reasons for creatinine-based eGFR underestimating true GFR.  
16. **Diagnostics:** Obtain CBC to assess for anemia or other systemic findings that could accompany chronic kidney disease or systemic illness.  
17. **Diagnostics:** Obtain fasting glucose or hemoglobin A1c to screen for diabetes despite normal blood pressure and absent albuminuria.  
18. **Diagnostics:** Obtain a fasting lipid panel as cardiovascular and CKD risk baseline if CKD is confirmed.  
19. **Diagnostics:** Check uric acid only if there is clinical concern for gout, nephrolithiasis, high purine intake, or unexplained renal dysfunction.  
20. **Diagnostics:** Repeat renal ultrasound if creatinine remains elevated or rises further, focusing on kidney size, echogenicity, hydronephrosis, stones, masses, and bladder emptying.  
21. **Diagnostics:** Add post-void residual bladder measurement if there are lower urinary tract symptoms, incomplete emptying, recurrent urinary infections, or ultrasound concern for obstruction.  
22. **Diagnostics:** Evaluate for nephrolithiasis with appropriate imaging only if flank pain, hematuria, recurrent stones, crystals, or obstructive symptoms develop.  
23. **Diagnostics:** Obtain renal Doppler imaging only if hypertension, asymmetric kidneys, recurrent unexplained acute kidney injury, abdominal bruit, or other renovascular features emerge.  
24. **Diagnostics:** Order ANA, complements, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, hepatitis B/C testing, HIV testing, and serum/urine protein electrophoresis only if hematuria, proteinuria, active sediment, systemic symptoms, anemia, hypercalcemia, or progressive renal decline appears.  
25. **Diagnostics:** Consider genetic kidney-disease evaluation only if there is a family history of early kidney disease, cystic disease, hearing loss, recurrent stones, congenital urinary anomalies, or unexplained progressive decline.  
26. **Diagnostics:** Confirm blood pressure with standardized office measurements and/or home blood-pressure monitoring, despite currently normal readings.  
27. **Medications:** Perform a complete medication, over-the-counter drug, supplement, performance-enhancing drug, and herbal-product reconciliation.  
28. **Medications:** Hold creatine supplements, if used, before repeat creatinine testing and reassess kidney markers after discontinuation.  
29. **Medications:** Avoid nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (including ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, and high-dose aspirin) when possible; if needed, use the lowest dose for the shortest duration.  
30. **Medications:** Avoid or minimize unregulated bodybuilding supplements, high-dose protein supplements, and herbal products with potential nephrotoxicity.  
31. **Medications:** Review for drugs that can raise serum creatinine without reducing true GFR, including trimethoprim, cimetidine, cobicistat, dolutegravir, fenofibrate, and some chemotherapy agents.  
32. **Medications:** If a medication-associated creatinine rise is suspected, consider holding, substituting, or repeating testing after the suspected agent is stopped, in coordination with the prescriber.  
33. **Medications:** Avoid starting an ACE inhibitor, ARB, SGLT2 inhibitor, diuretic, or other kidney-directed drug solely for an isolated mildly elevated creatinine in the absence of hypertension, albuminuria, diabetes, heart failure, or another established indication.  
34. **Medications:** Use renal-dose review for any newly prescribed medications if reduced GFR is confirmed by combined eGFR, measured GFR, or persistent abnormal testing.  
35. **Procedures:** Do not pursue kidney biopsy solely for stable creatinine of 1.2–1.4 mg/dL with normal cystatin C, bland urine sediment, and no proteinuria; reconsider biopsy if active urine findings or progressive dysfunction develops.  
36. **Referrals:** Refer to nephrology routinely if elevated creatinine/eGFR reduction persists for at least 3 months, if interpretation of discordant creatinine and cystatin C requires specialist input, or if measured GFR is being considered.  
37. **Referrals:** Expedite nephrology referral if creatinine rises rapidly, eGFR declines substantially, albuminuria/proteinuria appears, hematuria or casts are present, hypertension develops, or electrolyte/acid-base abnormalities occur.  
38. **Referrals:** Refer to a renal dietitian if there is a very high-protein diet, frequent supplement use, uncertainty about appropriate protein intake, or confirmed CKD requiring individualized nutrition guidance.  
39. **Counseling:** Counsel on maintaining consistent hydration before laboratory testing and avoiding dehydration from illness, heat exposure, alcohol excess, or intense exercise.  
40. **Counseling:** Counsel that serum creatinine can be influenced by muscle mass, exercise, dietary meat intake, creatine supplements, and certain medications, whereas cystatin C may better reflect filtration in some individuals.  
41. **Counseling:** Encourage regular physical activity and ergonomic breaks for a desk-based job, without restricting exercise unless there is concern for exertional rhabdomyolysis or another specific condition.  
42. **Counseling:** Advise a generally heart-healthy diet with moderate protein intake rather than extreme high-protein dieting until renal function status is clarified.  
43. **Counseling:** Advise avoidance of tobacco/nicotine products and caution with recreational drugs that may cause dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, hypertension, or nephrotoxicity.  
44. **Follow-up/monitoring:** If repeat creatinine, cystatin C, urinalysis, UACR, UPCR, blood pressure, and electrolytes are normal or stable, monitor kidney function and urine albumin approximately annually.  
45. **Follow-up/monitoring:** If creatinine remains around 1.4 mg/dL but cystatin-C or combined eGFR is normal and urine testing remains normal, document likely isolated creatinine elevation and monitor every 6–12 months.  
46. **Follow-up/monitoring:** If persistent eGFR is below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for 3 months or longer, classify and stage CKD using GFR and albuminuria categories and monitor at an interval appropriate to risk.  
47. **Contingency:** If creatinine increases by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, by at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or there is a substantial sustained rise from prior baseline, evaluate promptly for acute kidney injury.  
48. **Contingency:** If UACR is at least 30 mg/g, UPCR is elevated, microscopic hematuria persists, or urine sediment becomes active, repeat testing promptly and pursue nephrology evaluation.  
49. **Contingency:** If potassium is elevated, bicarbonate is low, edema develops, urine output falls, or uremic symptoms occur, obtain urgent clinical assessment.  
50. **Contingency:** If repeat ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, bladder retention, obstructing stone, or structural abnormality, arrange urgent urology and/or nephrology evaluation depending on the finding.

33. Refer to nephrology routinely if creatinine remains elevated for more than 3 months, eGFR is persistently below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², albuminuria/proteinuria is present, urine sediment is abnormal, or the creatinine trend is progressive.

49. If potassium is elevated, bicarbonate is low, edema develops, urine output decreases, or hypertension appears, reassess promptly for clinically significant kidney dysfunction.

21. Consider CT pulmonary angiography or V/Q imaging if symptoms or signs suggest pulmonary embolism, which would support systemic cancer-associated thrombosis.  
22. Review the surveillance CT for recurrent ovarian cancer, peritoneal disease, nodal disease, vascular compression, renal hilar involvement, or tumor thrombus.  
23. Obtain updated malignancy staging imaging, such as CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET/CT, if the surveillance study suggests recurrence or if cancer status is uncertain.  
24. Refer promptly to medical oncology/gynecologic oncology to assess current ovarian-cancer activity and whether the infarct represents cancer-associated arterial thrombosis.  
25. Review all current and recent medications for prothrombotic agents, including estrogen exposure, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, thrombopoietic agents, and cancer therapies associated with thrombosis.  
26. Stop or avoid exogenous estrogen-containing therapy if present, unless a specialist judges its benefit to outweigh arterial thrombotic risk.  
27. Review for recent interruption of anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, prior venous or arterial thrombosis, central venous catheters, and prior heparin exposure.  
28. Evaluate for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with platelet trend review and PF4/heparin antibody testing if there was recent heparin exposure and thrombocytopenia or new thrombosis.  
29. Obtain fasting lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c to assess atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk factors that could contribute to renal artery disease.  
30. Consider targeted antiphospholipid syndrome testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies) if the infarct is unexplained, recurrent, or disproportionate to cancer activity.  
31. Defer broad inherited thrombophilia testing until discussion with hematology, particularly because active malignancy and any anticoagulant exposure may confound interpretation and because results may not change management at age 60.  
32. Obtain ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, complement levels, and hepatitis serologies if imaging or symptoms raise concern for vasculitis, inflammatory arteriopathy, or glomerulonephritis.  
33. Check eosinophil count, inflammatory markers, and consider vascular imaging for polyarteritis nodosa or other medium-vessel vasculitis if there are systemic features, aneurysms, neuropathy, rash, or abdominal pain.  
34. Refer to hematology with expedited outpatient or inpatient timing depending on acuity to assess cancer-associated thrombosis, arterial thrombosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and anticoagulant choice/duration.  
35. Refer to nephrology if there is bilateral infarction, solitary kidney, declining eGFR, significant proteinuria/hematuria, difficult-to-control hypertension, or uncertainty about renal vascular disease.  
36. Refer urgently to vascular surgery or interventional radiology if CTA/MRA shows main renal artery occlusion, renal artery dissection, threatened renal function, bilateral disease, solitary kidney involvement, or potentially treatable vascular lesion.  
37. Discuss immediate therapeutic anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin infusion if the infarct appears acute/recent, an embolic or thrombotic cause is suspected, and bleeding risk is acceptable.  
38. Consider therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin, such as enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (with renal adjustment), as an alternative initial anticoagulant in active malignancy.  
39. Consider a direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days followed by 5 mg twice daily when appropriate, after evaluating renal function, drug interactions, gastrointestinal/genitourinary bleeding risk, and planned procedures.  
40. Consider warfarin with heparin bridging rather than a direct oral anticoagulant if antiphospholipid syndrome is confirmed or strongly suspected, or if drug interactions or cost/access issues limit alternatives.  
41. Consider antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin 81 mg orally daily if imaging supports atherosclerotic renal artery disease and anticoagulation is not indicated or is contraindicated.  
42. Avoid combining full-dose anticoagulation with antiplatelet therapy unless there is a separate clear indication because of increased bleeding risk.  
43. Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis, thrombectomy, angioplasty, or stenting only after urgent vascular/interventional consultation when there is acute main renal artery occlusion and a potentially salvageable kidney.  
44. Treat pain, if present, with acetaminophen as first-line therapy and avoid or minimize NSAIDs because of potential renal hemodynamic effects and bleeding risk during anticoagulation.  
45. Initiate antihypertensive therapy if persistent hypertension develops, with drug choice guided by renal function, renal artery anatomy, potassium, and presence of bilateral renal artery disease.  
46. Counsel the patient regarding urgent symptoms requiring emergency evaluation: new severe flank/abdominal pain, hematuria, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, focal neurologic deficits, syncope, reduced urine output, or bleeding while anticoagulated.  
47. Counsel regarding anticoagulant bleeding precautions, including avoidance of unnecessary NSAIDs, reporting melena/hematochezia/hematuria, and coordination before invasive procedures.  
48. Recheck CBC, creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, urinalysis, and blood pressure within approximately 1–2 weeks after diagnosis or anticoagulation initiation, sooner if clinically unstable.  
49. Repeat renal vascular imaging, commonly CTA/MRA or Doppler ultrasound, in approximately 1–3 months if an arterial thrombus, dissection, stenosis, or intervention is identified, with timing individualized by vascular specialists.  
50. If renal function worsens, blood pressure rises abruptly, infarcts recur, embolic events develop, or imaging identifies bilateral/main renal artery involvement, escalate to urgent inpatient evaluation with nephrology, hematology, cardiology, and vascular/interventional consultation.

1. Confirm the CT finding with radiology review, including infarct location, size, laterality, cortical involvement, and whether features suggest acute versus chronic infarction.  
2. Obtain contrast-enhanced CT angiography (CTA) of the abdomen/pelvis with arterial phase imaging to assess the renal arteries, aorta, dissection, aneurysm, plaque, thrombus, and renal arterial branch occlusion.  
3. Use MR angiography of the renal arteries/aorta if iodinated contrast is undesirable or CTA is nondiagnostic.  
4. Obtain renal artery duplex Doppler ultrasonography as a noninvasive assessment for renal artery stenosis, flow limitation, or major-vessel occlusion.  
5. Review prior surveillance CT scans for timing of infarct development, prior renal artery abnormalities, tumor recurrence, lymphadenopathy, or vascular compression.  
6. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy for hematuria, proteinuria, pyuria, casts, and evidence of alternative renal pathology.  
7. Obtain urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or albumin-to-creatinine ratio as a renal baseline.  
8. Repeat serum creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, bicarbonate, and estimated GFR within 24–48 hours to establish whether renal function remains stable.  
9. Obtain a baseline complete blood count with platelet count to evaluate anemia, thrombocytosis, thrombocytopenia, infection, and anticoagulation safety.  
10. Obtain PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, and D-dimer as baseline coagulation studies and to assess for cancer-associated coagulopathy/DIC.  
11. Obtain lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which may support acute renal infarction and provide a baseline trend.  
12. Measure inflammatory markers such as ESR and CRP if vasculitis, aortitis, or inflammatory vascular disease is clinically plausible.  
13. Obtain fasting lipid panel and hemoglobin A1c to assess atherosclerotic vascular risk factors.  
14. Obtain serial blood pressure measurements, including home blood-pressure monitoring or ambulatory monitoring if hypertension develops after infarction.  
15. Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for atrial fibrillation, flutter, prior myocardial infarction, or other arrhythmia.  
16. Place the patient on inpatient telemetry or arrange extended ambulatory rhythm monitoring (e.g., 14–30-day patch monitor) if no embolic source is immediately identified.  
17. Obtain transthoracic echocardiography to evaluate left ventricular thrombus, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, atrial enlargement, and shunt-related findings.  
18. Obtain transesophageal echocardiography if transthoracic echocardiography is unrevealing but suspicion remains for left atrial appendage thrombus, valvular vegetation, patent foramen ovale, or complex aortic atheroma.  
19. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if fever, leukocytosis, murmur, embolic phenomena, indwelling catheter infection, or other concern for infective endocarditis is present.  
20. Evaluate for active or recurrent ovarian cancer with review of current oncology imaging, tumor markers where relevant (e.g., CA-125), and assessment for metastatic or compressive disease.  
21. Review all cancer treatments, including recent surgery, chemotherapy, antiangiogenic therapy, hormonal therapy, central venous catheters, and radiation, for prothrombotic or vascular adverse effects.  
22. Review medication history for estrogen exposure, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, thrombopoietic agents, and drugs affecting renal perfusion.  
23. Obtain hematology input regarding whether thrombophilia testing is useful despite active or prior malignancy.  
24. If thrombophilia testing is pursued, test for antiphospholipid syndrome with lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I antibodies.  
25. If clinically indicated by recurrent/unusual arterial thrombosis or family history, test for inherited thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden mutation, prothrombin G20210A mutation, protein C/S deficiency, and antithrombin deficiency, recognizing acute thrombosis/anticoagulation can affect interpretation.  
26. Consider myeloproliferative-neoplasm testing, including JAK2 V617F (with CALR/MPL testing if appropriate), if thrombocytosis, erythrocytosis, splenomegaly, or unexplained arterial thrombosis is present.  
27. Consider paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria flow cytometry if unexplained hemolysis, cytopenias, or atypical thrombosis is present.  
28. Consult nephrology urgently or routinely depending on infarct extent, renal-function trend, bilateral involvement, proteinuria, hypertension, or diagnostic uncertainty.  
29. Consult vascular surgery or interventional radiology urgently if CTA/MRA shows main renal artery occlusion, dissection, aneurysm, fibromuscular dysplasia, threatened renal function, or a lesion potentially amenable to intervention.  
30. Consult cardiology if atrial fibrillation, intracardiac thrombus, valvular disease, suspected endocarditis, or another cardiac embolic source is identified.  
31. Consult hematology/oncology for assessment of cancer-associated arterial thrombosis and coordination of anticoagulation with cancer treatment and bleeding risk.  
32. Consider hospital admission for expedited embolic-source evaluation, serial renal-function testing, pain control, blood-pressure monitoring, and initiation of antithrombotic therapy if the infarct is acute or timing is uncertain.  
33. Start therapeutic anticoagulation with intravenous unfractionated heparin (weight-based bolus and infusion titrated to aPTT or anti-Xa) if acute renal arterial thrombosis/embolism is suspected and there is no contraindication.  
34. Use therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (or 1.5 mg/kg daily in selected patients) as an alternative initial anticoagulant when renal function is adequate.  
35. Transition to a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days followed by 5 mg twice daily, when an anticoagulation indication is established and drug interactions/bleeding risk permit.  
36. Use warfarin with heparin bridging, targeting INR 2.0–3.0, as an alternative when antiphospholipid syndrome, certain drug interactions, cost barriers, or other indications favor warfarin.  
37. Define anticoagulation duration based on etiology, such as at least 3–6 months for a provoked event, longer treatment for persistent active malignancy, or indefinite treatment for atrial fibrillation or recurrent embolism if bleeding risk allows.  
38. Consider antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 81 mg orally daily if imaging suggests atherosclerotic renal artery disease and full-dose anticoagulation is not indicated.  
39. Consider dual antiplatelet therapy only if renal artery stenting or another vascular intervention is performed, using an agent and duration specified by the procedural team.  
40. Start high-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin 40–80 mg orally daily or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg daily, if atherosclerotic disease is identified or overall cardiovascular-risk assessment supports it.  
41. Avoid routine NSAID use for flank pain because of potential renal perfusion effects; use acetaminophen and, if needed, short-course opioid analgesia instead.  
42. Avoid dehydration, and provide oral or intravenous isotonic fluids when clinically volume depleted while avoiding unnecessary volume expansion.  
43. Hold or reassess nephrotoxic medications and adjust renally cleared medications if creatinine rises or contrast exposure is planned.  
44. Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis, thrombectomy, angioplasty, or stenting if there is a recent main renal artery occlusion, ongoing ischemic pain, bilateral disease, solitary kidney, worsening renal function, or salvageable renal tissue.  
45. Avoid thrombolysis or invasive revascularization when infarction is clearly chronic, limited to a small segment, renal function is stable, procedural risk is high, or the anticipated renal benefit is low.  
46. Monitor for anticoagulant complications with periodic CBC, creatinine/eGFR, liver tests when relevant, medication-interaction review, and bleeding assessment.  
47. Recheck serum creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, urinalysis, and blood pressure approximately 1–2 weeks after diagnosis and again at 1–3 months.  
48. Repeat renal vascular imaging (CTA, MRA, or duplex) in approximately 1–3 months if dissection, stenosis, thrombus, aneurysm, or uncertain vessel patency is identified.  
49. Counsel the patient to seek urgent evaluation for new severe flank/abdominal pain, gross hematuria, reduced urine output, dyspnea, chest pain, neurologic deficits, unilateral leg swelling, syncope, or any major bleeding while anticoagulated.  
50. If fever or positive blood cultures develop, then pursue urgent endocarditis evaluation with echocardiography, infectious-disease consultation, and pathogen-directed intravenous antimicrobial therapy; if renal function worsens, bilateral infarction is identified, or blood pressure becomes difficult to control, then escalate urgently to nephrology and vascular/interventional evaluation.

1. Confirm the renal infarct on the surveillance CT by reviewing images with radiology, including infarct size, laterality, cortical distribution, renal arterial patency, and any renal mass or vascular abnormality.  

2. Obtain a dedicated contrast-enhanced CT angiogram or MR angiogram of the renal arteries and aorta to assess for renal artery thrombosis, dissection, aneurysm, fibromuscular dysplasia, aortic mural thrombus, or tumor-related vascular invasion.  

3. Consider renal Doppler ultrasound if CTA/MRA is contraindicated or as a noninvasive assessment of renal arterial flow and kidney size.  

4. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy to assess for hematuria, proteinuria, pyuria, casts, or findings suggesting glomerulonephritis/vasculitis rather than isolated embolic infarction.  

5. Obtain a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or albumin-to-creatinine ratio as a renal baseline and to evaluate for occult renal inflammatory disease.  

6. Repeat serum creatinine, BUN, electrolytes, bicarbonate, and estimated GFR to establish a post-infarct renal baseline.  

7. Obtain CBC with differential and platelet count to evaluate anemia, leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, thrombocytopenia, or hematologic evidence of malignancy-associated thrombosis.  

8. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel including liver tests and albumin before selecting anticoagulant therapy.  

9. Obtain PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, and D-dimer as baseline coagulation studies and to assess for consumptive coagulopathy or active thrombosis.  

10. Obtain LDH, which may support renal infarction and provide a baseline for evolution of tissue injury.  

11. Obtain ESR and CRP to screen for systemic inflammation, vasculitis, infection, or inflammatory autoimmune disease.  

12. Obtain blood pressure measurements, including repeat office measurements or home monitoring, because renal infarction can precipitate renin-mediated hypertension.  

13. Obtain ECG to evaluate for atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, prior infarction, or other arrhythmia-associated embolic sources.  

14. Arrange telemetry monitoring during acute evaluation if the infarct is recent or if there is concern for intermittent atrial fibrillation.  

15. Arrange ambulatory rhythm monitoring (e.g., 14–30-day patch monitor) if initial ECG and telemetry do not show atrial fibrillation but a cardioembolic source remains possible.  

16. Obtain transthoracic echocardiography to evaluate left ventricular thrombus, cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, intracardiac mass, and cardiac function.  

17. Obtain transesophageal echocardiography if transthoracic echocardiography is unrevealing and suspicion remains for left atrial appendage thrombus, valvular vegetation, patent foramen ovale, or aortic atheroma.  

18. Obtain blood cultures before antibiotics if fever, leukocytosis, heart murmur, emboli in other organs, or echocardiographic concern for infective endocarditis is present.  

19. Evaluate for embolic infarcts elsewhere with targeted imaging if symptoms or imaging suggest splenic, mesenteric, cerebral, or peripheral arterial embolization.  

20. Review all prior CT scans for chronicity of the renal lesion, prior renal perfusion defects, progressive aortic disease, recurrent cancer, lymphadenopathy, or compression/invasion of vessels.  

21. Reassess ovarian cancer status with oncology, including current disease burden, treatment status, tumor markers when clinically relevant, and evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease.  

22. Review current and recent cancer treatments for thrombosis risk, including chemotherapy, antiangiogenic agents, hormonal therapy, surgery, central venous catheters, and immune checkpoint inhibitors.  

23. Obtain antiphospholipid antibody testing, including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG/IgM, and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I IgG/IgM, particularly given an unexplained arterial thrombotic event.  

24. Repeat positive antiphospholipid antibody tests after at least 12 weeks if antiphospholipid syndrome is being considered.  

25. Obtain ANA with reflex connective-tissue disease testing if clinical review identifies rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, inflammatory arthritis, cytopenias, or other autoimmune features.  

26. Obtain ANCA testing (PR3-ANCA/MPO-ANCA) if there are clinical features of systemic vasculitis, active urinary sediment, pulmonary symptoms, sinus disease, neuropathy, or unexplained inflammatory marker elevation.  

27. Obtain complement C3/C4 levels if immune-complex disease, lupus, cryoglobulinemia, or endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis is suspected.  

28. Obtain rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP only if she has symptoms or examination findings of inflammatory arthritis; family history of rheumatoid arthritis alone should not be treated as diagnostic.  

29. Obtain hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV testing if vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, antiphospholipid syndrome, or immunosuppressive therapy becomes a consideration.  

30. Consider cryoglobulin testing if there are compatible findings such as purpura, neuropathy, low complement levels, arthralgias, or renal inflammatory findings.  

31. Consider JAK2 V617F mutation testing, with reflex CALR/MPL testing or hematology evaluation, if CBC shows persistent erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis, or other concern for a myeloproliferative neoplasm.  

32. Consider paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria flow cytometry if there is unexplained hemolysis, cytopenias, atypical thrombosis, or evidence of bone-marrow failure.  

33. Defer broad inherited thrombophilia testing unless hematology believes it would alter management, recognizing that protein C, protein S, antithrombin, and related assays may be unreliable during acute thrombosis, cancer, or anticoagulation.  

34. Consult hematology with expedited outpatient or inpatient timing depending on acuity to guide evaluation of cancer-associated arterial thrombosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and anticoagulant selection.  

35. Consult nephrology if there is rising creatinine, uncontrolled hypertension, substantial proteinuria/hematuria, bilateral infarction, recurrent infarction, or concern for renal vasculitis.  

36. Consult cardiology if atrial fibrillation, structural heart disease, intracardiac thrombus, valvular lesion, or a need for transesophageal echocardiography is identified.  

37. Consult vascular surgery or interventional radiology urgently if CTA/MRA shows renal artery dissection, occlusive thrombus amenable to intervention, aneurysm, or threatened renal function.  

38. Discuss initiation of therapeutic anticoagulation if the infarct is acute and an embolic, in-situ thrombotic, or malignancy-associated mechanism is suspected and bleeding risk is acceptable.  

39. If parenteral anticoagulation is selected, consider unfractionated heparin intravenously with a weight-based bolus/infusion and aPTT or anti-Xa monitoring, particularly if procedures or rapid reversal may be needed.  

40. If parenteral anticoagulation is selected, consider enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours (with renal-dose adjustment if kidney function declines) as an alternative to intravenous heparin.  

41. Consider transition to a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days followed by 5 mg twice daily, or an alternative standard therapeutic regimen, if cancer status, drug interactions, renal function, and bleeding risk permit.  

42. Consider warfarin with heparin bridging and INR target generally 2.0–3.0 if antiphospholipid syndrome is confirmed or strongly suspected, particularly after an arterial thrombotic event.  

43. Review all medications for interactions with anticoagulants, especially azole antifungals, anticonvulsants, antiemetics, targeted cancer therapies, antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs, and herbal supplements.  

44. Hold or avoid NSAIDs when possible if anticoagulation is started or renal perfusion is a concern; use acetaminophen as a potential first-line analgesic if pain is present and liver status permits.  

45. Consider antiplatelet therapy such as aspirin only if imaging or specialist assessment supports an atherosclerotic renal arterial mechanism or if another vascular indication exists, while accounting for bleeding risk when combined with anticoagulation.  

46. Consider catheter-directed thrombolysis, thrombectomy, angioplasty, or stenting only for a very recent infarct with demonstrable renal arterial occlusion, severe symptoms, bilateral involvement, solitary kidney, or threatened renal function after urgent interventional consultation.  

47. Counsel the patient on urgent symptoms requiring emergency assessment, including new flank/abdominal pain, gross hematuria, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, focal neurologic deficits, unilateral limb ischemia, syncope, or reduced urine output.  

48. Counsel regarding anticoagulant bleeding precautions if treated, including reporting melena, hematemesis, persistent epistaxis, severe headache, falls/head injury, heavy vaginal bleeding, or unexplained bruising.  

49. Counsel on home blood-pressure monitoring, avoidance of dehydration, smoking cessation if applicable, and management of cardiovascular risk factors such as diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and sedentary behavior.  

50. Repeat creatinine/eGFR, electrolytes, urinalysis, CBC, blood pressure, and anticoagulation-related monitoring within approximately 1–2 weeks after the event or treatment change, with repeat renal vascular imaging in roughly 1–3 months if vascular occlusion/dissection is identified or clinical status changes.

1. Quantify 24-hour urine volume (polyuria generally defined as >3 L/day in adults or >50 mL/kg/day) to distinguish true polyuria from urinary frequency with small voids.  
2. Have the patient complete a 2–3 day bladder/voiding diary documenting fluid intake, voided volumes, timing, nocturia, urgency, and incontinence.  
3. Repeat basic metabolic panel including serum sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, BUN, creatinine, glucose, and calcium.  
4. Obtain measured serum osmolality paired with simultaneous urine osmolality and urine specific gravity.  
5. Obtain a simultaneous urine sodium measurement with the serum/urine osmolality sample, recognizing low urine sodium alone is not diagnostic of diabetes insipidus.  
6. Obtain fasting or random serum glucose and urinalysis for glucosuria to reassess osmotic diuresis despite the prior normal A1c.  
7. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, urine culture, and sexually transmitted infection testing as indicated to reassess persistent urinary symptoms or urethritis.  
8. Measure serum calcium and phosphorus to evaluate hypercalcemia as a cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus/polyuria.  
9. Measure serum potassium and magnesium to evaluate hypokalemia or other electrolyte abnormalities contributing to renal concentrating defects.  
10. Measure BUN/creatinine/eGFR and consider urine protein/albumin testing to assess chronic kidney disease or tubular dysfunction.  
11. Review prior and current serum sodium values for hypernatremia, low-normal sodium, or hyponatremia patterns.  
12. Assess volume status clinically, including orthostatic vital signs, mucous membranes, weight change, and signs of dehydration or edema.  
13. Review total daily fluid intake, including habitual water drinking, sports drinks, caffeine, alcohol, and nighttime intake.  
14. Review all prescribed, over-the-counter, recreational, and supplement exposures that can cause polyuria or impaired concentrating ability.  
15. Specifically review for lithium exposure and obtain a serum lithium concentration if currently taking lithium or if toxicity is possible.  
16. Review for diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, demeclocycline, amphotericin B, cisplatin, foscarnet, ifosfamide, and other nephrotoxic/tubular medications.  
17. Review use of caffeine, alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, and high-solute/protein supplements that may increase urine output or worsen nocturia.  
18. Evaluate dietary solute load, including high sodium intake, high protein intake, tube feeds, creatine products, or recent large saline loads that can cause solute diuresis.  
19. Measure urine glucose, urea, sodium, potassium, and calculate daily osmole excretion if a 24-hour urine collection is obtained to distinguish water diuresis from solute diuresis.  
20. Obtain a 24-hour urine collection for volume, osmolality, sodium, potassium, urea nitrogen, glucose if applicable, creatinine, and calcium as clinically appropriate.  
21. Consider a formal supervised water-deprivation test with serial weight, vital signs, serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine output, and urine osmolality.  
22. Use strict stopping criteria during water deprivation, such as significant weight loss, symptomatic hypotension, rising serum sodium, severe thirst, or inability to safely continue fasting.  
23. Administer desmopressin only as part of a supervised diagnostic protocol after appropriate baseline testing to assess renal response.  
24. Consider a hypertonic-saline-stimulated copeptin test, where available, to distinguish central diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia.  
25. Consider an arginine-stimulated copeptin test where available as an alternative diagnostic approach for central diabetes insipidus versus primary polydipsia.  
26. Measure baseline plasma copeptin if available, particularly if serum sodium/osmolality is elevated and diabetes insipidus is strongly suspected.  
27. If central diabetes insipidus is suspected, obtain pituitary hormone evaluation including morning cortisol, ACTH as appropriate, TSH, free T4, prolactin, LH, FSH, and testosterone.  
28. If cortisol deficiency is possible, obtain urgent morning cortisol and consider endocrinology-directed dynamic testing before attributing symptoms solely to diabetes insipidus.  
29. Obtain MRI of the brain/pituitary with sellar protocol and contrast if central diabetes insipidus is confirmed or strongly suspected.  
30. Review for central diabetes insipidus causes including head trauma, neurosurgery, pituitary disease, autoimmune disease, infiltrative disease, malignancy, meningitis, encephalitis, and family history.  
31. If pituitary imaging is abnormal or symptoms suggest systemic infiltration, consider targeted evaluation for sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, tuberculosis, autoimmune hypophysitis, or malignancy.  
32. Obtain renal ultrasound if there is concern for obstruction, hydronephrosis, renal structural disease, recurrent stones, or chronic kidney disease.  
33. Measure post-void residual by bladder scan to assess incomplete bladder emptying, retention with frequency, or outlet obstruction.  
34. Consider uroflowmetry and formal urodynamic testing if the diary suggests reduced functional bladder capacity, overactive bladder, incomplete emptying, or neurogenic voiding dysfunction.  
35. Perform focused genitourinary examination, including abdominal, suprapubic, external genital, and prostate examination when clinically appropriate.  
36. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea symptoms, including snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence, and obesity, because sleep apnea can cause nocturnal polyuria.  
37. Consider sleep study referral if nocturia is prominent and obstructive sleep apnea screening is positive.  
38. Screen for anxiety, compulsive water drinking, psychosis, eating disorders, and other contributors to primary polydipsia.  
39. Refer to endocrinology on an expedited outpatient basis for interpretation of paired osmolality testing and supervised differentiation of central DI, nephrogenic DI, and primary polydipsia.  
40. Refer to nephrology if there is suspected nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, reduced kidney function, recurrent electrolyte abnormalities, or unclear renal concentrating defect.  
41. Refer to urology if true polyuria is not demonstrated, infection testing is negative, or urinary frequency/nocturia persists with suspected bladder, prostate, urethral, or retention pathology.  
42. Avoid empiric desmopressin outside a monitored diagnostic/therapeutic plan when primary polydipsia has not been excluded because of hyponatremia risk.  
43. Avoid intentional fluid restriction at home until serum sodium, serum osmolality, and the possibility of diabetes insipidus are assessed, particularly if dehydration or hypernatremia is possible.  
44. Counsel the patient to maintain reasonable access to water and to seek urgent care for confusion, severe weakness, syncope, inability to keep up with thirst, vomiting, or signs of severe dehydration.  
45. Counsel the patient to limit excessive evening caffeine, alcohol, and large late-night fluid intake while objective urine-volume assessment is underway.  
46. If urine output is high with elevated serum sodium or elevated serum osmolality and inappropriately dilute urine, arrange urgent endocrine evaluation and monitored assessment for diabetes insipidus.  
47. If serum sodium is severely elevated, mental-status changes occur, hypotension develops, or dehydration is clinically significant, send the patient for emergency evaluation and controlled fluid/electrolyte correction.  
48. If serum sodium is low or low-normal with very dilute urine and excessive intake, evaluate for primary polydipsia and avoid desmopressin unless specialist-supervised testing supports DI.  
49. If desmopressin is ultimately initiated for confirmed central diabetes insipidus, monitor serum sodium, weight, fluid intake, urine volume, and symptoms shortly after initiation and after dose changes.  
50. If nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is confirmed, address reversible causes such as lithium or electrolyte abnormalities and consider specialist-guided therapies such as dietary sodium reduction, thiazide therapy, amiloride for lithium-associated disease, or NSAID-based therapy with renal monitoring.

1. Quantify 24-hour urine volume with a formal 24-hour urine collection to distinguish true polyuria (>3 L/day in adults or >50 mL/kg/day) from urinary frequency with normal total output.  

2. Have the patient complete a 3-day bladder diary documenting fluid intake, timing/volume of voids, nocturnal voids, caffeine/alcohol intake, and overnight urine volume.  

3. Measure simultaneous early-morning serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality, and urine specific gravity before major changes in fluid intake.  

4. Repeat basic metabolic panel including sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, BUN, creatinine, glucose, and calcium.  

5. Measure serum magnesium and phosphate as contributors to renal concentrating defects when clinically appropriate.  

6. Obtain ionized calcium or repeat corrected calcium to exclude hypercalcemia-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus/polyuria.  

7. Measure serum potassium and replete/evaluate hypokalemia if present, because hypokalemia can impair urinary concentration and cause nephrogenic DI.  

8. Obtain fasting plasma glucose and/or repeat HbA1c if symptoms or prior testing create concern for intermittent hyperglycemia.  

9. Obtain urinalysis with microscopy, urine glucose, urine ketones, urine protein/albumin, and urine specific gravity.  

10. Obtain urine culture before additional antibiotic treatment if urinary symptoms persist or infection remains a concern.  

11. Test for sexually transmitted urethritis with NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia if dysuria, urethral symptoms, sexual exposure risk, or sterile pyuria is present.  

12. Measure urine electrolytes including urine sodium, potassium, urea, and glucose in the setting of a timed urine collection to evaluate osmole excretion.  

13. Calculate daily urine osmole excretion from 24-hour urine volume and urine osmolality to distinguish water diuresis from solute/osmotic diuresis.  

14. Review whether the low urine sodium and osmolality were measured during high fluid intake, IV fluid administration, fasting, or an acute illness that could affect interpretation.  

15. Assess volume status clinically, including orthostatic blood pressure/heart rate, mucous membranes, weight change, edema, and signs of dehydration.  

16. Obtain a detailed history of daily fluid intake, compulsive water drinking, dry mouth, psychiatric illness, exercise habits, and intentional “hydration” behaviors.  

17. Screen for medications and substances associated with polyuria or nephrogenic DI, including lithium, demeclocycline, amphotericin B, foscarnet, ifosfamide, cisplatin, diuretics, SGLT2 inhibitors, caffeine, alcohol, and herbal products.  

18. Review prior or current lithium exposure, including remote exposure, and obtain a lithium level if current use or toxicity is possible.  

19. Review dietary solute intake, including very low-protein diet, low-sodium diet, tube feeds, high-protein supplements, and high-salt intake, which can alter urine volume and urine osmoles.  

20. Assess for symptoms suggesting central nervous system or pituitary disease, including headache, visual changes, galactorrhea, libido/erectile changes, fatigue, weight change, and symptoms of other pituitary hormone deficiencies.  

21. Assess for history of head trauma, neurosurgery, pituitary surgery, meningitis/encephalitis, infiltrative disease, autoimmune disease, radiation, or intracranial tumors.
