30. Consider MRI of the brain and pituitary with contrast, including pituitary stalk and posterior pituitary evaluation, if central DI is biochemically supported or pituitary symptoms/signs are present.  
31. Consider chest imaging, inflammatory testing, ACE level, IgG4 evaluation, or targeted infectious/infiltrative workup if MRI or history suggests sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, Langerhans-cell histiocytosis, IgG4-related disease, or malignancy.  
32. Consider genetic evaluation for inherited central or nephrogenic DI if there is childhood onset, family history, unexplained lifelong polydipsia/polyuria, or suggestive syndromic features.  
33. Obtain post-void residual bladder volume by ultrasound to assess incomplete bladder emptying as a cause of urinary frequency/nocturia.  
34. Consider renal and bladder ultrasound if obstruction, hydronephrosis, stones, structural renal disease, elevated creatinine, hematuria, or recurrent urinary symptoms are present.  
35. Evaluate for lower urinary tract causes of frequency, including overactive bladder, interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, prostatitis, urethritis, and sexually transmitted infection when symptoms or risk factors support these diagnoses.  
36. Obtain gonorrhea/chlamydia nucleic acid testing and consider other STI testing if dysuria, urethral discharge, pelvic symptoms, or relevant sexual exposure is present.  
37. Consider urology referral for persistent urinary frequency without documented high urine volume, abnormal post-void residual, hematuria, recurrent infection, bladder pain, or suspected lower urinary tract pathology.  
38. Refer to endocrinology on a routine-to-urgent basis for confirmed hypotonic polyuria, abnormal serum sodium, suspected DI, need for dynamic testing, or suspected pituitary disease.  
39. Refer urgently to endocrinology or the emergency department if hypernatremia, rising serum osmolality, confusion, severe weakness, inability to maintain oral intake, syncope, or clinically significant dehydration develops.  
40. Hold or reduce nonessential agents contributing to polyuria when clinically feasible, including caffeine-containing products, alcohol, unnecessary diuretics, and medications identified during review, with prescriber oversight.  
41. If lithium is being used, coordinate with psychiatry and nephrology/endocrinology before dose reduction, discontinuation, or substitution; do not abruptly stop lithium without a psychiatric treatment plan.  
42. If central DI is confirmed, consider desmopressin therapy such as oral desmopressin 0.05–0.2 mg once or twice daily, intranasal desmopressin 10–20 mcg daily in divided doses, or parenteral desmopressin under specialist direction.  
43. If desmopressin is initiated, counsel on drinking to thirst rather than scheduled excess fluid intake and on holding or seeking advice for doses during vomiting, diarrhea, acute illness, or unusually high fluid consumption.  
44. Monitor serum sodium within several days of desmopressin initiation or dose change, again within 1–2 weeks, and periodically thereafter; assess urgently for nausea, headache, confusion, weight gain, or seizures suggesting hyponatremia.  
45. If nephrogenic DI is confirmed, address the underlying cause and consider specialist-directed therapies such as a low-solute diet, thiazide diuretic therapy (for example hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg orally once or twice daily), amiloride 5–10 mg orally daily for lithium-associated DI, or indomethacin in selected cases.  
46. If thiazide, amiloride, or NSAID therapy is considered for nephrogenic DI, monitor blood pressure, creatinine/eGFR, potassium, sodium, volume status, and gastrointestinal/renal adverse effects.  
47. Counsel on limiting excessive dietary sodium and excessive protein intake if nephrogenic DI or high-solute diuresis is present, while avoiding overly restrictive intake without dietitian or specialist guidance.  
48. Counsel to maintain access to water and to seek urgent care during intercurrent illness, inability to drink, prolonged travel, heat exposure, or reduced consciousness if DI remains possible.  
49. Reassess symptoms, 24-hour urine volume, fluid intake, weight, sodium, serum osmolality, and urine osmolality after completion of the initial diagnostic evaluation or after any treatment change.  
50. If 24-hour urine volume is not elevated and urine testing excludes infection, glucosuria, and renal dysfunction, redirect evaluation toward bladder-focused etiologies of urinary frequency/nocturia rather than DI.

1. Quantify total 24-hour urine volume with a measured collection to distinguish true polyuria (>3 L/day in adults or >40–50 mL/kg/day) from urinary frequency with normal total volume.  

2. Ask the patient to complete a 3-day bladder diary recording fluid intake, void timing, voided volumes, nocturnal urine volume, urgency, caffeine/alcohol intake, and sleep interruptions.  

3. Obtain an early-morning paired serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality, and urine specific gravity before substantial fluid intake if feasible.  

4. Repeat urine osmolality and urine sodium on a properly collected spot urine sample, because isolated low values may reflect high water intake rather than diabetes insipidus.  

5. Measure serum glucose at the time of urine testing and obtain urinalysis for glucose and ketones to exclude osmotic diuresis not captured by a prior A1c.  

6. Obtain a urinalysis with microscopy, urine culture, and sexually transmitted infection testing as indicated to reassess persistent urinary symptoms and exclude infection/urethritis.  

7. Check serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, potassium, bicarbonate, BUN, creatinine, and estimated GFR to evaluate renal concentrating defects, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, renal disease, and acid-base disorders.  

8. Obtain a complete metabolic panel including repeat sodium and chloride to identify hypernatremia, hyponatremia, or other electrolyte clues to water-balance disorders.  

9. Measure serum uric acid and consider fractional excretion indices if renal tubular disease or impaired concentrating ability is suspected.  

10. Review the timing and amount of daily fluid intake, including intentional water drinking, exercise-related intake, protein supplements, electrolyte drinks, and nighttime drinking.  

11. Screen for caffeine, alcohol, cannabis, energy drinks, and other substances that can increase urine output or worsen nocturia.  

12. Perform a detailed medication review for lithium, demeclocycline, loop diuretics, thiazides, SGLT2 inhibitors, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics, SSRIs, anticholinergics, and over-the-counter/herbal agents.  

13. Ask specifically about prior or current lithium exposure, even if the patient is no longer taking lithium, because nephrogenic diabetes insipidus may persist.  

14. Assess for symptoms of primary polydipsia or compulsive water intake, including anxiety, psychosis, xerostomia, exercise habits, and belief-driven excessive hydration.  

15. Assess for symptoms suggesting central diabetes insipidus, including abrupt onset polyuria/polydipsia, preference for cold water, history of head trauma, neurosurgery, pituitary disease, meningitis, encephalitis, infiltrative disease, or postpartum events where applicable.  

16. Assess for symptoms of anterior pituitary dysfunction, including fatigue, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, headaches, visual changes, weight changes, and symptoms of adrenal or thyroid insufficiency.  

17. Obtain morning cortisol and ACTH, with additional adrenal testing if abnormal, because adrenal insufficiency can alter water handling and may mask diabetes insipidus.  

18. Obtain TSH and free T4 to evaluate thyroid disease contributing to urinary symptoms or pituitary dysfunction.  

19. Obtain prolactin, LH, FSH, testosterone, IGF-1, and other pituitary hormone testing if central diabetes insipidus or pituitary disease is suspected.  

20. Assess vital signs including orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate for volume depletion or autonomic symptoms.  

21. Perform physical examination for dehydration, edema, neurologic abnormalities, visual field deficits, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary findings, and signs of systemic inflammatory or infiltrative disease.  

22. Calculate 24-hour osmole excretion using measured urine volume and urine osmolality to distinguish water diuresis from solute diuresis.  

23. If 24-hour urine volume is not elevated, shift the evaluation toward lower urinary tract causes of frequency/nocturia rather than diabetes insipidus.  

24. Measure post-void residual by bladder ultrasound to assess incomplete emptying, retention, or dysfunctional voiding as causes of frequent small-volume voids.  

25. Consider renal and bladder ultrasound if there is hematuria, renal dysfunction, recurrent infection, flank pain, retention, or concern for structural urinary tract disease.  

26. Consider uroflowmetry and formal urodynamic testing if the bladder diary suggests small-volume frequency, urgency, obstruction, or dysfunctional voiding.  

27. Consider screening for obstructive sleep apnea, including sleep history and validated screening questionnaire, because sleep apnea can cause nocturia through nocturnal natriuresis.  

28. Refer to endocrinology on a nonurgent but timely basis if true hypotonic polyuria is documented or if serum sodium/osmolality results suggest diabetes insipidus.  

29. Refer urgently to endocrinology or emergency care if hypernatremia, dehydration, altered mental status, inability to maintain oral intake, or rapidly increasing urine output is present.  

30. Perform a supervised water-deprivation test with serial weight, blood pressure, serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality, and urine volume if the diagnosis remains uncertain and appropriate expertise is available.  

31. Establish stopping criteria before a water-deprivation test, such as significant weight loss, hypotension, rising serum sodium/osmolality, severe thirst, dizziness, or inability to tolerate dehydration.  

32. Administer desmopressin at the end of a formal water-deprivation test and measure the change in urine osmolality to help distinguish central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.  

33. Consider hypertonic-saline–stimulated copeptin testing, where available, as an alternative or preferred diagnostic strategy to differentiate central diabetes insipidus from primary polydipsia.  

34. Consider arginine-stimulated copeptin testing where available as another diagnostic approach for suspected central diabetes insipidus versus primary polydipsia.  

35. Measure baseline copeptin if locally available; a markedly elevated level in the appropriate setting may support nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.  

36. Obtain MRI of the pituitary/hypothalamus with contrast if central diabetes insipidus is confirmed or strongly suspected, particularly with headache, visual symptoms, pituitary hormone abnormalities, or no obvious reversible cause.  

37. Consider chest imaging, inflammatory testing, or targeted evaluation for sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, histiocytosis, autoimmune disease, malignancy, or infiltrative disorders if MRI or systemic features suggest an infiltrative central cause.  

38. If nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is suspected, evaluate for reversible causes including hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, kidney disease, urinary obstruction, and medication exposure.  

39. Hold or discontinue a suspected causative medication, when clinically safe and coordinated with the prescribing clinician, such as lithium, demeclocycline, or an unnecessary diuretic.  

40. Avoid empiric desmopressin before establishing the diagnosis unless directed by an endocrinologist, because use in primary polydipsia can cause dangerous hyponatremia.  

41. If central diabetes insipidus is confirmed, consider initiating desmopressin with route and dose individualized by endocrinology (oral, intranasal, or subcutaneous) and with sodium monitoring.  

42. If desmopressin is started, counsel on limiting fluid intake to thirst rather than drinking excessively and provide education about symptoms of hyponatremia, including headache, nausea, confusion, and seizures.  

43. If nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is confirmed, consider dietary sodium reduction and moderate protein intake to reduce obligatory urine solute load.  

44. If nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is confirmed, consider treatment with a thiazide diuretic, such as hydrochlorothiazide or chlorthalidone, with electrolyte and renal-function monitoring.  

45. If lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is confirmed or strongly suspected, consider amiloride therapy in consultation with endocrinology/nephrology and monitor potassium and kidney function.  

46. Consider NSAID therapy such as indomethacin only in selected refractory nephrogenic diabetes insipidus cases under specialist supervision because of gastrointestinal, renal, and cardiovascular risks.  

47. Refer to nephrology if nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, chronic kidney disease, persistent electrolyte abnormalities, renal tubular dysfunction, or unclear renal concentrating impairment is identified.  

48. Refer to urology if total urine volume is normal but frequency/nocturia persists, particularly if post-void residual is elevated, urgency is prominent, hematuria is present, or bladder pathology is suspected.  

49. Counsel the patient not to intentionally restrict water intake at home as a diagnostic test and not to undertake water deprivation without medical supervision.  

50. Arrange follow-up after the bladder diary, 24-hour urine measurement, and paired serum/urine osmolality studies, with earlier reassessment for worsening thirst, dehydration, neurologic symptoms, fever, flank pain, dysuria, gross hematuria, or inability to maintain hydration.

1. Obtain a detailed headache history using a structured diary: onset, duration, location, character, severity, associated symptoms, triggers, aura, positional component, exertional/valsalva association, sleep relationship, and response to medications.  

2. Perform a complete neurologic examination, including mental status, cranial nerves, motor/sensory testing, coordination, gait, reflexes, visual fields, and fundoscopy for papilledema.  

3. Measure blood pressure and perform a general examination for systemic contributors to headache.  

4. Obtain brain MRI with and without gadolinium contrast to evaluate for structural sequelae of prior traumatic brain injuries and other secondary headache causes.  

5. Include susceptibility-weighted imaging/gradient-echo sequences on MRI to assess for chronic microhemorrhage or prior traumatic injury.  

6. Consider MRI angiography or venography of the head if history or examination suggests vascular pathology, venous sinus thrombosis, aneurysm, dissection, or intracranial-pressure disorder.  

7. Obtain noncontrast head CT urgently rather than outpatient MRI if he develops an acute “worst headache,” sudden thunderclap onset, new acute head trauma, seizure, altered mental status, or focal neurologic deficit.  

8. Compare any new imaging with prior head imaging if outside records are available.  

9. Screen for medication-overuse headache by documenting the number of days per month he takes aspirin, ibuprofen, acetaminophen, caffeine-containing products, or other acute headache medicines.  

10. Document vascular risk factors before using vasoconstrictive acute migraine therapies: hypertension, coronary disease, stroke/TIA, peripheral vascular disease, smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and family history of premature cardiovascular disease.  

11. Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, and renal function testing if frequent NSAID use is ongoing or preventive medication choices may affect renal/hepatic function.  

12. Consider liver-function testing before or during use of hepatically metabolized preventive agents such as valproate.  

13. Consider ESR and CRP only if new symptoms raise concern for inflammatory disease, such as scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, fevers, weight loss, polymyalgia symptoms, or atypical persistent pain.  

14. Refer to neurology/headache medicine for diagnostic confirmation, imaging interpretation, and management of chronic progressive unilateral headaches after repetitive head injury.  

15. Refer urgently to neurology or the emergency department if MRI is abnormal, the neurologic examination becomes abnormal, or red-flag features emerge.  

16. Classify the current phenotype using International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria, including possible migraine without aura, persistent post-traumatic headache, cervicogenic headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, neuralgia, or medication-overuse headache.  

17. Trial early-treatment ibuprofen 400–600 mg orally at headache onset, with food, subject to renal, gastrointestinal, bleeding, and cardiovascular risk assessment.  

18. Trial naproxen 500 mg orally at onset followed by 250–500 mg once 8–12 hours later if needed, instead of repeated mixed NSAID dosing.  

19. Avoid taking aspirin and ibuprofen together for the same attack unless specifically directed, because of increased gastrointestinal and bleeding risk and potential interference with aspirin’s antiplatelet effect.  

20. Limit NSAID or aspirin acute-treatment use to fewer than 15 days per month to reduce medication-overuse headache risk.  

21. Consider acetaminophen 1,000 mg orally at onset as an alternative acute agent, with a maximum total daily dose adjusted for liver disease, alcohol use, and other acetaminophen-containing products.  

22. Trial a migraine-specific triptan such as sumatriptan 50–100 mg orally at onset, repeatable once after at least 2 hours, with a maximum of 200 mg/day if no triptan contraindications exist.  

23. Consider sumatriptan 20 mg intranasally or 6 mg subcutaneously for attacks with nausea, inability to take oral medication, or need for faster onset.  

24. Consider rizatriptan 5–10 mg orally at onset as an alternative triptan; use the lower 5-mg dose when co-administered with propranolol.  

25. Limit triptans, gepants, ditans, combination analgesics, and opioids to fewer than 10 days per month to reduce medication-overuse headache risk.  

26. Avoid triptans or ergot derivatives if he has known coronary artery disease, prior stroke/TIA, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, brainstem aura, or other relevant vascular contraindications.  

27. Consider ubrogepant 50–100 mg orally at onset, with repeat dosing after at least 2 hours if needed, as a nonvasoconstrictive acute alternative.  

28. Consider rimegepant 75 mg orally disintegrating tablet once per attack as another nonvasoconstrictive acute option.  

29. Consider lasmiditan 50–200 mg orally for acute attacks when triptans are unsuitable; counsel that he must not drive or operate machinery for at least 8 hours after a dose.  

30. Add an antiemetic for attacks with meaningful nausea, such as metoclopramide 5–10 mg orally at onset or prochlorperazine 5–10 mg orally as needed, with counseling about sedation and extrapyramidal effects.  

31. Consider preventive migraine therapy because attacks occur 2–3 days per week, last approximately 8 hours, and impair work function.  

32. Trial topiramate 25 mg orally nightly, increasing by 25 mg weekly as tolerated toward 50 mg twice daily; monitor for cognitive slowing, paresthesias, weight loss, mood effects, metabolic acidosis, and nephrolithiasis.  

33. Obtain baseline serum bicarbonate and consider periodic bicarbonate/renal monitoring if topiramate is used.  

34. Trial propranolol 20–40 mg orally twice daily or a long-acting equivalent for prevention; monitor heart rate, blood pressure, fatigue, depression, erectile dysfunction, and exercise tolerance.  

35. Avoid or reconsider beta-blocker prophylaxis in asthma with bronchospasm, marked bradycardia, hypotension, heart block, or decompensated heart failure.  

36. Trial amitriptyline 10–25 mg orally at bedtime, titrating gradually as tolerated, particularly if insomnia, chronic pain, or mood symptoms coexist; monitor for sedation, weight gain, anticholinergic effects, and cardiac-conduction concerns.  

37. Consider nortriptyline 10–25 mg orally nightly as a potentially better-tolerated tricyclic alternative.  

38. Consider venlafaxine extended release 37.5 mg orally daily, titrating toward 75–150 mg/day, particularly if anxiety or depression accompanies headaches; monitor blood pressure and discontinuation symptoms.  

39. Consider candesartan 4–8 mg orally daily, titrating toward 16 mg/day for prevention; monitor blood pressure, potassium, and renal function.  

40. Consider a calcitonin gene-related peptide monoclonal antibody preventive, such as erenumab 70–140 mg subcutaneously monthly or another agent in the class, if standard oral preventive therapies fail, are contraindicated, or are poorly tolerated.  

41. Consider onabotulinumtoxinA injections using a chronic-migraine protocol if he reaches chronic migraine frequency (at least 15 headache days/month for more than 3 months, with migraine features on at least 8 days/month).  

42. Consider occipital nerve block or trigger-point injections if examination identifies occipital neuralgia, focal scalp tenderness, cervical muscle trigger points, or a prominent cervicogenic component.  

43. Assess for neck pain, reduced cervical range of motion, prior cervical injury, and reproducible headache provocation from the neck; refer to physical therapy if a cervical contribution is present.  

44. Refer to a concussion/TBI rehabilitation clinic, physiatry, neuropsychology, or behavioral-health service if cognitive, vestibular, sleep, mood, or occupational sequelae of repetitive TBI are identified.  

45. Counsel on regular sleep timing, hydration, consistent meals, gradual aerobic exercise, avoidance of prolonged fasting, and management of common individual triggers such as alcohol, dehydration, skipped meals, and excessive caffeine.  

46. Counsel to avoid abrupt caffeine withdrawal but to limit routine caffeine intake and avoid frequent caffeine-containing combination analgesics.  

47. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea, insomnia, depression, anxiety, PTSD, and substance use, and treat or refer for clinically significant findings because these can worsen headache burden.  

48. Provide a written acute-treatment plan: treat early in the attack, use one primary acute medication strategy at a time, record response, and avoid frequent rescue-medication use.  

49. Schedule follow-up in approximately 4–8 weeks after imaging and initiation or adjustment of therapy, with review of headache-day frequency, migraine-day frequency, disability, acute-medication days, adverse effects, blood pressure, and diary data.  

50. Escalate urgently for new focal neurologic signs, persistent vomiting, papilledema/visual loss, seizure, personality or cognitive decline, fever/meningismus, headache triggered by exertion or position, progressive worsening despite treatment, or sudden maximal-intensity headache.

19. Expedite neurologic evaluation if MRI is abnormal, headache frequency accelerates, headaches become continuous, or atypical neurologic symptoms emerge.  
20. Refer to a concussion/TBI rehabilitation clinic if he has ongoing cognitive, vestibular, mood, sleep, or functional sequelae of repeated head injuries.  
21. Use a headache diary for at least 4–8 weeks to document headache days, severity, duration, disability, acute medication days, triggers, and response to treatment.  
22. Limit aspirin, ibuprofen, and other simple analgesics to fewer than 15 days per month to reduce medication-overuse headache risk.  
23. Consider stopping or tapering excessive acute analgesic use if medication-overuse headache is identified, with a plan for bridge therapy and preventive treatment if needed.  
24. Avoid opioid analgesics and butalbital-containing products for recurrent headache because of medication-overuse, dependence, and chronification risks.  
25. For acute attacks, consider ibuprofen 400–600 mg orally at onset, with food, if there are no renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, anticoagulation, or bleeding contraindications.

37. Consider topiramate 25 mg orally nightly, titrating by 25 mg weekly as tolerated toward 50 mg twice daily; monitor cognitive slowing, paresthesias, mood effects, weight loss, nephrolithiasis, and glaucoma symptoms.

48. Counsel on regular sleep schedule, adequate hydration, consistent meals, gradual aerobic exercise, stress-management strategies, and avoidance of personally identified triggers.

Arrange follow-up within 4–8 weeks after imaging and treatment initiation to review imaging, headache diary, acute-medication days, adverse effects, blood pressure, functional impact, and need for preventive-treatment titration; seek emergency care immediately for thunderclap onset, new focal deficits, seizure, fever/meningismus, persistent vomiting, confusion, visual loss, or a major change in headache pattern.

1. Obtain a detailed headache history using a structured headache diary: onset, duration, location, quality, severity, associated symptoms, triggers, menstrual relationship, acute-medication use, disability, and number of headache/migraine days per month.

3. Measure blood pressure, BMI, and screen for sleep apnea risk, as hypertension, obesity, and sleep disorders can contribute to headache burden.  

4. Review the full traumatic brain injury history, including number of injuries, loss of consciousness, amnesia, mechanism, prior imaging, persistent cognitive symptoms, dizziness, mood symptoms, and neck injury.  

5. Screen for headache red flags using a formal approach such as SNOOP10, including positional headache, exertional/Valsalva precipitation, pregnancy/postpartum status, cancer/immunosuppression, fever, visual changes, seizure, altered mental status, and systemic inflammatory symptoms.  

6. Obtain MRI brain with and without contrast because of progressive unilateral headaches, change in pattern over two years, and history of repeated head trauma.  

7. Consider MRI brain without contrast initially if contrast is contraindicated or if local imaging protocols reserve contrast for abnormal noncontrast findings.  

8. Add vascular imaging (MRA or CTA of the head and neck) if symptoms/history raise concern for aneurysm, arterial dissection, vascular malformation, thunderclap onset, Horner syndrome, pulsatile tinnitus, or focal neurologic findings.

11. Consider cervical-spine imaging if examination/history suggests cervicogenic headache, neck trauma, radicular symptoms, myelopathy, or significant cervical range-of-motion limitation.  

12. Obtain baseline CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, renal function, and liver enzymes if frequent NSAID use or prescription acute/preventive medications are being considered.  

13. Obtain a pregnancy test before prescribing medications with pregnancy-related risks, especially valproate, topiramate, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, or certain CGRP-pathway therapies.  

14. Consider ESR and CRP only if systemic symptoms, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, polymyalgia symptoms, or another inflammatory/vasculitic syndrome becomes plausible.  

15. Refer to neurology or a headache-medicine specialist on a routine-but-timely basis for diagnostic confirmation, imaging interpretation, and preventive-treatment selection.  

16. Expedite neurology evaluation if imaging is abnormal, headaches escalate rapidly, neurologic examination is abnormal, or there is concern for secondary post-traumatic pathology.  

17. Document a working differential that includes migraine without aura, persistent post-traumatic headache with migrainous phenotype, cervicogenic headache, occipital neuralgia, medication-overuse headache, hemicrania continua, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia, and secondary intracranial causes.

**Diagnostics**

1. Obtain urgent stroke-neurology evaluation for high-risk transient ischemic attack despite negative initial CT/MRI.  
2. Confirm the episode history, including exact onset/offset, negative versus positive symptoms, gait symptoms, sensory symptoms, headache, seizure features, neck pain, and prior similar episodes.  
3. Perform a focused neurologic examination and document baseline NIHSS/mRS or comparable functional status.  
4. Obtain 12-lead ECG to assess for atrial fibrillation/flutter, conduction disease, prior infarction, or other arrhythmia clues.  
5. Complete the ordered 7-day Zio patch ambulatory rhythm monitor.  
6. Consider extended ambulatory rhythm monitoring for 14–30 days if the 7-day monitor is unrevealing and no alternative stroke mechanism is found.  
7. Consider implantable loop recorder placement if recurrent cryptogenic TIA/stroke occurs or if prolonged monitoring is otherwise indicated.  
8. Obtain urgent noninvasive cervical carotid imaging with carotid duplex ultrasound.  
9. Obtain CTA head and neck to assess extracranial and intracranial carotid/vertebral stenosis, occlusion, dissection, and intracranial atherosclerotic disease.  
10. Consider MRA head and neck instead of CTA when iodinated contrast, radiation exposure, or renal function makes CTA less suitable.  
11. Review the original MRI brain quality and timing; consider repeat MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging if the original study was early, technically limited, or clinical suspicion remains high.  
12. Assess for posterior-circulation ischemia with vascular imaging of vertebral and basilar arteries, even though symptoms were unilateral motor deficits.  
13. Obtain transthoracic echocardiography with Doppler to evaluate left ventricular function, valvular disease, intracardiac thrombus, chamber enlargement, and potential cardioembolic sources.  
14. Consider echocardiography with agitated-saline (“bubble”) study if there is concern for intracardiac shunt or if no other etiology is identified.  
15. Consider transesophageal echocardiography if transthoracic imaging is nondiagnostic and concern remains for left atrial appendage thrombus, valvular vegetation, aortic arch atheroma, or other cardioembolic source.  
16. Obtain fasting lipid panel, including LDL-C and triglycerides, as a secondary-prevention baseline.  
17. Obtain hemoglobin A1c and review home glucose data to assess glycemic control.  
18. Obtain CBC with platelet count as a baseline before and during dual antiplatelet therapy.  
19. Obtain serum creatinine/eGFR and electrolytes to guide contrast imaging and medication selection.  
20. Obtain liver enzymes as a baseline if initiating or intensifying statin therapy.  
21. Consider PT/INR and aPTT if there is concern for occult anticoagulant use, liver disease, bleeding risk, or future anticoagulation.  
22. Review medication list for agents that increase bleeding risk, including NSAIDs, systemic corticosteroids, anticoagulants, SSRIs/SNRIs, herbal supplements, and alcohol excess.  
23. Evaluate for TIA mimics when clinically suggested, including hypoglycemia, focal seizure/Todd paralysis, migraine aura, peripheral nerve pathology, cervical myelopathy, and functional neurologic disorder.  
24. Check glucose promptly during any recurrent focal neurologic episode to exclude hypoglycemia as a mimic.  

**Medications**

25. Continue aspirin 81 mg orally once daily indefinitely, with reassessment if a cardioembolic indication for anticoagulation is later identified.  
26. Continue clopidogrel 75 mg orally once daily for a total dual-antiplatelet duration of 21 days from initiation, with a documented stop date.  
27. Verify whether an appropriate clopidogrel loading dose was given or whether delayed initiation after the event changes the expected benefit-risk assessment.  
28. Consider extending aspirin-plus-clopidogrel therapy up to 90 days only if symptomatic severe intracranial arterial stenosis or another specific high-risk vascular indication is identified.  
29. Stop clopidogrel after the planned short-course period and continue single antiplatelet therapy unless another indication for dual therapy emerges.  
30. Consider aspirin monotherapy instead of clopidogrel-containing dual therapy if bleeding risk, intolerance, thrombocytopenia, active ulcer disease, or drug interactions are substantial.  
31. Consider clopidogrel 75 mg orally daily as long-term single antiplatelet therapy instead of aspirin if aspirin intolerance or recurrent ischemic events on aspirin occur.  
32. Start or intensify to high-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin 40–80 mg orally daily or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg orally daily, unless contraindicated.  
33. Add ezetimibe 10 mg orally daily if LDL-C remains above a secondary-prevention target despite maximally tolerated statin therapy.  
34. Consider a PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL-C remains elevated despite maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe and overall vascular risk supports escalation.  
35. Review current antihypertensive medications and titrate toward a long-term blood-pressure target commonly below 130/80 mmHg if tolerated.  
36. Avoid excessive blood-pressure reduction or medication over-titration if critical carotid/intracranial stenosis, orthostasis, recurrent hypoperfusion symptoms, or falls are present.  
37. Optimize diabetes therapy to an individualized A1c goal while avoiding hypoglycemia, particularly because hypoglycemia can mimic recurrent TIA.  
38. Consider adding or prioritizing an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist when compatible with renal function, cardiovascular risk, cost, and current diabetes regimen.  
39. Avoid routine anticoagulation unless atrial fibrillation, left ventricular thrombus, mechanical valve, venous thromboembolism, antiphospholipid syndrome, or another clear indication is found.  
40. If atrial fibrillation/flutter is detected, transition from antiplatelet-based stroke prevention to oral anticoagulation when appropriate, using a DOAC dose adjusted for renal function, age, and weight or warfarin when indicated.  
41. Avoid combining chronic anticoagulation with aspirin and/or clopidogrel unless there is a separate compelling indication such as recent coronary stenting.  
42. Consider gastroprotection with a proton-pump inhibitor during dual antiplatelet therapy when gastrointestinal bleeding risk is elevated; avoid or reassess omeprazole/esomeprazole if concern exists for reduced clopidogrel activation.  
43. Stop or minimize nonessential NSAIDs and other medications that materially increase bleeding risk during dual antiplatelet therapy.  

**Procedures / Vascular Interventions**

44. Refer urgently for carotid endarterectomy evaluation if imaging shows symptomatic ipsilateral extracranial internal carotid stenosis of approximately 70–99% and operative risk is acceptable.  
45. Consider carotid endarterectomy evaluation for symptomatic ipsilateral 50–69% carotid stenosis based on sex, age, anatomy, comorbidity, estimated perioperative risk, and expected benefit.  
46. Consider carotid artery stenting rather than endarterectomy when anatomy, prior neck surgery/radiation, restenosis, or surgical risk favors an endovascular approach.  
47. Avoid carotid revascularization for nonstenotic plaque, complete carotid occlusion, or stenosis not anatomically related to the neurologic event unless another indication is present.  
48. Consider neurointerventional consultation if severe symptomatic intracranial stenosis, recurrent ischemia despite intensive medical therapy, or an unusual vascular lesion is identified.  

**Referrals**

49. Refer to a stroke neurologist or dedicated TIA/stroke clinic on an urgent basis, ideally within days rather than routine follow-up.  
50. Refer to vascular surgery promptly if carotid imaging demonstrates potentially symptomatic moderate-to-severe extracranial carotid stenosis.  
51. Refer to cardiology if atrial fibrillation, significant structural heart disease, valvular disease, left ventricular thrombus, or a need for advanced cardiac monitoring is identified.  
52. Refer to primary care, endocrinology, or a diabetes-management service for coordinated control of diabetes, hypertension, lipids, renal function, and medication adherence.  
53. Refer to physical therapy, occupational therapy, or rehabilitation medicine if any residual weakness, gait instability, impaired dexterity, or fall risk is found.  

**Counseling**

54. Counsel the patient and family that recurrent unilateral weakness, facial droop, speech difficulty, vision loss, severe imbalance, or sudden severe headache warrants immediate EMS activation rather than waiting for clinic review.  
55. Provide education on the bleeding risks of aspirin plus clopidogrel, including melena, hematemesis, hematuria, persistent epistaxis, unusual bruising, severe headache after trauma, or symptomatic anemia.  
56. Counsel on medication adherence and use of a written antiplatelet calendar specifying the clopidogrel stop date.  
57. Counsel regarding smoking cessation, including pharmacotherapy and cessation-program referral if he smokes.  
58. Counsel on Mediterranean-style or DASH-style diet, sodium reduction, weight management, regular aerobic activity as tolerated, and limiting alcohol.  
59. Screen for and counsel about obstructive sleep apnea if snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, resistant hypertension, or obesity are present.  
60. Advise avoidance of dehydration, missed meals, and hypoglycemia-provoking diabetes regimens when these may contribute to neurologic symptom mimics or hypotension.  
61. Review driving, machinery, and fall precautions if recurrent neurologic spells, arrhythmia, orthostatic symptoms, or residual weakness are present.

49. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea symptoms and consider sleep-medicine referral or polysomnography if there is snoring, witnessed apnea, daytime sleepiness, resistant hypertension, or recurrent vascular events.  
50. Arrange close follow-up within approximately one week to review vascular imaging, rhythm-monitor results, echocardiography, blood pressure, glucose/A1c, LDL, medication adherence, adverse effects, and any recurrent events.

37. If anticoagulation is started for atrial fibrillation or another cardioembolic source, reassess whether aspirin and clopidogrel should be stopped to avoid unnecessary combined antithrombotic bleeding risk, unless there is a separate compelling coronary or vascular indication.  

38. Initiate or intensify high-intensity statin therapy, such as atorvastatin 40–80 mg orally daily or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg orally daily, unless contraindicated or not tolerated.  

39. Consider moderate-intensity statin therapy or the maximally tolerated statin dose if frailty, drug interactions, liver disease, adverse effects, or intolerance prevents high-intensity therapy.  

40. Consider adding ezetimibe 10 mg orally daily if LDL cholesterol remains above the secondary-prevention target despite maximally tolerated statin therapy.  

41. Consider a PCSK9 inhibitor or other lipid-lowering therapy if LDL remains inadequately controlled despite maximally tolerated statin plus ezetimibe, taking into account access, cost, and overall vascular risk.  

42. Review current antihypertensive medications, home blood-pressure readings, orthostatic symptoms, adherence, and secondary causes of poor control.  

43. Establish a long-term blood-pressure target generally below 130/80 mmHg if tolerated, with individualized adjustment for orthostasis, falls, renal disease, and cerebral hypoperfusion risk.  

44. Avoid overly rapid or excessive blood-pressure reduction during immediate evaluation if there is concern for critical carotid/intracranial stenosis, recurrent neurologic symptoms, or impaired cerebral perfusion.  

45. Review diabetes medications and consider adjustment toward individualized glycemic goals; evaluate whether an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist is appropriate for cardiovascular risk reduction if not contraindicated.  

46. Counsel on immediate emergency evaluation for any recurrent focal weakness, numbness, facial droop, speech disturbance, visual loss, severe imbalance, or other stroke symptoms, including calling emergency services rather than waiting for outpatient review.  

47. Counsel on bleeding precautions while taking dual antiplatelet therapy, including reporting melena, hematemesis, hematuria, persistent epistaxis, unusual bruising, severe headache, or head trauma.  

48. Counsel on smoking cessation if applicable, avoidance of secondhand smoke, limiting alcohol, Mediterranean-style dietary pattern, sodium reduction, gradual regular aerobic activity when cleared, weight management, and medication adherence.  

49. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea using history or a validated tool and arrange sleep-study referral if symptoms such as snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence, resistant hypertension, or obesity are present.  

50. Arrange stroke/TIA follow-up within approximately 1 week or sooner after vascular imaging and rhythm-monitor results, with repeat review at completion of clopidogrel therapy, lipid/BP/diabetes reassessment within 4–12 weeks, and immediate escalation if recurrent symptoms occur.

22. Assess whether beta-blocker dose, antihypertensive regimen, or diuretic therapy is causing symptomatic hypotension, bradycardia, dehydration, or cerebral hypoperfusion; adjust if documented.  
23. Continue omeprazole if GERD benefit remains clear, while reassessing long-term need and monitoring for B12 or magnesium deficiency associated with chronic use.  
24. Check oxygen saturation at rest and with ambulation; evaluate for nocturnal hypoxemia if symptoms or risk factors are present.  
25. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea using STOP-BANG or similar criteria, especially if snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, obesity, resistant hypertension, or postoperative hypoxemia are present.  
26. Order polysomnography or home sleep-apnea testing if screening suggests sleep-disordered breathing.  
27. Screen for depression, anxiety, post-ICU syndrome, and post-traumatic stress symptoms using PHQ-9, GAD-7, and targeted psychiatric history.  
28. Refer to neurology or a cognitive-disorders clinic for persistent cognitive impairment, delusions, or abnormal MRI/neuropsychological findings; arrange expedited assessment if symptoms are worsening.  
29. Refer to geriatric psychiatry or psychiatry for assessment of persistent paranoia, delusions, agitation, depression, sleep disturbance, or diagnostic uncertainty.  
30. Refer to neuropsychology for comprehensive testing if bedside screening is abnormal or family reports persistent functional decline despite normal clinic orientation.  
31. Consider EEG if episodes are brief, stereotyped, associated with unresponsiveness, automatisms, post-event confusion, or concern for focal seizures/nonconvulsive seizures.  
32. Consider vascular imaging (CTA/MRA head and neck or carotid duplex) if MRI reveals ischemic injury or if focal symptoms, transient neurologic episodes, carotid bruit, or embolic source concerns emerge.  
33. Obtain ECG and review postoperative rhythm monitoring for atrial fibrillation or other embolic arrhythmias if cerebral ischemia is suspected.  
34. Consider echocardiography and cardiology review if MRI suggests embolic infarcts or there is concern for cardiac thromboembolic source after CABG.  
35. Review vascular secondary-prevention therapy—antiplatelet agent, statin intensity, blood-pressure control, diabetes status, smoking status, and atrial-fibrillation anticoagulation indication—if cerebrovascular disease is identified.  
36. Avoid starting antipsychotic medication solely for mild intermittent paranoia without first evaluating reversible medical, medication-related, neurologic, sleep, and psychiatric contributors.  
37. If delusions cause dangerous agitation, severe distress, inability to receive essential care, or risk to self/others, consider short-term low-dose antipsychotic treatment under psychiatry/medical supervision, such as quetiapine 12.5–25 mg orally at bedtime or risperidone 0.25–0.5 mg orally daily, with ECG/QTc, orthostatic, metabolic, and stroke-risk monitoring.  
38. Avoid routine cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine initiation unless a neurocognitive disorder is established after appropriate neurologic and cognitive evaluation.  
39. Counsel family to maintain a structured daily routine, regular sleep-wake schedule, hydration, nutrition, daylight exposure, physical activity, hearing/vision aids, and frequent calm reorientation.  
40. Counsel avoidance of alcohol, recreational drugs, diphenhydramine-containing sleep aids, and nonprescribed sedatives while cognitive symptoms are being evaluated.  
41. Assess driving, medication-management, financial-management, firearm-access, wandering, and fall risks; advise temporary supervision or driving restriction if confusion or paranoia impairs safety.  
42. Arrange follow-up within 1–2 weeks after MRI and laboratory testing, with repeat cognitive assessment and review of symptom diary/collateral observations.  
43. Instruct the patient and family to seek emergency evaluation immediately for new focal weakness, facial droop, aphasia, severe headache, syncope, seizure, fever with confusion, rapidly worsening mental status, suicidal thoughts, or behavior creating imminent danger.  
44. If MRI, laboratory evaluation, medication review, sleep assessment, and neuropsychological testing are unrevealing but symptoms persist beyond several additional months, consider longitudinal cognitive follow-up with repeat testing at 3–6 months and reassessment for evolving neurodegenerative, autoimmune, infectious, or psychiatric etiologies.

1. Obtain collateral history from the wife regarding onset, fluctuation, frequency, duration, triggers, and functional impact of confusion, delusions, and paranoia.  
2. Perform a structured cognitive screen in clinic (e.g., MoCA) rather than relying on orientation alone.  
3. Arrange formal comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize cognitive domains affected and distinguish residual delirium, mild cognitive impairment, dementia, depression, or psychiatric disease.  
4. Assess instrumental activities of daily living, including medication management, finances, driving, cooking, and ability to use household electrical equipment safely.  
5. Screen specifically for ongoing delirium using a validated tool such as the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) or 4AT.  
6. Perform a detailed mental-status examination, including attention, executive function, thought content, hallucinations, insight, judgment, and suicidal or violent ideation.  
7. Screen for depression with PHQ-9 or Geriatric Depression Scale.  
8. Screen for anxiety and post-traumatic stress symptoms related to CABG/ICU hospitalization.  
9. Obtain a medication reconciliation including prescription drugs, over-the-counter agents, supplements, alcohol, cannabis, and other substances.  
10. Review for medications with anticholinergic, sedative-hypnotic, opioid, antihistamine, corticosteroid, or dopaminergic effects that could worsen cognition or psychosis.  
11. Consider tapering or discontinuing nonessential anticholinergic medications if present.  
12. Consider reducing or discontinuing benzodiazepines, sedative sleep medications, or opioids if present and clinically safe.  
13. Assess adherence, dosing errors, accidental double-dosing, and recent medication changes after discharge.  
14. Obtain CBC to evaluate for anemia, infection, or hematologic abnormalities contributing to cognitive symptoms.  
15. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel including sodium, calcium, renal function, hepatic function, and glucose.  
16. Obtain thyroid-stimulating hormone testing to exclude thyroid dysfunction.  
17. Obtain vitamin B12 level, with methylmalonic acid if the result is borderline.  
18. Obtain folate level if nutritional deficiency is plausible.  
19. Consider thiamine level or empiric thiamine supplementation if alcohol use, malnutrition, prolonged hospitalization, or poor intake is present.  
20. Obtain urinalysis and urine culture only if urinary symptoms, fever, leukocytosis, or other evidence suggests infection.  
21. Evaluate for hypoxemia with pulse oximetry; obtain arterial blood gas only if clinically indicated.  
22. Screen for sleep disruption, insomnia, circadian reversal, and symptoms of obstructive sleep apnea.  
23. Consider referral for sleep study if there is loud snoring, witnessed apneas, excessive daytime sleepiness, or refractory cognitive symptoms.  
24. Obtain MRI brain with and without contrast or MRI brain without contrast using a cognitive/vascular protocol to assess for silent infarcts, microhemorrhages, subdural collection, watershed injury, or structural lesions not seen on CT.  
25. Consider vascular imaging (CTA/MRA head and neck or carotid duplex) if MRI or clinical features suggest cerebrovascular disease.  
26. Consider EEG if episodes are stereotyped, transient, fluctuating, associated with unresponsiveness, or raise concern for focal seizures/nonconvulsive seizures.  
27. Consider lumbar puncture only if there are red flags for CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, rapidly progressive dementia, inflammatory disease, or unexplained progressive decline.  
28. Obtain HIV and syphilis testing if risk factors, atypical presentation, or unexplained cognitive decline warrants reversible-dementia testing.  
29. Assess alcohol intake and screen for alcohol withdrawal, alcohol-related cognitive disorder, or substance-induced psychosis.  
30. Ask about visual or hearing impairment and arrange correction of sensory deficits that could worsen confusion or paranoid interpretations.  
31. Refer to neurology or a cognitive-disorders clinic for evaluation of persistent postoperative cognitive dysfunction and alternative neurologic causes.  
32. Refer to geriatric psychiatry or psychiatry for assessment of persistent delusions, paranoia, mood symptoms, and possible psychotic disorder due to a medical condition.  
33. Consider referral to geriatrics for multidimensional assessment of cognition, medications, function, caregiver needs, and safety.  
34. Communicate with the cardiothoracic surgery and cardiology teams regarding the postoperative course, perioperative complications, cardiopulmonary bypass details, and current cardiac medications.  
35. Assess for recurrent cardiac ischemia, heart failure, arrhythmia, hypotension, or low cardiac output symptoms that could contribute to cerebral hypoperfusion.  
36. Obtain ECG and consider ambulatory rhythm monitoring if palpitations, syncope, episodic confusion, or concern for arrhythmia is present.  
37. Check orthostatic vital signs and review antihypertensive regimen for hypotension or excessive blood-pressure variability.  
38. Avoid starting cholinesterase inhibitors or memantine until a clearer cognitive diagnosis and trajectory are established.  
39. Avoid empiric antipsychotic treatment solely for intermittent paranoia unless symptoms create substantial distress, dangerous behavior, or inability to provide care.  
40. If antipsychotic treatment becomes necessary for severe psychosis or dangerous agitation, consider the lowest effective dose of an agent such as quetiapine, with ECG/QTc, orthostasis, metabolic, stroke-risk, and cardiac-risk monitoring.  
41. Counsel the patient and wife that cognitive and neuropsychiatric symptoms can persist for weeks to months after postoperative delirium, while emphasizing that persistent or worsening symptoms merit reassessment.  
42. Provide delirium-prevention and cognitive-support measures: regular sleep-wake schedule, daylight exposure, hydration, regular meals, activity, glasses/hearing aids, orientation cues, and avoidance of unnecessary sedatives.  
43. Advise temporary supervision of medications, finances, driving, and potentially hazardous activities until cognition and judgment are formally assessed.  
44. Counsel the wife to document episodes in a symptom diary, including time of day, sleep, medication timing, associated medical symptoms, and safety concerns.  
45. Arrange close primary-care follow-up within 1–2 weeks after initial testing, with serial cognitive testing over subsequent months.  
46. Escalate urgently to emergency evaluation for acute change from baseline, new focal neurologic deficit, severe headache, fever, syncope, chest pain, hypoxia, inability to maintain hydration, or markedly impaired consciousness.  
47. Arrange urgent psychiatric or emergency assessment if paranoia leads to threats, weapon access, inability to care for self, suicidal ideation, homicidal ideation, or risk to his wife.

1. Obtain brain MRI without contrast, including diffusion-weighted imaging/ADC, FLAIR, susceptibility-weighted imaging, and vascular sequences, to detect subacute ischemia, embolic infarcts, microhemorrhage, or other lesions missed by noncontrast CT.  
2. Add MR angiography of the head and neck if MRI suggests ischemia or if there are concern for vascular stenosis, embolic disease, or posterior-circulation pathology.  
3. Obtain a formal bedside cognitive screen such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), documenting domain-specific deficits in attention, executive function, memory, language, and visuospatial ability.  
4. Obtain collateral history from family/caregivers regarding baseline cognition before CABG, onset after surgery, fluctuation, functional decline, hallucinations, sleep changes, medication adherence, and safety concerns.  
5. Perform a detailed functional assessment of instrumental activities of daily living, including finances, medication management, driving, cooking, appointments, and technology use.  
6. Review the hospital/CABG records for perioperative hypotension, hypoxemia, arrhythmia, stroke concern, prolonged ICU stay, infection, renal failure, sedative exposure, and duration/severity of postoperative delirium.  
7. Perform repeat complete neurologic examination with focused testing of gait, eye movements, visual fields, coordination, extrapyramidal signs, frontal-release signs, and focal deficits.  
8. Screen for ongoing delirium features, including inattention, fluctuating alertness, altered sleep-wake cycle, acute medical illness, and waxing/waning cognition.  
9. Obtain CBC to assess for anemia, leukocytosis, and other hematologic contributors to cognitive symptoms.  
10. Obtain comprehensive metabolic panel, including sodium, calcium, renal function, hepatic function, glucose, and bicarbonate.  
11. Obtain thyroid-stimulating hormone with reflex free T4.  
12. Obtain vitamin B12 level, with methylmalonic acid if the B12 result is borderline or discordant with clinical suspicion.  
13. Obtain folate level if nutritional deficiency, macrocytosis, alcohol use, malabsorption, or poor diet is suspected.  
14. Obtain thiamine level or administer empiric thiamine if there is poor nutrition, alcohol use disorder, prolonged vomiting, diuretic-associated nutritional risk, or concern for deficiency.  
15. Obtain urinalysis and urine culture only if urinary symptoms, fever, leukocytosis, or other evidence raises concern for infection.  
16. Evaluate oxygenation with pulse oximetry and consider arterial blood gas only if hypoxemia, hypercapnia, severe lung disease, or respiratory symptoms are present.  
17. Screen for obstructive sleep apnea and sleep disruption; arrange sleep study if there is snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime somnolence, resistant hypertension, or nocturnal confusion.  
18. Screen for depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, and post-ICU psychological sequelae using validated instruments such as PHQ-9, GAD-7, and PTSD screening tools.  
19. Ask specifically about visual/auditory hallucinations, dream enactment behavior, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and neuroleptic sensitivity to assess for possible Lewy body disease.  
20. Assess alcohol intake, cannabis use, stimulant use, opioid use, nonprescribed sedatives, and other substance exposures; obtain toxicology testing when history is unreliable or exposure is plausible.  
21. Conduct a comprehensive medication reconciliation, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter agents, supplements, recently stopped medications, and adherence.  
22. Identify and taper or discontinue nonessential anticholinergic medications, such as diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, tricyclic antidepressants, or bladder antispasmodics.  
23. Identify and taper or discontinue nonessential benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, muscle relaxants, and other centrally sedating agents, avoiding abrupt cessation when withdrawal is possible.  
24. Reassess opioid use after CABG and reduce/discontinue opioids when clinically feasible, using a gradual taper if prolonged use has occurred.  
25. Review beta-blocker, antihypertensive, diuretic, and antianginal regimens for symptomatic hypotension, bradycardia, orthostasis, dehydration, or cerebral hypoperfusion.  
26. Measure orthostatic vital signs and review home blood-pressure readings, particularly if confusion occurs after standing, exertion, medication dosing, or low blood-pressure episodes.  
27. Refer to neurology or a cognitive-disorders clinic on an expedited outpatient basis for persistent cognitive impairment with new delusions after cardiac surgery.  
28. Refer for formal neuropsychological testing after acute reversible causes are assessed, to characterize deficits and establish a cognitive baseline for postoperative cognitive dysfunction versus emerging neurodegenerative disease.  
29. Consider EEG, preferably prolonged or ambulatory EEG if symptoms are episodic or stereotyped, to evaluate for focal seizures or nonconvulsive seizure activity.  
30. Obtain ECG and consider ambulatory rhythm monitoring if there are palpitations, syncope, transient neurologic symptoms, or concern for occult atrial fibrillation causing embolic events.  
31. Consider transthoracic echocardiography, with bubble study or transesophageal echocardiography when clinically indicated, if MRI identifies embolic-appearing infarcts or there is concern for cardioembolic source.  
32. Continue indicated secondary cardiovascular prevention medications, such as antiplatelet therapy and statin therapy, while evaluating for occult cerebrovascular injury, unless a contraindication emerges.  
33. Consider psychiatric consultation if delusions, paranoia, hallucinations, severe distress, agitation, impaired reality testing, or concern for a primary mood/psychotic syndrome is present.  
34. If psychosis causes dangerous agitation or severe distress after medical/neurologic evaluation, consider short-term low-dose antipsychotic treatment with psychiatry input, ECG/QTc monitoring, and attention to CAD/cardiovascular risk.  
35. Avoid routine antipsychotic use solely for mild non-dangerous confusion, and reassess whether symptoms are due to delirium, medication effects, sleep disturbance, or neurologic disease before starting treatment.  
36. Counsel the patient and family that persistent cognitive symptoms can follow postoperative delirium and CABG, while emphasizing that new focal symptoms, rapidly worsening cognition, or safety threats require urgent reassessment.  
37. Advise temporary avoidance of driving, unsupervised medication administration, management of major finances, firearms access, and hazardous equipment until cognition, delusions, and functional safety are clarified.  
38. Establish caregiver supervision and a written medication schedule, pill organizer, or pharmacy blister packs if there are medication errors, missed doses, or paranoid refusal of treatment.  
39. Optimize nonpharmacologic cognitive recovery measures: regular daytime activity, structured routine, hydration, adequate nutrition, hearing/vision correction, sleep hygiene, daylight exposure, and avoidance of alcohol/recreational drugs.  
40. Arrange close follow-up within 1–2 weeks to review MRI, laboratory results, medication changes, collateral history, symptom trajectory, and safety.  
41. Repeat cognitive screening at approximately 4–12 weeks after correcting reversible contributors and compare with the initial MoCA or equivalent assessment.  
42. Escalate to emergency evaluation immediately for acute focal weakness, facial droop, aphasia, new severe headache, seizure, syncope, sudden marked worsening of confusion, fever with altered mental status, or inability to maintain safety.  
43. If MRI demonstrates acute/subacute infarction, initiate stroke workup and secondary-prevention management, including vascular imaging, cardiac-source evaluation, risk-factor optimization, and stroke-neurology referral.  
44. If metabolic, endocrine, nutritional, infectious, hypoxic, or medication-related abnormalities are identified, correct the specific cause and reassess cognition after treatment.  
45. If symptoms persist despite normal MRI, reversible-cause testing, medication optimization, and resolution of delirium risk factors, proceed with neuropsychological testing and longitudinal evaluation for mild cognitive impairment, vascular cognitive impairment, Lewy body disease, or another neurodegenerative disorder.

1. Review the current CT images and radiology report directly, confirming the extent, distribution, and airway-centered nature of the right-lower-lobe tree-in-bud nodularity, mucus plugging, and bronchial wall thickening.  

2. Obtain and compare all available prior chest CTs or radiographs, including the study from 5 years ago, to determine whether any subtle chronic airway abnormality predated the new findings.  

3. Request thoracic-radiology over-read or multidisciplinary imaging review if the pattern is uncertain or if there is concern for an endobronchial obstructing lesion, aspiration, infection, or malignancy.  

4. Perform a focused respiratory history for recurrent cough, sputum production, wheeze, hemoptysis, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and declining exercise tolerance.  

5. Ask specifically about recent upper-respiratory infection, COVID-19, influenza, pneumonia, and the timing of the self-limited cough relative to the CT.  

6. Assess tuberculosis and nontuberculous mycobacterial exposure risks, including prior TB, known contacts, travel, congregate living, incarceration, homelessness, occupational exposure, and immunosuppressive medications.  

7. Assess aspiration risk factors, including dysphagia, choking, coughing with meals, stroke, Parkinson disease, alcohol use, sedatives, poor dentition, obstructive sleep apnea, and nocturnal regurgitation.  

8. Reassess for gastroesophageal reflux symptoms and consider “silent” reflux or nocturnal aspiration despite absence of typical heartburn.  

9. Obtain a focused exposure history for mold, hot tubs, birds, farming, soil exposure, dust, biomass smoke, vaping, and occupational inhalational exposures.  

10. Perform a complete physical examination including oxygen saturation, lung auscultation, lymph-node examination, weight/BMI, and signs of systemic infection or eosinophilic disease.  

11. Obtain a complete blood count with differential to quantify current absolute eosinophil count and assess for leukocytosis, anemia, or thrombocytopenia.  

12. Review the longitudinal eosinophil trend, prior hematology workup, medication list, allergic history, parasitic exposure history, and any previous organ involvement from eosinophilia.  

13. Obtain a basic metabolic panel and liver tests if contrast imaging, antimicrobial treatment, systemic therapy, or invasive testing may become necessary.  

14. Obtain inflammatory markers such as CRP and/or ESR if there is concern for active infection or inflammatory lung disease.  

15. Obtain baseline spirometry with bronchodilator testing if there is chronic cough, wheeze, smoking-related lung disease concern, or CT evidence of chronic airway disease.  

16. Consider full pulmonary function testing with lung volumes and DLCO if dyspnea develops, spirometry is abnormal, or there is concern for clinically significant chronic lung disease.  

17. Obtain expectorated sputum for routine bacterial culture and Gram stain if productive cough or purulent sputum is present.  

18. Obtain three sputum specimens for acid-fast bacilli smear/culture and mycobacterial speciation if symptoms persist, imaging progresses, there are TB/NTM risk factors, or bronchiectatic disease is suspected.  

19. Obtain sputum fungal culture or targeted fungal testing if there are relevant geographic, environmental, immune, or imaging features suggesting fungal infection.  

20. Obtain nucleic-acid testing for respiratory viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, only if new acute respiratory symptoms occur.  

21. Consider interferon-gamma release assay testing for latent TB when epidemiologic risk is present or if future immunosuppression is contemplated.  

22. Consider serum total IgE, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, and related testing if asthma, recurrent mucus impaction, central bronchiectasis, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis becomes a concern.  

23. Consider ANCA, urinalysis, creatinine, and other vasculitis-directed testing if eosinophilia is accompanied by asthma, sinus disease, neuropathy, renal findings, rash, or systemic features.  

24. Consider Strongyloides IgG and other parasite-directed testing before systemic corticosteroids if epidemiologic exposure or unexplained eosinophilia is present.  

25. Consider hematology reassessment for persistent marked eosinophilia, rising eosinophil counts, cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, or evidence of eosinophil-mediated organ injury.  

26. Schedule a short-interval repeat thin-section chest CT, potentially at approximately 3 months, to document resolution or persistence of the tree-in-bud abnormality after the presumed recent respiratory illness.  

27. Consider repeat chest CT at approximately 6–12 months instead of an earlier scan if the imaging appearance is judged low risk and there are no symptoms, microbiologic concerns, or concerning risk factors.  

28. Continue routine annual low-dose CT lung-cancer screening if he remains eligible under the relevant screening program criteria and if the acute imaging finding resolves or is stable.  

29. Use diagnostic chest CT rather than screening low-dose CT for follow-up if detailed airway assessment, evaluation for bronchiectasis, or assessment of interval progression is needed.  

30. Refer to pulmonology on a routine basis for assessment of new focal tree-in-bud nodularity in an older former smoker with mucus plugging and chronic eosinophilia.  

31. Escalate to expedited pulmonology review if follow-up imaging shows progression, a mass, lobar collapse, persistent focal obstruction, enlarging lymph nodes, or new respiratory symptoms.  

32. Consider infectious-disease referral if AFB cultures are positive, tuberculosis is suspected, recurrent unexplained tree-in-bud disease occurs, or unusual fungal/parasitic infection is identified.  

33. Consider speech-language pathology evaluation with bedside swallowing assessment if dysphagia, coughing during meals, recurrent lower-lobe infiltrates, or aspiration risk factors are identified.  

34. Obtain a modified barium swallow study or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing if aspiration is suspected after clinical screening.  

35. Consider bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures if sputum cannot be obtained and CT findings persist or progress.  

36. Consider bronchoscopy with airway inspection and possible endobronchial biopsy if a focal obstructing lesion, retained foreign body, abnormal airway narrowing, or malignancy is suspected.  

37. Consider CT-guided biopsy or surgical diagnostic evaluation only if a discrete suspicious nodule, mass, lymphadenopathy, or persistent lesion not explained by airway infection is subsequently identified.  

38. Do not initiate empiric antibacterial therapy solely for an incidental, asymptomatic tree-in-bud finding; reserve antibiotics for clinical bacterial infection or microbiologic evidence, with drug selection guided by likely pathogen and culture results.  

39. Avoid empiric systemic corticosteroids for the CT finding alone; consider corticosteroid therapy only if a defined eosinophilic, allergic, inflammatory, or vasculitic lung disorder is established and infection has been appropriately evaluated.  

40. Review current medications for agents that increase aspiration risk or suppress immunity, including sedatives, opioids, anticholinergics, proton-pump inhibitors, systemic steroids, biologics, and chemotherapy; adjust or deprescribe when clinically appropriate.  

41. Counsel on reporting new cough lasting more than several weeks, sputum, fever, dyspnea, hemoptysis, weight loss, night sweats, reduced exercise tolerance, choking with meals, or recurrent respiratory infections.  

42. Counsel on continued smoking abstinence, avoidance of vaping and inhaled irritants, diabetes control, oral/dental hygiene, and staying current with influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, and RSV vaccination as appropriate.  

43. If repeat CT demonstrates complete resolution, document the finding as likely transient infectious/inflammatory bronchiolitis and return to the planned lung-screening or clinically indicated surveillance schedule.  

44. If repeat CT is unchanged but the patient remains asymptomatic and cultures/testing are unrevealing, consider longer-interval imaging surveillance and pulmonary follow-up for possible indolent airway disease.  

45. If repeat CT shows increasing tree-in-bud burden, new bronchiectasis, cavitation, consolidation, lymphadenopathy, or a suspicious focal lesion, obtain sputum/BAL microbiology and expedite pulmonology evaluation.  

46. If he develops fever, hypoxemia, significant dyspnea, hemoptysis, confusion, or rapidly worsening respiratory symptoms, arrange urgent in-person assessment, chest imaging, and evaluation for acute infection, pulmonary embolism, or other serious cardiopulmonary disease.

1. Review the current CT images with thoracic radiology to confirm that the right-lower-lobe findings are true tree-in-bud centrilobular nodules rather than motion artifact, dependent atelectasis, or vascular structures.  

2. Compare the current CT directly with all available prior chest CTs, not only the study from 5 years earlier, to establish interval onset and any subtle pre-existing bronchiectasis or airway disease.  

3. Obtain a dedicated thin-section high-resolution CT chest, including inspiratory images and, if appropriate, expiratory images, to characterize small-airway disease, bronchiectasis, air trapping, mucus impaction, and distribution of nodularity.  

4. Schedule a short-interval repeat noncontrast chest CT in approximately 6–12 weeks to document resolution after the reported self-limited respiratory illness.  

5. Use a repeat chest CT interval of approximately 3 months rather than 6–12 weeks if radiology considers the pattern low risk and likely postinfectious.  

6. Obtain repeat CT sooner than planned if cough, sputum, dyspnea, fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or declining exercise tolerance develops.  

7. Resume annual low-dose CT lung-cancer screening only if the tree-in-bud abnormalities resolve or remain stable in a manner considered benign by radiology/pulmonology.  

8. Obtain a detailed respiratory history including chronic cough, sputum production, wheeze, recurrent “bronchitis,” exertional breathlessness, hemoptysis, prior pneumonia, tuberculosis exposure, and environmental mold/water exposure.  

9. Obtain a detailed aspiration-risk history, including dysphagia, choking with meals, coughing while eating, denture problems, prior stroke, neuromuscular disease, sedative use, and nocturnal regurgitation.  

10. Screen for gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, including heartburn, sour taste, nocturnal cough, hoarseness, and regurgitation, despite his denial of known reflux.  

11. Review medication history for drugs associated with aspiration risk or impaired airway clearance, including opioids, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, anticholinergics, and inhaled medications.  

12. Perform a focused pulmonary examination, including resting oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, lung auscultation, and assessment for signs of chronic lung disease.  

13. Obtain baseline spirometry with bronchodilator testing to assess for COPD, asthma, or obstructive small-airway disease in this former smoker.  

14. Obtain full pulmonary function testing with lung volumes and diffusing capacity if spirometry is abnormal, if CT suggests emphysema/air trapping, or if respiratory symptoms emerge.  

15. Obtain a complete blood count with differential to document the degree and trajectory of eosinophilia and assess for leukocytosis or anemia.  

16. Review prior absolute eosinophil counts, duration of eosinophilia, prior hematology evaluations, and any evidence of organ involvement from hypereosinophilic syndromes.  

17. Obtain serum total IgE as part of evaluation for allergic airway disease or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis if bronchiectasis, asthma symptoms, or mucus impaction are prominent.  

18. Obtain Aspergillus-specific IgE and IgG testing if imaging or clinical features raise concern for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis or chronic pulmonary aspergillus-related disease.  

19. Obtain serum Aspergillus galactomannan and/or fungal serologies only if there are compatible symptoms, progressive imaging abnormalities, immunosuppression, cavitation, or other concern for invasive or chronic fungal infection.  

20. Obtain three separate expectorated sputum specimens for acid-fast bacillus smear and mycobacterial culture if he can produce sputum, particularly to evaluate for nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease.  

21. Include nucleic-acid testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis on sputum if there are epidemiologic risks, systemic symptoms, upper-lobe disease, cavitation, or concern for communicable tuberculosis.  

22. Obtain routine sputum bacterial culture and Gram stain if productive cough recurs or if persistent mucus plugging is seen on follow-up imaging.  

23. Obtain fungal sputum culture if there is persistent or progressive tree-in-bud disease, bronchiectasis, substantial eosinophilia, or immunocompromising conditions.  

24. Consider induced sputum collection if sputum cultures are clinically indicated but he cannot spontaneously expectorate.  

25. Refer to pulmonology on a routine but timely basis for interpretation of persistent tree-in-bud nodularity, mucus plugging, possible bronchiectasis, and consideration of bronchoscopy.  

26. Refer to pulmonology more urgently if follow-up imaging shows progression, new cavitation, enlarging nodules, lobar collapse, significant bronchiectasis, or symptoms suggestive of active infection.  

27. Consider bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage if serial CT shows persistent/progressive abnormalities and noninvasive sputum studies are unavailable or nondiagnostic.  

28. Send bronchoalveolar lavage, if performed, for bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, cytology, cell differential including eosinophils, and tuberculosis testing when clinically indicated.  

29. Consider bronchoscopic airway inspection and removal of obstructing mucus if there is persistent focal mucus plugging, lobar/segmental atelectasis, or concern for an endobronchial lesion.  

30. Consider a modified barium swallow study or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing if aspiration symptoms, recurrent lower-lobe infiltrates, or persistent dependent tree-in-bud disease develops.  

31. Refer to speech-language pathology for swallowing assessment and aspiration-prevention strategies if dysphagia or aspiration is identified.  

32. Consider gastroenterology referral and/or reflux testing if recurrent aspiration-pattern imaging occurs despite absent classic reflux symptoms.  

33. Consider evaluation for immunodeficiency, including quantitative immunoglobulins, if there is a history of recurrent sinopulmonary infection, unexplained bronchiectasis, or persistent unusual respiratory pathogens.  

34. Consider hematology referral if eosinophilia is marked, rising, associated with pulmonary infiltrates, accompanied by systemic symptoms, or not previously adequately characterized.  

35. Consider parasitic evaluation guided by travel, exposure, dietary, and medication history if eosinophilia is substantial or pulmonary eosinophilic disease is suspected.  

36. Do not initiate empiric antibacterial therapy while asymptomatic unless there is clinical evidence of acute bacterial pneumonia, such as fever, purulent sputum, focal consolidation, leukocytosis, or physiologic instability.  

37. If acute community-acquired pneumonia develops, obtain chest radiography and/or CT as appropriate and treat with guideline-concordant antibiotics tailored to comorbidities, allergies, local resistance, and microbiologic results.  

38. Do not start empiric multidrug therapy for nontuberculous mycobacterial disease solely on the basis of one CT finding; require compatible clinical, radiographic, and microbiologic criteria before treatment consideration.  

39. If diagnostic criteria for clinically significant nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease are met, refer to pulmonology and/or infectious diseases for species-directed multidrug treatment planning and toxicity monitoring.  

40. Do not start systemic corticosteroids solely for tree-in-bud nodularity and eosinophilia unless a defined corticosteroid-responsive diagnosis, such as eosinophilic lung disease, asthma exacerbation, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, is established.  

41. Consider an inhaled bronchodilator trial if spirometry demonstrates obstruction or if wheeze, exertional dyspnea, or chronic bronchitic symptoms develop.  

42. Consider inhaled corticosteroid-containing therapy only if there is a separate indication such as asthma or frequent COPD exacerbations, balancing potential infection and pneumonia risks.  

43. Counsel regarding airway-clearance measures if mucus plugging or bronchiectasis persists, including hydration, regular physical activity, directed coughing/huff coughing, and possible use of an oscillatory positive-expiratory-pressure device.  

44. Consider respiratory therapy teaching for airway-clearance techniques if follow-up CT confirms bronchiectasis or recurrent mucus retention.  

45. Counsel to avoid smoking relapse, secondhand smoke, inhaled irritants, and aerosolized exposures that may worsen small-airway inflammation.

43. Counsel him to report promptly any cough lasting more than 2–3 weeks, sputum production, hemoptysis, dyspnea, wheezing, fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, or declining exercise tolerance.

39. Consider a trial of airway-clearance measures if mucus plugging persists, such as hydration, regular ambulation, huff coughing, oscillatory positive-expiratory-pressure device use, or respiratory-therapy instruction.

43. Reinforce smoking abstinence and avoidance of vaping, inhaled cannabis, and significant particulate or occupational airway irritants.  

44. Review and update influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, RSV, and Tdap vaccination status as appropriate for age, diabetes, and pulmonary risk.  

45. Schedule clinical follow-up after the short-interval CT, or sooner within 4–8 weeks if symptoms recur, to review imaging, sputum results if obtained, eosinophil trend, pulmonary function testing, and need for escalation.
